This is a digital copy of a book that was preserved for generations on library shelves before it was carefully scanned by Google as part of a project to make the world's books discoverable online.

It has survived long enough for the copyright to expire and the book to enter the public domain. A public domain book is one that was never subject to copyright or whose legal copyright term has expired. Whether a book is in the public domain may vary country to country. Public domain books are our gateways to the past, representing a wealth of history, culture and knowledge that's often difficult to discover.

Marks, notations and other <term>marginalia</term> <note>Handwritten notes or marks made in the margins of a book by previous readers or librarians.</note> present in the original volume will appear in this file—a reminder of this book's long journey from the publisher to a library and finally to you.

## Usage guidelines

Google is proud to partner with libraries to digitize public domain materials and make them widely accessible. Public domain books belong to the public and we are merely their custodians. Nevertheless, this work is expensive, so in order to keep providing this resource, we have taken steps to prevent abuse by commercial parties, including placing technical restrictions on automated querying.

We also ask that you:

+ *Make non-commercial use of the files* We designed Google Book Search for use by individuals, and we request that you use these files for personal, non-commercial purposes.

+ *Refrain from automated querying* Do not send automated queries of any sort to Google's system: If you are conducting research on machine translation, optical character recognition or other areas where access to a large amount of text is helpful, please contact us. We encourage the use of public domain materials for these purposes and may be able to help.

+ *Maintain attribution* The Google “watermark” you see on each file is essential for informing people about this project and helping them find additional materials through Google Book Search. Please do not remove it.

+ *Keep it legal* Whatever your use, remember that you are responsible for ensuring that what you are doing is legal. Do not assume that just because we believe a book is in the public domain for users in the United States, that the work is also in the public domain for users in other countries. Whether a book is still in copyright varies from country to country, and we can’t offer guidance on whether any specific use of any specific book is allowed. Please do not assume that a book’s appearance in Google Book Search means it can be used in any manner anywhere in the world. Copyright infringement liability can be quite severe.

## About Google Book Search

Google’s mission is to organize the world’s information and to make it universally accessible and useful. Google Book Search helps readers discover the world’s books while helping authors and publishers reach new audiences. You can search through the full text of this book on the web at <insert>http://books.google.com/</insert>

<meta>This page serves as the preface to the third volume of the Oxyrhynchus Papyri series, establishing the editorial timeline and acknowledging scholarly contributions.</meta>

# PREFACE

In accordance with the chronological arrangement adopted by us in the publication of the Oxyrhynchus Papyri <note>A massive collection of ancient manuscripts discovered in an Egyptian rubbish mound at the site of Oxyrhynchus.</note>, the present volume is devoted to second century texts, with the exception of the theological and some of the classical papyri. The selection of documents here published in full or described probably represents less than half the second century material discovered in 1897, but it is our intention in future volumes to deal with successive centuries up to the sixth, and then to return to the older papyri temporarily passed over. In the spring of this year excavations at Oxyrhynchus were resumed, and another large find of papyri was made, including a certain number of the late Ptolemaic period <note>The era of Greek rule in Egypt, roughly 305–30 BCE, ending with the death of Cleopatra VII.</note>. These, together with a selection of the more important literary texts from the new find, will be published in Part IV, which we hope to issue within a year.

In proportion to the space in the present volume occupied by the literary fragments our debt is the greater to Professor Blass <note>Friedrich Blass, a renowned German classical scholar and expert in Greek philology.</note>, to whom is due the identification of several of the classical pieces, and to a large extent their reconstruction, together with many suggestions in the commentary. Mr. J. G. Smyly has rendered us much assistance, especially in connexion with questions of ancient mathematics; the help which we have received on special points from other scholars is acknowledged in connexion with the individual papyri.

->BERNARD P. GRENFELL.<-
->ARTHUR S. HUNT.<-

**Oxford,**
*June, 1903.*

<summary>The editors outline their chronological plan for publishing the Oxyrhynchus collection, focusing here on 2nd-century documents while announcing new discoveries from the 1903 excavation season. They acknowledge the vital assistance of scholars like Professor Blass and J. G. Smyly in reconstructing and interpreting the fragments.</summary>

<keywords>Oxyrhynchus Papyri, Bernard P. Grenfell, Arthur S. Hunt, Friedrich Blass, J. G. Smyly, Ptolemaic period, papyrology, archaeological excavations, ancient mathematics</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the editorial introduction for the Oxyrhynchus collection, transitioning from the general description of the archaeological find to the specific typographic and editorial conventions used in this volume. It establishes the "scholarly shorthand" necessary for readers to understand how missing text and corrections are represented in the translated and transcribed documents that follow.</meta>

## NOTE ON THE METHOD OF PUBLICATION AND
## LIST OF ABBREVIATIONS

In the following pages, the same general method is followed as in preceding volumes. Of the new literary texts <note>Literary texts include works of poetry, philosophy, or drama, as opposed to "documentary" texts like receipts or letters.</note>, a few are printed in a dual form: a reconstruction in modern style is added to a literal transcript. In most other cases, as well as in the fragments of existing authors, the originals are reproduced except for the division of words, the addition of capital initials to proper names, the expansion of abbreviations, and the filling in—where possible—of <term>lacunae</term> <note>original: "lacunae"; refers to physical gaps or holes in the papyrus where text has been lost.</note>.

In document **413**, however, accents and punctuation have been introduced to make the text clearer. This system has also been adopted for the majority of the literary fragments in the "miscellaneous" section (IV). Additions or corrections made by the original scribe are shown in a small, thin font; those added later by a different person are shown in **thick, bold type**. Non-literary texts (such as business documents) are given in modern style only.

Abbreviations and symbols are "resolved" (written out in full), and these are all of the common variety. Additions and corrections are usually built directly into the text, with a record of them kept in the critical notes. In the few instances where it was necessary to show changes exactly as they appear on the original papyrus, a later hand is distinguished by **thick type**, just like in the literary texts. Mistakes in <term>orthography</term> <note>original: "orthography"; the conventional spelling system of a language.</note> and other errors are corrected in the notes whenever they might cause confusion. 

The <term>iota adscript</term> <note>A small Greek letter "i" (iota) written next to a long vowel.</note> is printed when it was actually written on the papyrus; otherwise, the <term>iota subscript</term> <note>A small "i" (iota) written underneath a vowel, common in modern Greek printing but often omitted in ancient handwriting.</note> is used. 

**Guide to Editorial Symbols:**
*   **Square brackets [ ]** indicate a <term>lacuna</term> (a hole or gap in the paper).
*   **Round brackets ( )** indicate the completion of an abbreviation or symbol.
*   **Angular brackets < >** indicate a word or letter the original scribe accidentally left out.
*   **Double square brackets [[ ]]** mean the letters inside were deleted or crossed out in the original.
*   **Braces { }** mean the letters inside were written by mistake and should be ignored.
*   **Dots inside brackets [...]** represent the approximate number of lost or deleted letters.
*   **Dots outside brackets . . .** indicate letters that are visible but too damaged to read.
*   **Letters with dots underneath them** (e.g., ẹ) are doubtful readings.

Heavy Arabic numerals refer to the specific <term>Oxyrhynchus papyri</term> <note>Thousands of ancient documents recovered from an ancient Egyptian rubbish heap at the city of Oxyrhynchus.</note> published in this volume and in Parts I–II; ordinary numerals refer to lines; small Roman numerals refer to columns.

## 401. ST. MATTHEW'S GOSPEL, I-II.

->7 x 9.5 *cm.*<-

THESE few verses from the end of the first and the beginning of the second chapter of the Gospel according to St. Matthew are contained on part of a leaf from a vellum book. Unless the text was in double columns, which would make the book a very unlikely shape, the leaves were unusually small in size; for though the columns are incomplete at both top and bottom only two or three lines are missing between the last line of the *verso* <note>The back side of a manuscript leaf.</note> and the first of the *recto* <note>The front side of a manuscript leaf.</note>. The handwriting, which is in well-formed slightly sloping <term>uncials</term> <note>A style of script written entirely in capital letters, common in Greek and Latin manuscripts from the 4th to 8th centuries.</note> of medium size, may be assigned to the fifth or sixth century. It is somewhat faded, and a second hand has here and there rewritten letters and lectional signs with a darker ink, besides correcting mistakes made by the original scribe, who was not very careful. To judge from this fragment, the text followed by the manuscript was a good one, having affinities with the <term>Codex Sinaiticus</term> <note>A famous 4th-century Greek manuscript of the Bible, one of the most important for establishing the original text.</note>. We give a <term>collation</term> <note>A line-by-line comparison of different manuscript versions to identify variations.</note> with the text of Westcott and Hort and with the <term>Received Text</term> <note>original: "Textus Receptus." The standard Greek text of the New Testament used by translators for centuries, including those of the King James Version.</note>.

->*Verso.*<-

[so that] it might be fulfilled which was spo[ken]

5. Above and below the superfluous "th" <note>original: "$\theta$"</note> are short horizontal strokes by the second hand.
6. "You shall bear" <note>original: "τεξετε"</note> is for "she shall bear" <note>original: "τεξεται"</note>; the final "e" has been partially rewritten by the later hand, but was also apparently the original reading.
7. "They shall call" <note>original: "καλεσουσι"</note>: "they shall call" <note>original: "καλέσουσιν"</note> in the Westcott and Hort edition, following most manuscripts.
10. "Having been raised" <note>original: "εγερθεις"</note>: so found in <term>Codex Sinaiticus</term>, <term>Codex Vaticanus</term>, <term>Codex Ephraemi Rescriptus</term>, and <term>Codex Dublinensis</term> <note>These are major 4th and 5th-century manuscripts denoted by the symbols ℵ, B, C, and Z respectively.</note>, as well as Westcott and Hort; "Having been awakened" <note>original: "διεγερθεις"</note> appears in other versions like the <term>Received Text</term>.
11. The spacing suits "But Joseph" <note>original: "δε] Ἰ[ω]σηφ"</note> better than "But the Joseph" <note>original: "δε ο] Ἰ[ω]σηφ"</note> found in the <term>Received Text</term>.
14-5. The remaining traces do not clearly decide between "son" <note>original: "υιον"</note> and "her firstborn son" <note>original: "τον υιον αυτης τον πρωτοτοκον"</note>, since with either reading the letters "au" <note>original: "αυ"</note> would appear in the same position in line 14, and there is not enough left of line 15 to show if the word was abbreviated.
15. Or perhaps "he called [the" <note>original: "εκαλεσε [το"</note>, which would suit the length of the line rather better.
22. The final "s" of "saying" <note>original: "λεγοντες"</note> seems to have been accidentally omitted by the original scribe.
23. The correction of "born" <note>original: "τεχθεις"</note> is by the second hand.

### 402. FIRST EPISTLE OF ST. JOHN, IV.

->8 x 5.2 *cm.*<-

A fragment of a leaf from a papyrus book, written in a clear <term>semi-uncial</term> <note>A script style that combines features of formal capital letters (uncials) and faster, cursive writing.</note> hand towards the end of the fourth or in the fifth century, and containing part of 1 John 4:11-17. The usual contractions found in biblical manuscripts <note>original: "MSS."</note> occur, such as <term>nomina sacra</term> <note>Abbreviated forms of sacred names like "God" or "Lord," usually marked with a horizontal line above.</note>, and a horizontal stroke at the end of lines is used apparently to indicate abbreviations. The text is curiously corrupt <note>In manuscript studies, "corrupt" means the text contains many errors or deviates significantly from the likely original.</note>, considering its early date, and bears evidence of extremely careless copying.

### 403. THEOLOGICAL FRAGMENTS

<columns>
...no one has ever [seen
God; if we love [one an-
<margin>5</margin> other, God [abides] in us [and
his love [is perfected]
. . . . . .

<column-break/>

[confesses that Jesu]s is the [So]n of [
God, God] abides [in] him and
<margin>5</margin> [God] is in [him] and we
[have known] and [believed]
the [love] which God <note>original: "χθς̅", likely a scribal error mixing "Christ" (χς) and "God" (θς)</note>
has in us. [God] is love, [and]
he who abides i]n love abides in
<margin>10</margin> God, [and] God [abides] in him.
[In this is per]f[ected...]
. . . . . .
</columns>

---

*Front side.* 1. *taprisen* <note>original: "ταπρισεν"</note> is a corruption of "loved" <note>original: "ηγαπησεν"</note>.
3-4. "No one has ever seen God" <note>original: "θεὸν οὐδεὶς πώποτε τεθέαται"</note> is the word order in the standard manuscripts, but the reconstruction at the end of line 2 is already long enough, and *tonein* <note>original: "τονειν"</note> is an easy scribal error for "the God" <note>original: "τὸν θν"</note> <note>An abbreviated form of the Greek word for God in the accusative case.</note>.
*Back side.* 4-5. Instead of "and he [remains] in God" <note>original: "καὶ αὐτὸς ἐν τῷ θεῷ"</note>, which is the reading of the manuscripts, the papyrus seems to have "and God is in him" <note>original: "καὶ ὁ θεὸς ἐν αὐτῷ ἐστιν"</note>, i.e., a repetition of the preceding words with the substitution of "is" <note>original: "ἐστιν"</note> for "abides" <note>original: "μένει"</note>. The "is" <note>original: "ις"</note> of "we" <note>original: "ημεις"</note> is written above the line, owing to a lack of space.
7. The scribe seems to have mixed up the <term>Nomina Sacra</term> <note>Traditional abbreviations for sacred names.</note> for "Christ" <note>original: "χς̅"</note> and "God" <note>original: "θς̅"</note>. "God" <note>original: "θεὸς"</note> is the reading of the manuscripts.
8. *ka* <note>original: "κα̅"</note> stands for "and" <note>original: "καί"</note>.
10. After "in him" <note>original: "ἐν αὐτῷ"</note>, <term>Codex Sinaiticus</term> and <term>Codex Vaticanus</term> <note>original: "ℵ and B"</note> have "abides" <note>original: "μένει"</note> which is omitted by <term>Codex Alexandrinus</term> <note>original: "A"</note>, while other manuscripts are divided. It is not certain that a letter is lost after "him" <note>original: "αυτω"</note>, but since "in" <note>original: "εν"</note> is required to fill the gap in line 11, and the horizontal stroke is used by this scribe merely as a sign of abbreviation (as seen in line 8), "abides" <note>original: "[μ]ε̅(νει)"</note> is more probable than just "in" <note>original: "ε̅"</note>.

## 408. APOCALYPSE OF BARUCH, XII-XIV.

->14 X 11 cm. PLATE I (front).<-

Of the numerous theological works of a visionary character composed shortly before or after the beginning of the Christian era, one of the most interesting is the *Apocalypse of Baruch*. Like many other ancient religious works not included in the standard Bible, it is preserved only in a translation from the Greek. To the recovery of a considerable fragment of the Greek original of the *Ascension of Isaiah* (P. Amh. I. 1), previously known in its entirety only from the ancient Ethiopian version, now succeeds a small fragment of the *Apocalypse of Baruch* in the language from which the existing Syriac translation is derived. However, whether the Greek text itself was originally translated from Hebrew is a matter of debate. Professor Charles, who has published the latest and most complete edition of that Apocalypse, is strongly in favor of a Hebrew original.

# THE OXYRHYNCHUS PAPYRI

But his reasons are not very convincing, and the present fragment illustrates the precarious character of arguments based on retranslations into a supposed original through a version which is itself not extant.

The papyrus is part of a leaf from a book, written in brown ink in a large slightly sloping <term>uncial</term> <note>A script consisting entirely of capital letters, common in Greek and Latin manuscripts from the 4th to 8th centuries.</note> hand of a moderately early Byzantine type, probably not later than the fifth century, and perhaps as early as the end of the fourth. The high point is frequently used, and there is a tendency to increase the size of the initial letters of lines. The text, so far as can be judged from the very imperfect condition of the lines preserved, is not very good; one certain error ("having witnessed" <note>original: μαρτυρήσαντες</note> for "having sinned" <note>original: ἁμαρτήσαντες</note> in line 28) of the first hand has been corrected by another person, and "midday heat" <note>original: μεσημβρία</note> is misspelled "midday heat" <note>original: μεσεμβρία</note> in line 4. The curious tendency to omit the definite article (cf. lines 16 and 24), which produces a certain harshness, is, however, not likely to be due to the scribe. But in spite of its smallness the fragment is of much interest as affording for the first time a direct opportunity of testing the fidelity of the Syriac translation. The impression created by a comparison of the two versions is that the Syriac translator was much less accurate than, for instance, the Ethiopic translator of the *Ascension of Isaiah*. In one passage (lines 6–8) he has expanded the three verbs of the Greek into six by adding a synonym in each case. In another he seems to have misapprehended the meaning of the Greek, and to have introduced an idea which is quite inappropriate to the context (cf. note on lines 25–7).

The references at the side of the text and the translation of the Syriac version are taken from the edition of Prof. Charles, whom we have to thank for several suggestions in the reconstruction of the fragment. The first ten lines of the *verso* <note>The "back" side of a leaf of papyrus or parchment.</note> are the conclusion of a prophecy of Baruch against Babylon (i.e. Rome). The *recto* <note>The "front" side of a leaf of papyrus or parchment.</note> is part of a prophecy against the Gentiles by ‘a voice from the height,’ and is a passage which has caused commentators much difficulty, but which the Greek helps to explain.

The Syriac here agrees verbally with the Greek, for the equivalent of "the continual" <note>original: τὸ διηνεκές</note> which is translated as an adjective by Prof. Charles <note>Professor R.H. Charles (1855–1931), a famous scholar of biblical apocrypha</note>, who supplies 'always' with the verb, is, as the Greek shows, to be constructed adverbially.

6-8. 'And do not thou expect to rejoice, nor condemn greatly.' The Syriac has 'Do not conclude or expect that thou wilt always be prosperous and rejoicing, and be not greatly uplifted and do not oppress' (the last verb emended by Prof. Charles to 'be not boastful'), thus duplicating all the three verbs of the Greek, but no doubt wrongly. "To condemn" <note>original: καταδικάζειν</note> is equally possible in lines 7-8.

8-10. 'For assuredly in its season the wrath will be awakened against thee which now is restrained by long-suffering as it were by a rein.' This agrees with the Syriac. Prof. Charles translates 'which now in long-suffering ...'; but the traces before "long-suffering" <note>original: μακροθυμίας</note> are incompatible with "in" <note>original: ἐν</note>, the second letter being either *s* or *e*.

10-16. 'And having said these things I fasted seven days. And it came to pass after this that I, Baruch, was standing upon Mount Zion, and lo! a voice came forth from the height and said to me "Stand upon thy feet, Baruch, and hear the word of the mighty God."' Here too the Syriac shows no variation. For the omission of the definite article before "mighty" <note>original: ἰσχυροῦ</note> compare line 24 "orders of the times" <note>original: καιρῶν τάξεις</note>.

18. [The word starting with] *stē*: the first letter may be *sigma* <note>original: σ</note>, and the second *nu* <note>original: ν</note> but not *tau* <note>original: τ</note>. The Syriac version of verses 10-11 has 'They were therefore chastened then that they might receive mercy. But now, ye peoples and nations, ye are debtors because all this time ye have trodden down the earth, and used the creation unrighteously.'

21-2. 'For ye were always being benefited but were always ungrateful.' The Syriac has 'For I have always benefited you and ye have always denied the beneficence,' which differs by the introduction of the first person, and the use of an active instead of a passive verb in the first half of the sentence. Prof. Charles notes that the order of the words in the Syriac is unusual, and a corruption may be suspected.

23-5. 'And I answered and said "Behold, thou hast shown me the methods of the times and that which will be."' The Syriac differs slightly by having a singular word for "orders" <note>original: τάξεις</note> and by inserting 'after these things' after 'will be.'

25-7. It is clear that the Greek and Syriac here diverged from each other. The Syriac has 'and thou hast said unto me that the retribution which was spoken of by thee will be of advantage to the nations.' As Prof. Charles acutely remarks, the idea of a remedial chastisement of the Gentiles seems out of place, and something is probably wrong with the Syriac text. The verb found in the Greek, "will be endured" <note>original: ὑπενεχθήσεται</note>, does not suggest anything like 'be of advantage to,' and taken in conjunction with "action" or "practice" <note>original: πρᾶξις</note> the meaning 'endured' is in every way more satisfactory. Of the two doubtful letters at the beginning of line 26 the second could be *pi* <note>original: π</note>, *ēta* <note>original: η</note>, or *iota* <note>original: ι</note>, but the first, if not *nu* <note>original: ν</note>, can only be *rho* <note>original: ρ</note>, and *rē* <note>original: ρη</note> or *ros* <note>original: ρ[ο]ς</note> is very intractable, while a compound of "to bear" <note>original: φέρω</note> is required. The phrase 'will be of advantage to,' to which Prof. Charles objected, may therefore be regarded as an error of the Syriac translator. In some other respects Prof. Charles seems to us to have slightly exaggerated the inconsistencies in chapters x-xiv; compare page 24 of his edition. "Orders of the times" <note>original: καιρῶν τάξεις</note> does not seem an impossible description of the prophecy in chapter xiii, and if 'the retribution spoken of by thee' is first mentioned by the cities, not by God, nevertheless it occurs in a speech put by the 'voice from the height' into the mouth of the 'prosperous cities,' of whom the abrupt mention (compare ibid. p. 22) is not so very surprising after a section devoted to Babylon and the 'land which is prospering.'

27-32. The Syriac has 'And now I know that those who have sinned are many and they have lived in prosperity and departed from the world, but that few nations will be left in those times to whom those words shall be said which thou didst say.' The Greek does not materially differ. In line 27 there is room for a word not expressed

## 404. SHEPHERD OF HERMAS.

->Fragment (c) 7.8 × 5.3 cm. PLATE IV (Fragment (c) *front*).<-

Three fragments of a leaf from a papyrus book, inscribed on both sides in a sloping uncial <note>a style of handwriting using large, rounded capital letters</note> hand of the late third or fourth century; the surface of the *back* <note>original: verso</note> is much damaged. No line is complete, and indeed very few complete words are preserved, so that all the greater credit is due to Mr. V. Bartlet for recognizing the scraps as belonging to the lost Greek ending of the *Shepherd of Hermas* (specifically the *Parables* <note>original: Similitudines</note> book 10, chapter 3, section 3 to chapter 4, section 3). They thus form a useful supplement to P. Amh. 190, Fr. (h) *back*, another papyrus fragment of the missing Greek portion of the same work, and demonstrate with equal clearness that Simonides’ <note>Konstantinos Simonides (1820–1890), a notorious manuscript forger who claimed to have found the original Greek of this text</note> version of the last leaf of the Athos codex <note>an ancient manuscript found at Mount Athos</note> was a forgery; compare the introduction to P. Amh. 190.

The text of the present papyrus seems to have differed in many points of detail from those which were the basis of the extant translations of the last chapters of the *Parables*, and only a few lines on the *front* <note>original: recto</note> can be restored with any approach to certainty, while the *back* is for the most part illegible. Fragments (a) and (b) all but join each other; but there seems to be a narrow gap <note>original: lacuna</note> between the bottom of Fragment (b) and the top of Fragment (c), causing the loss of a whole line on the *front*. In Fragment (c) the ends of lines 18–22 are preserved, and since these are by no means even, the number of letters lost at the ends of lines 11–17 may vary from 0 to 3. We have reconstructed lines 15–21 on the hypothesis that about 11 letters are lost at the beginnings. From the lines of breakage in Fragments (a) and (b) it is probable that the gaps at the end of lines 4–8 are of the same size as those in lines 11–17, and that the gaps at the beginning of lines 2–6 correspond to those at the beginnings of lines 15–22.

We are indebted to Mr. V. Bartlet for several suggestions in the reconstruction of the fragments.

**Vocabulary:** <term>Shepherd of Hermas</term> (an early Christian literary work from the 2nd century), <term>papyrus</term> (writing material made from reeds), <term>uncial</term> (capital letter script), <term>codex</term> (an early form of a book), <term>Parables</term> (a section of the Shepherd of Hermas), <term>V. Bartlet</term> (Vernon Bartlet, a church historian), <term>Simonides</term> (a famous 19th-century forger), <term>Athos codex</term> (a manuscript from a Greek monastery), <term>lacuna</term> (a missing or damaged section of text).

404. THEOLOGICAL FRAGMENTS

(2) *The Palatine Codex <note>original: Codex Palatinus; a 15th-century Latin manuscript of the Shepherd of Hermas</note>: ... and having all grace with the Lord. If therefore they find your house pure, they will remain with you; but if your house is in any way defiled <note>original: spurca</note>, they immediately withdraw from your house. For these virgins do not love defilement. And I said: Lord, I hope I will please them so [that] they may live in my house willingly and always. And just as this one, to whom you handed me over, complains nothing about me, so neither will those virgins complain anything about me. Then he said to that shepherd: I know this man keeps the commandments, and will settle these virgins in a clean dwelling. When he had said these things, he handed me over again to the same shepherd, and called those virgins and said to them ...*

(3) *The Ethiopic Version in Latin <note>original: Versio Aethiopica Latine; a Latin translation of the ancient Ethiopic version of the text</note>: ... and they have grace with the Lord. And as soon as they find your house pure, they will remain with you; but if it is slightly impure in some matter, they will immediately leave your house. For those virgins do not desire impurity at all. And I said to him: I trust, Lord, that I will please them so that they may live joyfully in my house always; just as he to whom you handed me over has nothing for which to rebuke me, so they will have nothing for which to rebuke me. And he said to the shepherd: I know the servant of the Lord wants life, and will keep these commandments, and will please the virgins in purity. And after he handed me over again, he called the virgins and said to them ...*

4. The word in this line ought to correspond to *scant* <note>original: pusillum; in Greek: ελαχιστον τι (elachiston ti)</note>, *stained* <note>original: inquinationis; in Greek: ρυπαρον (ryparon)</note>, or *happens/occurs* <note>original: acciderit; in Greek: γενηται (genētai) or συμβη (symbē)</note>, but the remnants of the letters are very difficult to interpret. Those of the third letter suit a "beta" (β) better than anything else, but unfortunately no other "beta" occurs elsewhere in this papyrus to compare. The fifth letter is very uncertain; "lambda" (λ) is possible, but not "nu" (ν). The last letter of the line is represented only by the bottom of a vertical stroke and may be an "iota" (ι). Neither "stained," "defiled" <note>original: μιαρον (miaron)</note>, "happens," nor "receiving" <note>original: λαμβανον (lambanon)</note> are acceptable readings here.

5. Possibly: "they will depart fro[m | you" <note>original: αποχωρησουσιν α[πο | σου (apochōrēsousin apo sou)</note>.

7-8. Perhaps: "at all they do not love [the] filthiness" <note>original: πανταπασιν ουκ αγαπωσιν τ[ην] ρυπαροτητα (pantapasin ouk agapōsin tēn ryparotēta)</note>, but the noun <note>term: substantive (the word functioning as a noun)</note> in line 8 no doubt corresponded to the adjective in line 4 which seems not to have been "stained" <note>original: ρυπαρος (ryparos)</note>.

11. Perhaps: "th]ese [to dwell] for [eternity" <note>original: ταυ]τας εις τ[ον αιωνα κατοικη]σαι (tautas eis ton aiōna katoikēsai)</note>.

15. "I know" <note>original: οιδα (oida)</note>: the letter "delta" (δ) has been corrected from an "iota" (ι) (?). The papyrus thus agrees with the Palatine Codex and Ethiopic version (*I know* <note>original: scio</note>) against the common Latin Bible version <note>original: Versio Vulgata</note> which reads "I see" <note>original: video</note>.

18. "In puri[ty" <note>original: εν καθαροτη[τι (en katharotēti)</note>: so the Ethiopic version reads *in purity* <note>original: in puritate</note>; the Latin versions have *in a clean dwelling* or *into a clean dwelling*.

22. The word or words lost at the beginning of this line have nothing corresponding to them in the other known versions of the text.

40-2. The corresponding passages of the versions (*Similitudes* 10. 4. 3) are as follows:— (1) *Common Version <note>original: Versio Vulgata</note>: he who therefore knows the calamity of such a man and does not rescue him, commits a great sin and becomes guilty of his blood. Easily therefore, etc.* (2) *Palatine Codex: [he who therefore knows] his distress and does not redeem him commits a great sin and becomes guilty of his blood.* (3) *Ethiopic Version in Latin: he who however knows the affliction of him who is in such a state and does not save him, commits a great sin and becomes his killer.* The papyrus differs from these considerably; not only is the plural "guilty ones" <note>original: ενοχοι (enochoi)</note> found in place of the singular *guilty* <note>original: reus</note>, but the remains of line 40 do not in the least support anything like *commits a great sin*. Apparently the papyrus omitted that phrase and in its stead had a participial phrase depending upon the preceding words which is not represented in the translations. The letter "gamma" (γ) of the word "they become" <note>original: γινονται (ginontai)</note> has been corrected, probably from a "beta" (β) or "delta" (δ).

<summary>This page provides a comparative analysis of Fragment 404, a papyrus of the "Shepherd of Hermas," using Latin and Ethiopic versions to reconstruct missing Greek text. The editor highlights where the papyrus agrees with or diverges from established manuscripts, particularly regarding the theme of purity and the moral guilt of failing to help those in distress.</summary>
<keywords>Shepherd of Hermas, Similitudes, papyrology, textual criticism, Codex Palatinus, Ethiopic Version, Greek paleography, moral purity, guilt of blood</keywords>

# THE OXYRHYNCHUS PAPYRI

### 405-406. THEOLOGICAL FRAGMENTS.

->PLATE I (**405** and **406** *reverse*).<-

We here group together fragments of two different theological works, which we have not been able to identify, both containing quotations from the New Testament.

**405** consists of seven fragments written in a small neat uncial hand <note>a style of writing using large, rounded capital letters</note>, which is not later than the first half of the third century, and might be as old as the latter part of the second. The ordinary contractions for God, Christ, and Jesus <note>original: θ̅σ̅, χ̅σ̅, ι̅η̅σ̅</note> occur; and it is clear that the use of these goes back far into the second century. Besides its early date (it is probably the oldest Christian fragment yet published), **405** is interesting on account of a quotation from St. Matthew iii. 16–7 describing the Baptism, which is indicated by wedge-shaped signs in the margin similar to those employed for filling up short lines, e. g. in Fragment (*a*) lines 9 and 13.

**406** is part of a leaf from a papyrus book and contains the quotation from Isaiah vi. 10 also found in Matthew xiii. 15 and Acts xxviii. 27. The citation appears here in its New Testament form, omitting the "their" after "ears" <note>original: αὐτῶν after ὠσίν</note> found in the Septuagint <note>the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible</note> version. The large and upright uncial hand is comparable with that of **25** and **224** and is probably to be assigned to the third century. Besides the ordinary contractions we have the abbreviation for "crucified" <note>original: ε̅σ̅τ̅ρ̅ν̅ο̅σ̅ for ἐσταυρωμένος</note> in line 21.

16–22. Because there are many differences in the versions of this passage (Matthew 3:16–17) and because the edges of the papyrus are uneven, as seen in Column 1, some of the reconstructed words are uncertain. Both the word **heavens** <note>original: ουρανοι</note> in line 14 and **of the heavens** <note>original: ουρανων</note> in line 18 might have been written in a shortened form. In line 15, if the word **spirit** <note>original: πνευμα</note> was written out in full, then the words **the** and **of the** <note>original: το and του</note> (which are missing from the famous manuscripts *Codex Sinaiticus* and *Codex Vaticanus*) might also have been left out of this papyrus. It is also quite certain that the word **and** <note>original: και</note>, which appears in some manuscripts before the word **coming** <note>original: ερχομενον</note>, was not in this papyrus. The suggested text for line 17 is a bit short; the only known variation that would be longer is the word **to/towards** <note>original: προς</note> instead of **upon** <note>original: επ'</note>, which is found in several other ancient handwritten copies. In line 19, there is definitely not enough space for the most common version of the text, **"This is my beloved Son"** <note>original: ουτος εστιν ο υιος μου ο αγαπητος</note>. Either this papyrus matched *Codex Bezae* in reading **"You are"** <note>original: συ ει</note> instead of **"This is,"** or else the phrase **"my son"** <note>original: ο υιος μου</note> was left out or moved to come after the word **"beloved"** <note>original: αγαπητος</note>.

> ‘O God Almighty, who madest heaven and earth and sea and all that is therein, help me, have mercy upon me, wash away my sins, save me in this world and in the world to come, through our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, through whom is the glory and the power for ever and ever. Amen.’

## II. NEW CLASSICAL FRAGMENTS

### 408. ODES OF PINDAR.

->Fragment (*a*) 13 x 15 *cm.* &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; PLATE II.<-

FOUR fragments of a lyric work in Pindaric dialect <note>the specific literary language used by the Greek poet Pindar</note> written in medium-sized uncials <note>a style of rounded capital letters used in ancient manuscripts</note>, with a few corrections and marginal notes in various hands. On the *back* <note>original: verso</note> are some money accounts in a second-century cursive script. The writing on the *front* <note>original: recto</note>, which bears much resemblance to that of the semi-capitalized legal contracts from Oxyrhynchus from the period of the Emperors Domitian and Trajan (e.g., **270**), belongs to the early part of the second century or even to the end of the first. Sub-divisions of the poem are indicated by paragraphi <note>lines placed in the margin to mark the end of a section</note>, while an elaborate coronis <note>a decorative symbol shaped like a bird or flourish</note> apparently marks the beginning of a new poem, as seen in the Bacchylides papyrus; the high stop <note>a punctuation mark placed at the top of the line</note> is employed, and occasional marks for breathing, accents, and indicators of vowel length or shortened words occur. Fragment (*b*) probably belongs to the second column of fragment (*a*), and since this arrangement accounts for forty-eight lines in this column, it is unlikely that more than two or three lines, if any, are lost between those two fragments. The position of fragments (*c*) and (*d*) is unclear.

<summary>This page concludes a late 3rd or 4th-century Christian prayer based on the Psalms and introduces a significant 1st or 2nd-century manuscript of Pindar's lyric odes.</summary>
<keywords>Christian prayer, Psalm 146, Psalm 51, Pindar, Greek lyrics, Oxyrhynchus Papyri, uncial script, ancient accounts, paleography</keywords>

<header>THE OXYRHYNCHUS PAPYRI</header>

The authorship of the piece is made certain, as was perceived by the scholar Blass, by the correspondence of the last line of fragment (*b*) **]of the dolphin beneath[** <note>original: ]υ δελφινος υπ[</note> with the beginning of Pindar, *Fragment* 235 (Christ edition), a quotation found in Plutarch’s *Table Talk* <note>original: Quaest. Symp. vii. 5. 2</note> (compare also *On the Cleverness of Animals* <note>original: De soll. anim. 36</note>) of a passage in which the poet compares himself to a dolphin:—**"Pindar says he was moved to song in imitation of a sea-dolphin: ‘whom the lovely melody of flutes moved in the open sea of the waveless deep.’"** <note>original: ὁ Πίνδαρός φησι κεκινῆσθαι πρὸς ᾠδὴν ἁλίου δελφῖνος ὑπόκρισιν τὸν μὲν ἀκύμονος πόντου ἐν πελάγει αὐλῶν ἐκίνησεν ἐρατὸν μέλος.</note> Another extant Pindaric fragment (200) occurs in lines 58-59; see the note for that specific location. Dismissing the first twenty-two lines, of which only the smallest fragments remain, we have in lines 23-42 most of the last **antistrophe** <term>the second section of a choral ode, answering the first</term> and in lines 43-54 part of the last **epode** <term>the third part of a choral ode, following the strophe and antistrophe</term> of one poem, and in lines 54-69 part of the first strophe of the next poem. The subject of the antistrophe, which has suffered much damage through the fading of the ink in the latter parts of several lines, is the vengeance taken by the hero Heracles upon King Laomedon <note>In mythology, Heracles saved Laomedon's daughter from a sea monster, but Laomedon refused the promised reward, leading Heracles to sack Troy.</note>. Although the general thread of the sentence structure in lines 23-35 has yet to be discovered, their restoration is by no means a hopeless task, for the traces of letters in the faded parts are generally sufficient to confirm the correct guesses when they are made. The second poem has in the margin at the beginning traces of what seems to have been its title, but these are too small to give a clue to the subject. The first strophe contains an interesting tribute by Pindar to one of his predecessors in the field of lyric poetry, which may be compared with the conclusion of the recently discovered *Persians* <note>original: Persae</note> by the poet Timotheus.

In this, as in the other new classical fragments, many of the restorations of missing text <note>original: lacunae</note> and suggestions in the commentary are provided by the scholar Blass.

33. The doubtful E after PAUS may be A.

36. **remember** <note>original: "μνάσθηθ'"</note> is for **remember** <note>original: "μνάσθητι"</note>, Apollo being addressed; compare line 35 **far-darting** <note>original: "ἑκάβολε," a traditional title for Apollo</note>. The subject of **settled** <note>original: "ἔσσατο"</note> is Heracles, who, according to Apollodorus (Book 2, Section 99), came to Paros when on his quest for Hippolyte's girdle, after which enterprise he went to Troy. **Cronian father** <note>original: "πατρὶ Κρονίῳ"</note> means Zeus; compare *Olympian Ode* 2. 13 **Son of Cronus** <note>original: "Κρόνιε παῖ"</note>.

55 sqq. '... song and harmony... were devised by one of the Locrians who dwell beside the white-crested hill of Zephyrium in furthest Ausonia <note>An ancient name for Italy</note>, a rich city; he dedicated... a single paean <note>A song of praise or triumph</note> meet for Apollo and... : I hearing his brief melody, plying an art of ceaseless words, am moved to song like a sea-dolphin...'

55. Perhaps **of the Ionians** <note>original: "Ιώνων"</note>, but **of the Iaonians** <note>original: "Ιαόνων"</note> would be the form expected. In the marginal adscript the doubtful *m* in the first line might be *d* or *l* preceded by another letter, and the doubtful *a* might be *o*, while a narrow letter such as *i* may have been lost between them. For **hymn** <note>original: "υ[μ]νος"</note> there is not space enough. Instead of **kh** in the third line **kai** is possible, and the last word may be **to Apollo** <note>original: "Απόλλ(ωνι)"</note>; compare line 64. Pindar wrote several **hymns** to Apollo; compare Pausanias (Book 10, page 858) **Pindar used to sit and sing whatever songs were for Apollo** <note>original: "καθέζεσθαί τε τὸν Πίνδαρον καὶ ᾄδειν ὁπόσα τῶν ᾀσμάτων ἐς 'Απόλλωνά ἐστιν"</note>.

58. The reference is to Xenocritus (or Xenocrates) who invented the Locrian mode <note>original: "Λοκριστί," a musical scale or style associated with the Locrian Greeks</note>; compare Westphal, *Metrik der Griechen*, I. page 286. For the restorations of this line and the next compare Pindar Fragment 200 quoted by the commentator on *Olympian Ode* 10. 17: **It might reasonably be called rugged, being hilly and by the sea; for he himself says: "and those who [dwell] by the white-crested hill of Zephyrium."** <note>original: "τραχεῖα δὲ εἰκότως λέγοιτο (Locri) λοφώδης οὖσα καὶ ἐπιθαλασσίδιος· αὐτὸς γάρ φησιν· οἵ τ' ἀργίλοφον πὰρ Ζεφυρίου κολώνων"</note>.

60. **AOUSUPE** is rather long for the gap, and possibly **hill [dwelling above]** <note>original: "ΚΟΛΩ[Ν(ΑΝΥΠΕ]Ρ"</note> should be read.

61. **ANTH . [** : above **A** is what may be a mark of quantity, probably short (˘). **E** can be read in place of **TH**.

62. For **vehicle** <note>original: "ὄχημα," often used metaphorically by Pindar for a "chariot of song"</note> compare Pindar Fragment 124 **the lovely vehicle of songs** <note>original: "ἐρατᾶν ὄχημ' ἀοιδᾶν"</note>.

63. For the form **paean** <note>original: "παυίο[να"</note> compare Bacchylides 15. 8.

67. For **I am stirred** <note>original: "ἐρεθίζ[ομαι"</note> compare Plutarch, *On the Cleverness of Animals* 36: **Pindar, likening himself to a dolphin, says he is stirred to the imitation of a (sea) dolphin, etc.** <note>original: "δελφῖνι Πίνδαρος ἀπεικάζων ἑαυτὸν ἐρεθίζεσθαί φησιν (ἁλίου) δελφῖνος ὑπόκρισιν κ.τ.λ."</note>. ### 409. Menander, The Flatterer.

->21.5 x 34.1 *centimeters.* PLATES II and III.<-

A notable increase has been effected during the last few years in the fragments of Menander, the discovery of the Geneva fragment of **The Farmer** <note>original: "Γεωργός"</note> being rapidly followed by that of the Oxyrhynchus fragment of **The Girl with Shorn Hair** <note>original: "Περικειρομένη"</note>. Another welcome addition is now made by the following considerable fragment of **The Flatterer** <note>original: "Κόλαξ"</note>, a comedy previously represented only by a few short quotations, and some mutilated lines in P. Petrie I. iv. 1 assigned with much probability to this play by Blass (*Hermes*, 33. p. 654, *Rhein. Museum*, 55. p. 102). The identification is established by the fortunate occurrence in the papyrus (lines 42-4) of

# THE OXYRHYNCHUS PAPYRI

three lines quoted from *The Flatterer* <note>original: "Κόλαξ"</note> by Stobaeus, *Anthology* <note>original: "Floril. 10. 21"</note> (Fragment 294 of the Menander fragments in Kock's *Fragments of Greek Comedy* <note>original: "Fragmenta Comicorum"</note>); while another line and a half formerly placed among the *uncertain plays* <note>original: "ἄδηλα δράματα"</note> (Kock, Fragment 731) occur in lines 49-50.
As is well known, this play was utilized by Terence in his *The Eunuch* <note>original: "Eunuchus"</note>, a fact which he himself states in the prologue (lines 30-2):

> *The Flatterer* is by Menander: in it there is a parasite, the Flatterer,
> and a boastful soldier. He does not deny that he
> transferred these characters into his own *Eunuch*,

<note>original Latin: "Colax Menandri est: in ea est parasitus Colax / et miles gloriosus. eos se non negat / personas transtulisse in Eunuchum suam"</note>

the "parasite" Gnatho representing Menander's Struthias <note>original: "Στρουθίας"</note>, and the "boastful soldier," who in *The Flatterer* <note>original: "Κόλαξ"</note> was called Bias <note>original: "Βίας"</note> (compare line 32), appearing as Thraso (compare Kock, Fragment 293, Plutarch, *Moralia* 57 *a*). But not much can be inferred from this concerning the plot of *The Flatterer*, since *The Eunuch* was the product of a *combination* <note>original: "contaminatio," a Roman playwright's practice of blending two Greek plays into one Latin play</note> of two Menandrian dramas, the second being *The Eunuch* <note>original: "Εὐνοῦχος"</note>; and where Terence was following the one and where the other cannot be accurately determined. Unfortunately on this point the present papyrus, notwithstanding its length, does not bring much enlightenment. Throughout the first column the beginnings of the lines are lost; and though different speakers are occasionally distinguished, and the sense of a line or two may here and there be caught, it is impossible either to follow the course of the dialogue or evolve a connected idea of the action. In lines 1-13 the speaker is possibly Struthias, the parasite, and a comparison with Terence, *The Eunuch* Act 2, Scene 2, would then suggest itself; but the resemblance, if indeed there can be said to be a resemblance, was not more than a general one. A closer parallel is obtainable between lines 11-3 and Terence, *The Eunuch* Act 3, Scene 4, a speech by Antipho. Lower down in the column other characters appear and the names Doris and Phidias (lines 18-9) are mentioned; perhaps therefore a change of scene occurred in the course of this column, and the transition may be marked by the space between lines 13 and 14. Column ii, which succeeds without a break, is in a more satisfactory condition. Probably a new scene opens at line 39, from which point as far as line 53 we have a dialogue between two persons who are walking in the street followed by a slave carrying wine-jars (line 47). One of them is infuriated by the sight of the parasite, Struthias, whom he declares (lines 45-53) he would like to unmask in the open market-place. Below line 53 is a <term>coronis</term> <note>a flourish-like symbol in papyri indicating the end of a section</note> and a short line; and then another dialogue succeeds in which the speakers are the familiar young man (A.) and his tutor (B.; compare line 55 **young master** <note>original: "τρόφιμε"</note>), the latter of whom makes a speech of some length upon the iniquities of the race of parasites (lines 55-63). It would at first sight be natural to suppose that a change of scene occurred at line 54, and that the short line is a stage direction. But what remains of line 54 does not seem to suit this view, while

<sig>C 2</sig>

on the other hand it can be easily connected with what follows; and, moreover, the speech of the tutor would succeed so appropriately upon the outburst in lines 45–53 as to give strong support to the hypothesis that the speakers in the upper half of this column are the same as in the lower. Line 54 must then be assumed to be defective. In the third column a different and apparently more dramatic scene opens, the transition to which is lost with the first few lines. This column is detached from the preceding two, but that it followed them immediately is rendered almost certain by the fact that this accords not only with the front of the sheet <note>original: *recto*</note>, where we have the correct amount of margin, but also with the back of the sheet <note>original: *verso*</note>, which has been used for an account. The break in the papyrus separates the figures of a column from the items to which they relate, and though the latter are too much defaced for the connection to be established with certainty, the coincidence of the lines with the figures and the width of the resulting column, which exactly corresponds with that following it, suffice to make this relation of the fragments extremely probable. There is then hardly room for doubt that this was the next scene of the play; but although twenty lines remain, of which not more than a few letters or syllables are missing, the situation is very obscure. There is apparently only one change of speaker (line 89); the soldier *Bias*, a pimp <note>original Latin: *leno*</note>, and a girl seem to be involved; but their relations are not made clear, and *The Eunuch* <note>original Latin title: *Eunuchus*</note> seems to provide no definite clue. The mention of soldiers <note>original Greek: *stratiōtai*</note> in line 82, with the passage in the next speech (lines 91–4) ‘If he perceives it he will come bringing sixty comrades, even as many as Odysseus took with him to Troy, with shouts and threats,’ may recall the scene (*The Eunuch*, Book IV, Scene 7) where Thraso with his comrades prepares to attack the house of Thais, a passage with which the scholar Blass also connects the Fayûm fragment referred to above; but it is difficult to work out the analogy.

The manuscript is written in rapidly formed medium-sized uncials <note>a style of Greek handwriting using large, rounded capital letters</note> which we should assign to about the middle of the second century. This date is also indicated by the two marginal notes, one of which is of some length, written by the original scribe in a smaller and more cursive hand, and also by the accounts already mentioned on the back of the sheet <note>original: *verso*</note>, which are not later than the first half of the third century, and may belong to the end of the second. Changes of speaker are marked by double dots and paragraph-marks <note>original: *paragraphi*, horizontal lines placed in the margin to indicate a new speaker</note> as in *The Girl with Shorn Hair* <note>original Greek: *Perikeiromenē*</note> fragment (211); stops <note>punctuation marks</note> are frequently added, the high point <note>a dot placed at the top of the line, similar to a period or semicolon</note> as a rule being used, though the middle point (so apparently at the ends of lines 6 and 35) and low point (line 44) also occur, and accents, breathings, etc., are found here and there: most or all of these reading aids <note>original: "lection signs"</note> are by the first hand. The text is but mediocre in quality, for in addition to minor errors half a line may be missing at line 54 (see above), and the blank space after line 13 is suspicious.

## 409. NEW CLASSICAL FRAGMENTS

28. **double-pay soldier**: the meaning of the word is explained in the marginal note; it is equivalent to the Latin *duplicarius* <note>original: "duplicarius" — a Roman soldier receiving double pay as a reward for service or rank.</note>.
31. The line probably ran *but now all these things are unfortunate, etc.*, as the scholar Blass suggests.

39-67. **A** (a young man). ‘What [evil]... has swooped down on us and whence is it? ... that he is a knave is evident.
**B** (tutor of **A**). How?
**A**. No honest man ever grew rich quickly. For while he is putting by and living thriftily, the man who lays a trap for his patient watchfulness gets everything.
**B**. How unjust it is what you say.
**A**. I swear by the sun that if the slave were not following me carrying the Thasian jars <note>original: "Θασίων" (Thasion) — large vessels of wine from the island of Thasos, known for its high quality and luxury status.</note> and there were no suspicion of my being drunk, I would at once pursue him in the market-place crying: “Fellow, last year you were poor and an outcast, but now you are rich. Say what trade you have been working at; answer me this, whence have you got all this? Won’t you be off ... somewhere else? Why do you teach men wrong? Why do you declare to us that there is profit in evil-doing?”
**B**. There is one character, my boy, only one which has brought utter ruin upon the world, and so I tell you. This alone it is that has ruined all the cities which you have seen laid waste, as I have now discovered. All the tyrants, all the great rulers, satraps, captains, founders, generals—I mean those who have come to complete ruin—this alone has been their destruction, namely the miserable parasites <term>parasite: in the context of Greek comedy, this is a social climber or "hanger-on" who trades flattery for free meals at a wealthy person's table.</term> who attend them.
**A**. That is a violent speech; but I am not sure what is the meaning of this.
**B**. Any one might be so mistaken as to suppose the man who was intriguing against him to be his friend.
**A**. But if the intriguer is powerless?
**B**. Every one has power to do evil.’

34. The supposed point after **IF** <note>original: "ΕΙ"</note> may be a vestige of another letter.
39. *What evil...* would be suitable, but it would then be quite impossible to get two more feet into the remaining space, which seems in any case almost too short for the requirements of the verse; but something may have dropped out.
42-4 = Stobaeus, *Anthology* 10. 21. <note>Stobaeus was a 5th-century compiler who preserved many fragments of lost Greek plays.</note> The word *no one* is also found in the Paris manuscript; *no one* according to Kock. *Himself* in line 43 is the reading in Stobaeus, but *the man himself* is a probable correction.
49-50 = Eustathius 1833. 58. <note>Eustathius was a 12th-century archbishop and scholar who quoted ancient texts.</note> The scholar Grotius’ emendation of *now* to *even now* is confirmed by the papyrus.
52. *From the [city]* is an obvious restoration, but it seems impossible to get so much into the gap; *market-place* is also too long.
54. For a discussion of this passage see the introduction.
58. The vestiges would suit **HOUSE**, and *he who is now at home* is a just possible reading.
62. **THEY HAVE DESTROYED** <note>original: "ΑΝΗΡΗΚΑΝ"</note> must be altered to *it has destroyed*; the mistake was a natural one, given the mention of *the parasites* in the next line.
63. To find a restoration of this passage which at once suits the sense and the papyrus is not easy. *Who are present* naturally suggests itself, but the letter after **O** is almost certainly **U**, not **I**, and before the ending **-ESIN** the traces would be consistent with the tip of a letter like **A, L** or **M** but hardly with **R**. On the other hand, *...eioin* seems a fatal obstacle to the alternative of making *wretched ones* refer to the *tyrants*, etc., and reading *whom... for themselves wretched ones.*
89. **starvelings**: ‘hungry ones’ or ‘scoundrels’ as in the poet Poseidippus, Fragment 26. 12: *calling them all cumin-splitters <note>a "cumin-splitter" was a slang term for a stingy person or a miser.</note> or starvelings.* For the phrase *having [life] in [their] hands* <note>original: "[βίον] ἔχον[τ]ες ἐν τ[αῖς] χερσίν"</note> compare the compound words for "living from hand to mouth" or "earning a meager living by manual labor."

105. The letter before **of the** <note>original: "των"</note> was the figure giving the number of the book.

106. **the circuit**: <note>original: "τὴν περίοδον"</note> i.e. the four great public games; <note>The "circuit" (Periodos) consisted of the Olympic, Pythian, Nemean, and Isthmian games. Winning all four was the highest honor for an ancient athlete.</note> compare, for example, Athenaeus x. 415 a: “he won the circuit ten times.”

### 410. RHETORICAL TREATISE.

->25.4 x 23.2 *cm.* PLATE IV (Cols. i–ii).<-

A treatise on Rhetoric in the Doric dialect <note>Doric was a regional dialect of ancient Greek, often associated with Sparta and the Pythagoreans; its use in a rhetorical manual is highly unusual as most were written in the Attic or Common Greek dialects.</note> is something of a surprise, but that such was the character of the work from which these fragments are derived admits of no doubt. The dialect, though occasionally corrupt, is the same as that found in the fragments of Archytas of Tarentum and other Pythagoreans, and in the anonymous *Ethical Discourses* <note>original: "Διαλέξεις 'Ηθικαί"</note>, the composition of which is attributed to the beginning of the fourth century B.C. (compare Mullach, *Fragments of Greek Philosophy* i. pp. 544 ff.; ii. pp. 9 ff.). To the same period and probably to the same school the present treatise is also to be assigned. The precepts inculcated by the writer are of a simple and practical character, and their principal object is the attainment of **magnificence** <note>original: "μεγαλοπρέπεια" — a stylistic quality of grandeur or dignity.</note>, which, as we also know from Quintilian (*Institutes of Oratory* iv. 61–3), was specially included among the **virtues of narration** <note>original: "narrandi virtutes"</note> (compare l. 15: **and in [the] narration**) by certain authorities. Poetical quotations are freely introduced, a circumstance which forms another connecting link with the *Discourses*; compare Mullach, *op. cit.* i. pp. 546, 548.

The greater part of four consecutive columns is preserved, the first of these being practically complete. They are written in a neat, rather small, round uncial hand which we should place in the latter half of the second century A.D., though the contents of the *verso* <note>The back side of the papyrus sheet.</note>, a series of epigrams (**464**) in a semi-uncial...

> 1-20. ‘... And others will esteem you; and also if in speaking at the commencement of the address of ingratiation <note>original: "ἔφοδος" (ephodos); the technical term for a subtle introductory speech used when the audience is hostile or indifferent.</note> one appears to use common phrases and not written ones, and speaks of nothing as a matter of certain knowledge, but of opinion and hearsay, whether from the jury or others. Such are the points in the exordium <note>An "exordium" is the beginning or introduction of a speech.</note> which are useful as giving an impression of fairness. In the narration of facts, the following directions serve to produce an appearance of a superior and high-minded character.’

## 411. LIFE OF ALCIBIADES.

->21.6 x 18 cm.<-

A leaf from a vellum codex <note>A "codex" is an early form of a book with pages, rather than a scroll</note> of a historical work, written in double columns in a calligraphic uncial hand <note>A formal style of uppercase Greek lettering</note> resembling that of the Codex Alexandrinus <note>A famous 5th-century manuscript of the Greek Bible</note>. The fragment was found with papyri of the later Byzantine period but is certainly not later than the sixth century, and more probably it is to be assigned to the fifth.

<meta>This page continues the scholarly introduction and transcription of Oxyrhynchus Papyrus 411, a biographical fragment concerning the Athenian general and politician Alcibiades, following the discussion of rhetorical fragments on the previous page.</meta>

<page-num>32</page-num>

# THE OXYRHYNCHUS PAPYRI

The leaf is a good deal worm-eaten, and the writing being on very thin vellum <term>vellum: a high-quality parchment made from animal skin</term> has a tendency to come through on to the other side. There are no lection-marks <note>marks used to guide the reader, such as accents or punctuation</note> of any kind, nor are initial letters of lines larger than the rest. The letter N at the end of a line is generally represented by a horizontal stroke.

The fragment, which despite its brevity covers the period from the mutilation of the Hermae <note>The "Hermae" were sacred statues in Athens that were vandalized in 415 BCE, sparking a political crisis</note> to Alcibiades' arrival at Sparta, clearly belongs to a life of Alcibiades rather than to a general history. This fact, coupled with the use of such a phrase as "to dance out the mysteries" <note>original: ἐξορχήσασθαι τὰ μυστήρια (exorchēsasthai ta mystēria); this refers to the illegal parodying of the sacred Eleusinian Mysteries</note>, which is found in Lucian, Achilles Tatius, and other late writers, indicates that the work in question was a composition of the Roman period. Thucydides is the principal authority, several phrases from him being incorporated; but that he was not the exclusive source is shown by the mention of Poulytion <note>original: Πουλυτίων</note>, whose name is recorded by Andocides (*On the Mysteries*, p. 7, Reiske) and Plutarch (*Life of Alcibiades* 19, 22), but not by Thucydides; compare line 57, where the papyrus comes into conflict with Thucydides. There is no reason to think that the writer borrowed from the much more detailed narrative of Plutarch, whom it is as likely as not that he preceded.

So brief an account of well-known events could hardly be expected to contain new historical information, but the papyrus is interesting as a specimen of one of Plutarch's rivals in the sphere of biography who must have enjoyed considerable vogue for a time. There are a few errors on the part of the copyist, but the style of the fragment is fairly good. The sympathies of the writer were obviously on the side of Alcibiades.

**9–12.** Compare the digression of **Thucydides** upon the **Pisistratidae** <note>The family of tyrants who ruled Athens in the 6th century BC; Thucydides uses their story to explain the Athenian public's paranoia regarding Alcibiades.</note> at this point (Book vi. 54–9).
With large rewards for information <note>original: μηνυτροις μεγαλοις (mēnytrois megalois)</note>: compare Thucydides vi. 27. 2.
**16.** Suspicions <note>original: υποψιαι(ς) (hypopsiais)</note>: the singular "suspicion" is less likely, both on account of the gap between vowels and because the silent "i" (iota adscript) is elsewhere omitted in this manuscript, as was common during this period.
**23.** Concerning the statues of **Hermes**, nothing <note>original: περι των μεν Ερμων ουδεν (peri tōn men Hermōn ouden)</note>: compare Thucydides vi. 28. 1.
**25–7.** See the introduction.
**34.** To hold back <note>original: κατασχειν (kataschein)</note>: compare Thucydides vi. 29. 3, "to hold back the departure."
**40–43.** Compare Thucydides vi. 29. 3 and 61. 5: "wishing not least for the **Mantineans** and **Argives** <note>Allies of Athens whose loyalty was tied specifically to Alcibiades.</note> to stay, thinking that through him they were persuaded to join the campaign," and **Plutarch**, *Life of Alcibiades* 19. The doubtful "i" in line 42 could be a "k."
**48.** The word "not" <note>original: ουκ (ouk)</note> is a little short for the gap in the papyrus, in which there is room for one or two more letters.
**57.** Almost all [cities] <note>original: σχεδον πασας (schedon pasas)</note>: this statement is in flagrant contradiction with the facts recorded by **Thucydides**, vi. 50–2, from which it appears that the **Athenians** met with little support. Compare **Plutarch**, *Life of Alcibiades* 20: "having sailed to **Sicily** he won over **Catana**, but did nothing else before being summoned back, etc." <note>original: πλεύσας εἰς Σικελίαν προσηγάγετο Κατάνην ἄλλο δὲ οὐδὲν ἔπραξε μετά-πεμπτος κ.τ.λ.</note>
**61.** Above this line are some traces of ink, perhaps the number of the page.
**62–63.** Compare Thucydides vi. 53. 1.
**74.** The remains of the letters do not suit the phrase "and others" <note>original: [αλλ]ους [τε]</note>. Possibly "also others" <note>original: [και] αλλ[ους]</note>, though this too is not satisfactory.
**80.** Was accustomed <note>original: ειωθε(ι) (eiōthei)</note>: the correction seems necessary, for the perfect tense used as a present could not be true of the period at which this work was composed. The fact that the **Salaminia** <note>The Athenian state trireme used for official missions.</note> required an explanation is an indication of the late date of the text. The division of the word for "property" <note>original: ουσια (ousia)</note> is noticeable, for the manuscript elsewhere follows the ordinary rules concerning the division of words.
**95.** Of the **Thurians** <note>original: Θουριων (Thouriōn)</note>: compare Thucydides vi. 61. 6.
**96.** Having escaped to the **Peloponnese** <note>original: αποδρας εις Πελοποννησον</note>: compare Plutarch, *Life of Alcibiades* 23.
**101.** Later <note>original: υστερον (hysteron)</note>: compare Thucydides vi. 88. 9: "**Alcibiades** . . . having crossed then immediately on a merchant vessel from **Thuria** to **Kyllene** in **Elis** first, then later to **Lacedaemon**." <note>original: Ἀλκιβιάδης . . . περαιωθεὶς τότ' εὐθὺς ἐπὶ πλοίου φορτηγικοῦ ἐκ τῆς Θουρίας ἐς Κυλλήνην τῆς Ἠλείας πρῶτον, ἔπειτα ὕστερον ἐς τὴν Λακεδαίμονα.</note> There is some corruption in lines 101–2, for "the evils" <note>original: των κακων</note> has no verb to govern it. Unless we assume some words are missing, the simplest alteration is to read "concerning" <note>original: υπερ (hyper)</note> for "later."
**105–107.** Compare Thucydides vi. 89. 2 (speech of **Alcibiades**): "and while I continued to be zealous, you, in making peace with the **Athenians**, gave power to my enemies through them, and cast dishonor upon me." <note>original: καὶ διατελοῦντός μου προθύμου ὑμεῖς πρὸς Ἀθηναίους καταλλασσόμενοι τοῖς μὲν ἐμοῖς ἐχθροῖς δύναμιν δι' ἐκείνων πράξαντες, ἐμοὶ δὲ ἀτιμίαν περιέθετε.</note> Thucydides does not mention **Nicias** by name in this passage; for the circumstances see Plutarch, *Life of Alcibiades* 14.
**107–120.** Compare Plutarch, *Life of Alcibiades* 23: "one thing he immediately accomplished was to rouse and provoke those who were hesitating and delaying to help the **Syracusans**, to send **Gylippus** <note>The Spartan general who would eventually turn the tide of the war in Sicily.</note> . . . secondly, to stir up the war from there against the **Athenians**, and thirdly and most importantly, to fortify **Decelea**," <note>original: ἐν μὲν εὐθὺς ἐξειργάσατο μέλλοντας καὶ ἀναβαλλομένους βοηθεῖν Συρακουσίοις ἐγείρας καὶ παροξύνας πέμψαι Γύλιππον . . . , ἕτερον δὲ κινεῖν τὸν αὐτόθεν πόλεμον ἐπὶ τοὺς Ἀθηναίους, τὸ δὲ τρίτον καὶ μέγιστον ἐπιτειχίσαι Δεκέλειαν</note> the source of both passages being of course Thucydides vi. 89–92.

### 412. JULIUS AFRICANUS, <term>The Girdles</term> <note>original: Κεστοί (Kestoi)</note>.

->26.5 x 22.3 cm. PLATE V.<-

Two columns containing the conclusion of Book 18 of *The Girdles* <note>The title *Kestoi* refers to the "embroidered girdle of Aphrodite," signifying a collection of varied and decorative knowledge.</note> of Julius Africanus, as is expressly stated in the title preserved at the end. This title clears up at once two moot points concerning *The Girdles*. Joseph Scaliger (*Observations on the Chronicle of Eusebius* <note>original: Animadv. in Chron. Eusebii</note>), in spite of the unanimous testimony of antiquity, distinguished between Sextus Africanus—the author of *The Girdles*—and Julius Africanus—the Christian chronographer and friend of Origen. This view has found little favor with subsequent critics and is contested at length by H. Gelzer in his recent book on Africanus. Its lack of basis is finally proved by this papyrus, whose testimony must carry the utmost weight in view of the fact that it is separated by little more than a generation at most from the "flourishing period" <note>original: floruit</note> of the author. The chronological work of Africanus was brought down to the year 221, and *The Girdles* are supposed to have been composed subsequently; while this manuscript is earlier than the year 275–6, since on the back <note>original: verso</note> is a document dated in the reign of the Emperor Tacitus. Secondly, a doubt has existed as to the number of the books of *The Girdles*, which is given by Photius (*Library* <note>original: Bibl.</note> 34) as fourteen, and Suidas (under the entry "Africanus" <note>original: s.v. 'Αφρικ.</note>) as twenty-four; Syncellus, who speaks of the work as *consisting of nine books* <note>original: ἐννεάβιβλος (enneabiblos)</note> (p. 359 *b*), no doubt only knew it in an incomplete copy. The similarity of the figures fourteen and twenty-four naturally suggested that the difference was due to a clerical error, but there was no reason to prefer one to the other. We now know that there was an 18th book, and may accordingly accept the higher figure.

*The Girdles* are described by Suidas as "as it were matters of natural science, containing healings and other effects produced by words and incantations and certain written characters" <note>original: οἱονεὶ φυσικά, ἔχοντα ἐκ λόγων τε καὶ ἐπαοιδῶν καὶ γραπτῶν τινων χαρακτήρων ἰάσεις τε καὶ ἀλλοίων ἐνεργειῶν</note>. A number of excerpts have survived dealing with military matters, the care of animals, and agriculture (*Ancient Mathematicians* <note>original: Math. Vet.</note>, ed. Thievenot, pp. 275 sqq.), and on the latter subject large extracts are embodied in the *Geoponica* <note>A 10th-century collection of agricultural lore.</note>. The present fragment exhibits another side of this multifarious composition, being concerned with a question of literary criticism. The author produces twenty-seven lines, mainly consisting of a magical incantation, which were to be inserted in the passage in Book 11 of the *Odyssey* where Odysseus calls up the ghosts. For these new lines definite authority is cited, references being given to manuscripts in Palestine, Caria, and Rome; and a doubt is expressed as to whether this ‘precious product’ was cut out by the poet himself or by the family of the tyrant Pisistratus <note>The Pisistratidae, who were often credited with or blamed for the standard arrangement of the Homeric epics.</note>! We do not suppose that Homeric scholars will be inclined to accept either of those alternatives. They will

...perhaps be more likely to include this passage in the list of things which <note>original: "ὁ ἀνὴρ οὗτος ἐν τοῖς Κεστοῖς αὐτοῦ τερατολογεῖ καὶ διέξεισι"</note> "this man in his *Girdles* relates and details as marvels" (Psellus, *in the Ancient Mathematicians* <note>original: "ap. Math. Vet."</note> p. xvi). Nevertheless it affords a valuable insight into the writer’s methods and standards of criticism; and though we may not admire his judgement, there is no ground for suspecting his facts. Of especial interest is the statement (lines 65–8) that he had arranged a library in the Pantheon at Rome ‘for the Emperor.’ According to Syncellus (*in the place cited* <note>original: "loc. cit."</note>) the *Girdles* <note>original: Κεστοί</note> were dedicated to Severus Alexander, from which Gelzer has inferred that Africanus was on a footing of friendship with the imperial house, a conclusion to which the new autobiographical detail of the papyrus gives strong support.

The manuscript is written in well-formed round uncials <note>A script using large, rounded capital letters, common in Greek and Latin manuscripts of this period.</note> of medium size, and being dated within such narrow limits, its paleographical evidence is of much value. To suppose an interval of ten years between the writing of the literary text on the *recto* <note>The front or "right" side of the papyrus sheet, where the fibers usually run horizontally.</note> and the cursive document on the *verso* <note>The back side of the papyrus.</note> would be a very moderate estimate. The date of the former therefore is fixed with certainty in the period between the years 225 and 265 A.D. But notwithstanding its proximity in time to the author the text is far from being a good one; several lines of the incantation especially are clearly corrupt, and one of them is incomplete. In these circumstances little weight can be attached to the variants from the ordinary text in the quotations from Homer. The two columns are numbered at the top respectively 35 and 36; thirty-four columns had therefore preceded, and if, as is most probable, these all formed part of the same book, its total length would be about 1530 lines.
