6. <note>original: "νεοπενθε αυτον" (neopenthe auton)</note> **newly mourning him**: the manuscripts read <note>original: "νεοπενθέα θυμόν" (neopenthea thymon)</note> **newly mourning spirit**. The word "him" is unintelligible in this context.
7. <note>original: "χ]αλκηρεσσιν" (chalkeressin)</note> **with bronze weapons**: the doubled "ss" is also found in other fragments; read as <note>original: "χ]αλκήρεσιν"</note> **with bronze weapons**.
9. <note>original: "παρα" (para)</note> **beside**: so in one manuscript; <note>original: "περί" (peri)</note> **around** in other manuscripts and the Ludwich edition.
11-13 = *Odyssey* book 11, lines 48-50.
11. <note>original: "[αυταρ] εγω" (autar ego)</note> **[but] I**: the same reading was entered by a second hand in the margin of another manuscript; <note>original: "αὐτὸς δέ" (autos de)</note> **but he himself** in other manuscripts and Ludwich.
13. <note>original: "και αμειβομενος επος ηυδων" (kai ameibomenos epos audon)</note> **and in answer I spoke these words**: the standard manuscripts read <note>original: "πρὶν Τειρεσίαο πυθέσθαι" (prin Teiresiao puthesthai)</note> **before inquiring of Tiresias**. The variation in this papyrus provides a standard introductory formula for what follows.
14. Neither here nor in line 21 was anything written before the word <note>original: "δει" (dei)</note> **it is necessary**, which in both cases is preceded by a short blank space.
15-17 = *Iliad* book 3, lines 278-80, with the word "and" replaced by another Greek particle in line 15, and a phrase meaning **"you shall fulfill"** etc. replacing **"keep your oaths faithful."**
16. <note>original: "τ[ι]νυσθον" (tinysthon)</note> **you two who punish**: this (as edited by Ludwich) or a similar spelling is the reading of most manuscripts; a different spelling of "punish" does not seem to be found elsewhere.
19. Compare *Iliad* book 6, line 467: **"the child against the breast of the well-girdled nurse."**
22-36. For this incantation, compare the magical papyri (for example, the collections of Wessely and Kenyon). However, the similarity is only general, involving the identity of a few names, such as **Anubis** <note>The jackal-headed Egyptian god of the dead</note> and **Ththa** <note>Likely a variant of Thoth, the Egyptian god of wisdom</note>. The word **Ablanathaw** in line 28 is a variant of **Ablanathanalba** <note>A common magical palindrome used in ancient spells, often translated from Hebrew as "Thou art our father"</note>, which is common in magical texts. The word <note>original: "εισι" (eisi)</note> in line 29 is a mistake for <note>original: "επι" (epi)</note> **upon**. In line 31, **"father of the bears"** can be read.
39 = *Iliad* book 11, line 741, with **"he knows"** for **"he knew."**
43 = *Odyssey* book 11, line 51.

44-68. '... and so on. Whether then the superfluous part of the incantation stood thus and the poet himself passed over it on account of the dignity of his work, or whether the **Pisistratidae** <note>The family of the Athenian tyrant Peisistratus, who were said to have commissioned the first "official" written edition of Homer's poems in the 6th century BCE</note>, when they combined the various poems, cut out these verses judging them to be alien to the march of the poem, I should much like to know. I have myself set them down here as being a most valuable product of the epic art (?); and you will find the whole work preserved in the archives of your (?) old home, the colony of **Aelia Capitolina** <note>The Roman name for Jerusalem after its destruction and rebuilding by Emperor Hadrian</note> in Palestine, at Nysa in Caria, and as far as the thirteenth verse at Rome, near the baths of Alexander, in the beautiful library at the **Pantheon** <note>The famous temple in Rome; Africanus claims to have designed a library within its complex for the Emperor</note> which I myself designed for the **Emperor** <note>original: "Σεβαστω" (Sebasto) — the Greek title for the Roman Emperor, likely Severus Alexander</note>.'

44-46. This passage can be understood as it stands by treating the phrase <note>original: "εχον ... το περιεργον" (echon... to periergon)</note> **"the extraordinary part... having"** as an absolute construction, but the word order is awkward, and the phrase **"the other things"** should not mean the same as **"the extraordinary part."** A simpler meaning is found if **"the other things"** is omitted; the words may have been accidentally repeated from line 49.
53-54. We take the word <note>original: "εγνων" (egnon)</note> **"I knew"** as equivalent to **"I would have known,"** and suppose a connecting word is missing after <note>original: "ατε" (ate)</note> **"since."** Perhaps a mark in the margin opposite this line indicates an omission in the original text.
55. The word <note>original: "επεικ[η]ς" (epeikes)</note> **"suitable"**, if correct, refers to **"art"** or **"poetry."** The scholar Blass suggests the word <note>original: "επιεικώς" (epieikos)</note> **"reasonably,"** but there is not enough room in the gap for the required letters.
56. This is another difficult passage. The letter in the damaged word must be an 'e' or an 'o', and there is only room for one narrow letter. Therefore, the phrase **"and [mine]"** <note>original: "την τ ε[μ]ην" (ten t' emen)</note> is not suitable. Blass suggests **"and [yours]"** <note>original: "την τε [σ]ην" (ten te sen)</note>, assuming the person being addressed (who **"will find"** the work in line 58) is a Jew to whom this work, the *Kestoi*, was dedicated. This fits the phrase **"of your ancient native country"**; though the idea that the author has to tell someone where to find the person's own work is not quite satisfactory. To understand **"ancient native country"** as Africanus’s own home is difficult, unless it means 'the country in which I used to live.'

### 413. FARCE AND MIME.

->22.9 X 42.3 cm.<-

Both sides of this remarkable papyrus are occupied with literary compositions of an unusual type. On the **recto** <note>the front side of the papyrus, where the fibers run horizontally</note> are three columns, of which the two latter are almost complete, of a low comedy or farce, written in a good-sized **semi-uncial** <note>a clear, rounded script often used for literary texts</note> hand, the **dramatis personae** <note>the list of characters in the play</note> being carefully distinguished and stage directions added. Adhering to the right of the third column about halfway down is an uninscribed fragment of some size, showing that the work did not extend beyond half a column more at most. 

On the **verso** <note>the back side of the papyrus, where the fibers run vertically</note> are, firstly, two columns in a much smaller and more **cursive** <note>flowing, "joined-up" handwriting</note> hand, preceded by a few letters of a third upon the projecting fragment already referred to, from what may best be described as a **mime** <note>a popular, often improvised dramatic performance, usually featuring everyday characters</note>, which is mainly, at the least, a monologue. The second of the two complete columns is shorter than the other, and there are some 6 centimeters of blank space below it. 

Secondly, adjoining this to the right is another column of dialogue in the style of the **recto**, and with the same characters, written in a somewhat larger and more careful hand, but evidently by the same person who was responsible for the foregoing mime. This column was intended to supersede the latter portion of the first column of the **recto**; see the note on lines 30-36. To assign both sides of the papyrus to one scribe is out of the question, but we are not inclined to think that the two documents were separated by a considerable interval of time. The hand of the **recto** we attribute with little hesitation to the **Antonine period** <note>the era of the Roman Empire from 138 to 192 AD</note>; that of the **verso** no doubt falls within the second century.

As we have already seen, the manuscript apparently was not continued more than a few lines beyond the third column of the **recto**, if it did not actually end at that point. This fact is quite in accordance with the internal evidence, for the...

The impression given by the lower part of this column is that it is the <term>exodium<note>original: "exodium" — a comic after-piece or conclusion to a theatrical performance</note></term> or conclusion of the whole piece. Metrical passages are introduced, a system of <term>Sotadean verses<note>a rhythmic meter used in ancient Greek poetry, often associated with satirical, coarse, or ribald themes</note></term> in lines 88-91 being followed after a short interval by a series of <term>trochaic tetrameters<note>a fast-paced poetic meter often used in ancient drama for lively dialogue or intense action</note></term> (lines 96-106); and there was an accompaniment of music and dancing (see lines 88-89, 92-93). The close of the play is also probably indicated by the word <note>original: "καταστολή" (katastolē)</note> **conclusion** or **denouement** in line 95, which heads the concluding section. The scene is the coast of a barbarian country bordering upon the Indian ocean (see lines 88-91), and the subject is the adventures in those remote regions of a party of Greeks, chief among whom is Charition, the heroine of the drama. Such themes are familiar from the pages of the early Greek romances, and the plot of this piece seems to have run on lines very similar to theirs. Charition had not improbably been carried off in the usual way by pirates, and had so come into the hands of the barbarians, whose Greek-speaking king (see lines 88 and following) is one of the characters of the play. She had apparently taken up her abode in a temple (see lines 215, 225); and the present fragment describes her rescue by her brother and others who had arrived by sea, and who succeed in effecting their escape after making their captors drunk. Professor Crusius, to whom we are much indebted in the reconstruction and interpretation of this papyrus, acutely suggests that the position in which Charition found herself placed may have been similar to that of the heroine in the romance of Xenophon of Ephesus, Antheia, who in order to repel the advances of the Indian prince Psammis represented herself as dedicated to the goddess Isis (see line 88 <note>original: "θεὰ Σελήνη" (thea Selēnē)</note> **Goddess Moon**, and line 106 <note>original: "τὴν σὴν πρόσπολον" (tēn sēn prospolon)</note> **your handmaid**), and lived for some time in that capacity under Psammis’ protection (*Ephesian Tale* iii. 11). 

A large number of characters are introduced. Besides Charition, whom the stage directions call **A**, her brother (**Γ**, see lines 97-99), and the barbarian king, called **king**, we have the buffoon (**B**) who largely supplies the comic element. This, as might be expected, is often of a coarse kind. **B** is of the Greek party and does not understand the barbarian language (see lines 58, 66); but some non-Greek words are assigned to him in lines 75 and 79-80. Another well-identified character is **Δ**, the captain of the ship (line 101). The personality of others is less easy to ascertain. In the fourth column of the <term>verso<note>original: "verso" — the back side of the papyrus sheet</note></term>, **ς**, who goes to fetch the ship, seems to belong to the brother’s party, and is consequently to be distinguished from the speaker in lines 70-71 and 74, who uses only the barbarian language, but is designated by a symbol which might otherwise be supposed to represent **ς**. It is, however, formed quite differently from the **ς** on the back, and is more like the sign for 200. **Z**, who figures only in lines 31 and 71-73, is another barbarian. There remains **κοι( )**, whose remarks are also with one exception (line 104) in the barbarian tongue. We are indebted to Professor G. Wissowa for the suggestion that the abbreviation is to be expanded to <note>original: "κοι(νῇ)" (koinē)</note> **altogether** or **in unison**, referring either to...

the body of the barbarians or of the Greeks as the case may be. This hypothesis satisfies all the conditions, and accounts for the appearance of <note>original: "κοι( )" — likely an abbreviation for "koinē," meaning "in common" or "together"</note> **together** in line 104, which would on any other view be a difficulty. In lines 195 and following, a party of barbarian women, who have just returned from a hunting expedition, is introduced. They are armed with bows and arrows, and nearly succeed in shooting the buffoon (lines 207-8).

Apart from the distribution of the various parts, the manuscript includes a number of symbols and abbreviations which are to be interpreted as stage directions. The commonest of these are a letter <term>tau<note>the Greek letter 'τ'</note></term> with a dot and a horizontal dash above it (in line 211 there is no dash), and a pair of short strokes curving towards each other at the centre (e.g. line 11) which is sometimes followed by a straight stroke (e.g. line 39). The <note>original: "τ̄̇"</note> **dotted tau** (which we print simply as **τ**) is probably to be connected with the music, and might stand for <term>tympanismos<note>original: "τ(υμπανισμός)" — a rhythmic drumming or beating of a hand-drum</note></term>; compare line 92 <note>original: "τ(υμπανισμός) πολ(ύς), κροῦσ(ις)"</note> **much drumming, striking of instruments**, and lines 69 and 95 where **τ** is similarly combined with <note>original: "πολ( )"</note> **much**, and line 87 <note>original: "τ(υμπανισμός) (πεντάκις?)"</note> **drumming (five times?)**. The two curved strokes, which sometimes stand before or after **τ** (e.g. lines 65, 72), but more commonly are by themselves, may also have a musical signification, or may refer in some other way to the accompanying action; their use is not like that of mere marks of punctuation. The word <note>original: "πορδ(ή)" (pordē)</note> **fart**, which is repeatedly associated with the remarks of B, the buffoon, seems also to be of the nature of a stage direction; compare line 22 <note>original: "πέρδ(εται)" (perdetai)</note> **he farts**¹. The speeches in the barbarian language are usually written continuously, like the Greek, without separation of words; but in one passage (lines 61-4) the words are divided by points, while in others the insertion of one of the symbols described above serves a similar purpose. The language is no doubt to a large extent of an imaginary nature, but it may include some genuine non-Hellenic elements; compare the note on line 83.

The mime of which two columns are preserved upon the <term>verso<note>the "back" or reverse side of a papyrus sheet, where the fibers usually run vertically</note></term> of the papyrus is of a simpler character. The chief figure here is again a woman, upon whom the action centres throughout; most of the other actors are slaves. The motive of the first scene (Column ii) is that of the fifth mime of Herondas, titled the <term>Zelotypos<note>original: "ζηλότυπος" — The Jealous Woman</note></term>. The young mistress makes proposals to one of her slaves, Aesopus (line 115), to which he declines to listen, whereupon she orders him to be put to death along with a female slave (? Apollonia, line 120) whom she supposes to be the object of his affections. These cruel commands, however, are not actually carried out, for the male slave manages to escape, and his assumed paramour is only placed in confinement. In the next scene (Column iii) the bloodthirsty mistress is engaged in plotting the death of an old man, to whom she appears

to have been unhappily married. Her accomplices are two slaves, Spinther and Malacus, who also figured in the previous scene; and a ‘parasite’ <note>In ancient comedy, a 'parasite' was a character who hung around wealthy households, offering flattery or services in exchange for free meals.</note> acts as a go-between. The column ends in a rather obscure manner without her nefarious purpose having been accomplished, and the piece seems to have been left unfinished.

Whether at any point in these two columns the monologue of the mistress is interrupted by other speakers is a matter of some doubt. The sentences are in the original divided off by an oblique dash (see the critical notes); and at two points (at the end of line 117 and in the middle of line 185) the dash is preceded by three short horizontal strokes. Possibly this sign should be interpreted as an indication of a change of speaker, which would in either case suit the context. Thus in line 117 **Mistress** <note>original: "κυρί’", likely "κυρία" (kyria)</note> would be the natural mode of address from a slave to his mistress; and in line 187 **Master** <note>original: "δέσποτα" (despota)</note> implies the entrance of a new character (the old husband?), to whom may be attributed the words **Woe is me** <note>original: "οὐαί μοι" (ouai moi)</note>. But if so the scribe was not consistent in the use of this sign, which should have been repeated when the previous speaker resumed; and if omitted in these cases, it may be absent entirely in some others where an interchange of speakers might be supposed to occur, e.g. line 172 **What sort?** <note>original: "τὸ ποῖον" (to poion)</note>, line 178 **Ah, how? Certainly, etc.** <note>original: "αἳ πῶς ; μάλιστα, κ.τ.λ."</note>. But this is not necessary, and we do not feel satisfied that the other two passages cannot be explained on the hypothesis that the piece is a monologue throughout.

With regard to the date of the composition of these two productions, Crusius <note>Otto Crusius (1857–1918) was a noted German classical scholar who specialized in Greek proverbs and mimes.</note> considers that the mime belongs to the Roman period, while the farce may be rather earlier, though not a product of the better Hellenistic age. Their literary quality cannot of course be ranked very high, but they are not devoid of merit. The situations disclosed in the farce show some skill in construction, and when on the stage may have been amusing enough even without the coarser elements; while the mime, though without the accompanying action it is sometimes obscure, has considerable vigour and dramatic force. Not improbably these two pieces were once performed in the theatre of Oxyrhynchus, and they may be regarded as typical of the performances upon the provincial stages at this time. In short, they afford a most interesting glimpse into the music-hall of the period immediately following that which is represented by the Alexandrian Erotic Fragment (P. Grenf. I. 1).

These lines are enclosed in the papyrus by a circular stroke which passes through line 30, and there can be no doubt that it was intended that their place should be taken by Column 4 of the *verso*. This is indicated by the note at the bottom, which is in the same handwriting as the *verso*. The fact that in relation to the foregoing column the letters of the note are upside down is unusual, and "the outside" would be expected rather than "the inside"; but "the inside" would represent the point of view of the writer of the mime, and the practical identity of line 30 with lines 188-189 adds a conclusive proof that the column on the *verso* was meant to be inserted at this point. Line 30 is accordingly to be restored as "Lady Charition, rejoice with me," the speaker being character "Ϛ" as in line 188; it may also be noted that the word *alemmaka* found in line 35 also occurs in line 205 in the scene with the barbarian women, to whom "them" in line 33 probably refers. <meta>This page provides scholarly commentary and textual analysis for the previously translated "Charition Mime" (P.Oxy. 413). It focuses on the linguistic challenges of the "barbarian" dialogue, metrical patterns in the verses, and the distribution of roles among the actors.</meta>

# 413. NEW CLASSICAL FRAGMENTS

### Page 55

75-80. The distribution of the parts in this passage causes some difficulty. ***B.***, the buffoon, elsewhere speaks Greek only, and appears not to understand the barbarian language. Yet in lines 75 and 79 he is assigned non-Greek speeches, and the speaker who intervenes either at the end of lines 75 or 76 may also be ***B***. It will be noticed that in either case there is a beta <note>original: "β"</note> near the end of the line; but in both instances the letter following is closer than it should be if the beta was meant to represent the character. If the attribution of lines 75 and 79-80 to ***B.*** is correct, he may be supposed to be emboldened by the conviviality of the barbarians to address them in a meaningless jargon intended to imitate their language.

82. At the end of the line we should perhaps read *ouenit* <note>original: "ov<ε>νιt"</note>, as in lines 83-5.

83. Assuming that it is worth while to attempt to bring the barbarian language in this piece into relation with any known speech, the key is possibly to be found in late <term>Pali|A Middle Indo-Aryan language</term> or old <term>Prakrit|A group of medieval Indic languages</term>. We owe to Dr. G. A. Grierson the suggestion that in the present passage, for instance, *panoumbriti* <note>original: "πανουμβρητι"</note> may represent *pānō amṛta*, ‘drink’ (or ‘life’) and ‘nectar,’ which suits the context remarkably well. Similarly he would connect *alem(m)aka* <note>original: "αλεμ(μ)ακα"</note> in lines 35 and 205 with the Pali *alam* ‘enough,’ ‘stop,’ *-ka* being a substantival suffix which an ignorant Greek might use incorrectly. But we must leave the consideration of this question to <term>Sanskrit|The ancient classical language of India</term> scholars.

89. 1. *aneton*? <note>original: "ἀνετόν" — meaning relaxed or loosened</note>

90. *erothroun* <note>original: "ἐ[ε]ρόθρουν" — likely meaning red-sounding</note>, though a new compound, seems certain; cf. *ligythrous* <note>original: "λιγύθρους" — clear-voiced</note>, etc. Some syllables are missing at the end of the line, and a substantive is required to complete the sentence; perhaps *typanon* <note>original: "τύπανον" — drum</note> followed by a long syllable.

91. *Serikon* <note>original: "[Σ]ηρικόν" — referring to the Seres, or Silk-people (ancient Chinese/East Asians)</note> (Crusius) is very attractive, though it hardly fills the available space. At the end of the line the doubtful lambda <note>original: "λ"</note> may be a nu <note>original: "ν"</note>.

93. *orchisai* <note>original: "ὀρχῆσαι" — to dance</note> reproduces the sound of the barbarian *orkis[ . ]*.

94. ***B.*** is probably still the speaker.

96-106. The verses with which the scene closes are <term>trochaic tetrameters|A poetic meter consisting of four pairs of "stressed-unstressed" feet</term>, but the text seems faulty in places, and some alteration is required to reduce the metrical system to order. Thus lines 98 and 104 are each a syllable short, and lines 101-2 are considerably too long. Crusius suggests that in line 101 "the helmsman" <note>original: "ὁ κυβερνήτης"</note> is a <term>gloss|An explanatory note written in the margin or between lines</term> on "I" <note>original: "ἐγώ"</note>; and if these two words be omitted and *pirotos* <note>original: "πι[ρ]ώτως"</note> (for *protos* <note>original: "πρώτως" — first</note>) and "I" <note>original: "ἐγώ"</note> transposed, the metre is restored. Line 98 may be amended by reading "surely all" <note>original: "ἦ ῥα (or ἆρα) πάνθ'"</note>, which also improves the sense. The <term>iambic trimeter|A common meter for spoken drama</term> in line 105 is unexpected, and a <term>cretic|A foot consisting of a long, a short, and a long syllable</term> may be lost at the beginning; but it is perhaps better not to demand exact regularity, especially since lines 95-6 are also not trochaic tetrameters.

95. *katastole* <note>original: "καταστολή"</note> in the original is written after the manner of a title in larger letters, with little dashes above and below. It is probably equivalent to <term>katastrophe|The resolution or final turn of the plot in a drama</term>, as in the Scholium on Aristophanes' *Peace* <note>original: "Schol. on Aristoph. Pax 1204"</note>: "he made the **conclusion of the drama** <note>original: "τὴν δὲ καταστολὴν τοῦ δράματος"</note> similar to the *Acharnians*."

100. The first letter may be a pi <note>original: "π"</note>.

116. The word before "self" <note>original: "αὐτ( )"</note> seems to be some part of either *arassein* (to strike) or *tarassein* (to disturb).

117. *Kyri* <note>original: "κυρι'"</note> may be either "Lord" <note>original: "κύριε"</note> or "Lady" <note>original: "κυρία"</note> according to the view taken as to whether a change of speaker occurs at this point; cf. introduction. It is not quite clear where the words added above line 118 and in the <margin>margin</margin> were intended to be inserted. Crusius supposes that "all then . . . nurtured together" <note>original: "πάντων οὖν . . . συντεθραμμ(ένον)"</note> is resumptive of the previous conditional sentences, to which the <term>apodosis|The 'then' clause of a conditional statement</term> is "appeared empty" <note>original: "κενός . . . ἐφάνη"</note>, the general sense being: ‘If women had the hard work to do that I have, you would be as little inclined to love as I.’ The "you" <note>original: "σ[ε]"</note> after "if however" <note>original: "εἰ δέ"</note> is quite doubtful; the fibres of the <term>papyrus|Ancient writing material made from the pith of the papyrus plant</term> are displaced.

119. There is barely room for an alpha <note>original: "α"</note> at the beginning of the line, and the supposed *a* of "you boast" <note>original: "αὐχ(εῖς)"</note> is more like an omicron <note>original: "ο"</note>.

### 414. PHILOSOPHICAL FRAGMENT.

->Fr. (a) 14.3 x 11.8 cm.<-

Several fragments from a work of a philosophical nature, written in a good-sized and well-formed hand which seems to be a rather early specimen of the oval sloping style. In the formation of the letters and general appearance this manuscript bears a decided resemblance to **26**, and probably falls within the second century rather than the third. Columns iii and iv are on a detached piece of papyrus, but very likely succeed Column ii immediately. The subject under discussion is poets and the poetic faculty. There is no indication that the treatise was cast in the form of a dialogue.

### 418. SCHOLIA ON HOMER, *Iliad* I.

->*27.7 X 12 cm.*<-

An imperfect column of a commentary upon Book I of the *Iliad*, written in a large and clear cursive <note>A flowing style of handwriting where letters are joined, common in everyday documents of the era.</note> hand at the end of the first or early in the second century. The information provided is principally of a mythological character, and since line 399 is discussed immediately after line 264 the papyrus very likely consists of a series of excerpts. There are very close resemblances to *Schol. A* <note>The main set of ancient notes found in the famous Venetus A manuscript of Homer.</note>, which in several passages exhibits an inferior text; and considering the early date of the papyrus it is not unlikely that the commentary in question was one of the sources used in compiling the scholia in A which give mythological details. It shows traces of Didymean <note>Referring to Didymus Chalcenterus, a prolific scholar in Alexandria known for his work on Homer.</note> influence (cf. l. 24, note), but was probably derived directly or indirectly from Apollodorus <note>Apollodorus of Athens, a 2nd-century BC scholar who wrote extensively on Greek mythology.</note> (cf. ll. 9–22, note). The lines commented on are for the sake of clearness printed in capitals.

9-22. Compare with the Scholion A on line 264: **"Caeneus was the son of Elatus and king of the Lapiths <note>A legendary people of Thessaly</note>; previously he was a beautiful maiden, but after Poseidon mated with her, the young woman asked to be changed into a man and became invulnerable, having emerged as the most noble of those of his time. And once, having fixed a spear in the very middle of the marketplace, he commanded this to be honored as a god. For which reason Zeus, being indignant, exacted punishment from him for his impiety. For while he was fighting the Centaurs and being invulnerable, Zeus made him subject to them; for the aforementioned [Centaurs], striking him with oaks and fir-trees, crushed him into the earth."** <note>original: "ὁ Καινεὺς Ἐλάτου μὲν ἦν παῖς... ἐλάταις ἤρεισαν εἰς γῆν."</note> This is almost identical with the papyrus, but is more compressed in some parts and more expanded in others. As before, the papyrus exhibits the better text, (1) by avoiding the repetition of **was** <gloss>ἦν</gloss> in the first sentence, (2) by having **young man** <gloss>νεανίας</gloss> in place of **the young woman** <gloss>ἡ νεᾶνις</gloss> which is detrimental to both sense and construction, and in the light of the papyrus should be corrected to **young man**. Blass <note>Friedrich Blass, a prominent 19th-century German classical scholar.</note> suggests **"because of [his] beauty"** <note>original: "δία | δε το καλλος"</note> for the lacuna <note>A gap or missing part in a manuscript.</note> in lines 11-2, and **"the great pride"** <note>original: "τον [με]γαν ογκον"</note> for that in lines 14-5.

In the epitome of Apollodorus <note>A summary of a vast handbook of Greek mythology attributed to Apollodorus of Athens.</note> I. 22 (edited by Wagner, page 181) the story of Caeneus is related more briefly: **"That Caeneus was previously a woman, but after Poseidon came together with her, she asked to become an invulnerable man; wherefore also in the battle against the Centaurs, despising wounds, he destroyed many of the Centaurs, but the rest, standing around him and striking him with fir-trees, buried him in the earth."** <note>original: "ὅτι Καινεὺς πρότερον ἦν γυνή... ἔχωσαν εἰς γῆν."</note> The version of the papyrus may well represent another epitomizing of Apollodorus.

24. It is remarkable that the variant **"Phoebus Apollo"** in place of **"Pallas Athena"** occurs in line 400 not in line 399, and that the story of the conspiracy of Hera, Poseidon, and Apollo against Zeus follows as a kind of justification for the variation. As Apollo played an important part in the legend, this order is really more logical than that found in Scholion A, which first gives the story of the plot in connection with line 399 and then discusses the variant **"Phoebus Apollo,"** which is ascribed to Zenodotus <note>The first librarian of Alexandria and a pioneer of Homeric criticism.</note> but rejected as inappropriate. The account in Scholion A is as follows:—**"Zeus, having taken over the administration of heaven, used his freedom of speech excessively, performing many self-willed acts. Poseidon, Hera, Apollo, and Athena wished to bind and subdue him. But Thetis, having heard of the plot against Zeus from her father Nereus (for he was a seer), hurried to him, bringing along Aegaeon as a terror to the plotting gods; this sea-spirit even outmatched his father Poseidon. Zeus, having heard of the plot from Thetis, hung Hera in the bonds he had prepared against him, and for Poseidon and Apollo he decreed a period of service under Laomedon <note>The King of Troy; the gods were punished by being forced to build the city's walls.</note>, while for Thetis he set aside the honor of Achilles for a later time. Didymus <note>A Greek scholar in Alexandria (c. 63 BC – 10 AD) known for his prolific commentaries.</note> records this."** <note>original: "Ζεὺς παραλαβὼν τὴν ἐν οὐρανῷ διοίκησιν... ἱστορεῖ Δίδυμος."</note> The parallelism between this and the papyrus is marked, though the papyrus is somewhat shorter and varies the phraseology. The mention of Athena in the scholium, but not in the papyrus, is due to the slightly different point of view from which the legend is brought forward. If the scholium gives the actual words of Didymus, the papyrus would seem to be a secondary commentary based upon his notes; but on the other hand the papyrus may express Didymus' language more exactly, and the scholium be an expansion.

### 421-434. POETICAL FRAGMENTS.

We here group together a number of miscellaneous fragments in verse, which do not seem to be extant <note>Meaning they are "lost" works not found in surviving medieval manuscripts</note> and which are too small to be of much value. Of these four (421-3 and 434) are in <term>hexameters</term> <note>A poetic meter consisting of six "feet" per line, typical of epic poetry like the Iliad</note>, three (424-6) are lyrical <note>Song-like verses</note>, seven (427-33) are in <term>iambics</term> <note>A metrical foot consisting of one short syllable followed by one long syllable, common in dramatic dialogue</note>, chiefly comic.
**421** consists of the ends of nineteen hexameter lines written in a second century <term>uncial hand</term> <note>A style of handwriting using rounded capital letters, common in Greek and Latin manuscripts from the 4th to 8th centuries</note> with occasional breathings, accents, stops, and marks of quantity. The subject of the fragment is the parentage of Bellerophon and the gift of Pegasus (who is not mentioned by Homer). There are no indications that the poem was a late epic, and several phrases suggest Hesiod <note>An early Greek poet, often grouped with Homer</note> as the author.
**422** contains parts of eleven much mutilated hexameter lines, written in

rather large and well-formed <term>uncials</term> <note>A style of script using large, rounded capital letters common in Greek manuscripts from the 3rd to 8th centuries</note> of the square sloping type, and dating probably from the third century. A battle scene is apparently being described; Heracles is mentioned in line 9 and part of another name occurs in line 4. The vocabulary suggests that the fragment comes from some Alexandrian epic.

**423** is a strip from the bottom of a column, containing on the *verso* <note>The "back" or reverse side of the papyrus</note> parts of thirteen <term>hexameters</term> <note>A line of verse consisting of six metrical feet, the standard meter for epic poetry like the Iliad</note> in a large and rather rough uncial hand apparently of the third century. The *recto* <note>The "front" or primary side of the papyrus, where the fibers usually run horizontally</note> of the papyrus is blank. The high stop <note>A punctuation mark similar to a period but placed at the top of the line</note> occurs several times and marks of elision and accents were used. The subject of the fragment is obscure; a reference to the Nile is noticeable in line 13, while Hermes is mentioned in line 4.

**424** contains a fragment of three stanzas in <term>Sapphic metre</term> <note>A specific four-line poetic structure named after the poetess Sappho</note>, probably by Sappho herself, written in a heavy uncial hand of the third century resembling that of the Oxyrhynchus Sappho fragment already published (**7**). Accents and stops are found, the high point in lines 6 and 10, the middle point in line 5 (?). The form <term>aterais</term> <note>original: "ἀτέραις"</note> (equivalent to <term>heterais</term> <note>original: "ἑτέραις"</note>, meaning "to others") in line 9 is of some interest, since the *a* was hitherto doubtful for the Lesbian dialect; compare Meister, *Greek Dialects* page 41.

**425** is a short extract from some lyric poem copied out as a school exercise. This is indicated partly by the character of the handwriting, which is a large irregular uncial, partly by the fact that the papyrus is complete in itself; and the inferior spelling points to the same conclusion. Below the last line are a series of dashes. The excerpt is of the nature of an invocation such as might have come at the beginning of the poem, which does not appear from this specimen to have been of a very high-class quality. The metrical scheme is short-short-long, short-short-long, short-short-long. The date of the manuscript is second or third century.

A more valuable fragment is **426**, a long narrow strip containing parts of thirty-two lines from a lyric poem in <term>dactylo-epitritic metre</term> <note>A rhythmic structure commonly used in Greek choral lyric and victory odes</note> and Pindaric style, which is not improbably to be attributed to Pindar himself. Unfortunately the piece is so mutilated that little can be done in the way of restoration, though a few lines in the middle which concern Melampus <note>A legendary healer and soothsayer in Greek mythology</note> are intelligible. The text is written on the *verso* of the papyrus in a rather uncultivated uncial hand which may be assigned to the third century; on the *recto* is part of a cursive document dating from the latter half of the century preceding.

**427** is also a fragment of some importance. It consists of the latter parts of the three closing lines of a play, below which is the title <term>...anes | ...pogonia</term> <note>original: "]ανους | ]πογονια"</note>. There can be little question that Blass <note>Friedrich Blass, a prominent German classical scholar</note> is right in reading this as <term>Antiphanes' Anthropogonia</term> <note>original: "[Ἀντιφ]άνους [Ἀνθρω]πογονία", meaning "The Creation of Mankind"</note>, and that the papyrus furnishes another example of the dangers of rejecting definite ancient evidence on logical grounds alone. A <term>Theogonia</term> <note>original: "Θεογονία", meaning "The Genealogy of the Gods"</note> of Antiphanes is mentioned by Irenaeus (ii. 14), who gives a lengthy excerpt from it; this, however, was rejected by Meineke (*i. pp. 38 sqq.*), who maintained that it was derived from

<summary>This page describes a series of papyrus fragments (423-427) including possible works by Sappho and Pindar, as well as a significant find confirming a play by the comic poet Antiphanes.</summary>

The text is written on the *verso* <term>verso</term> <note>The back side of the papyrus sheet</note> of the papyrus in a square or oval sloping <term>uncial</term> <note>A formal style of handwriting using large, rounded capital letters</note> hand (cf. **420**) of the third century; on the *recto* <term>recto</term> <note>The front side of the papyrus, where the fibers usually run horizontally</note> are parts of three lines in second century <term>cursive</term> <note>A faster, flowing style of handwriting used for everyday documents</note>.

**428** contains the ends of nine <term>iambic</term> <note>A rhythmic meter common in Greek drama, mimicking the natural cadence of speech</note> lines of a comedy, or possibly a tragedy, written in a small semi-uncial hand, which is more likely to belong to the second century than to the third. A short diagonal dash at the top of the line is used as a mark of punctuation.

**429** is another comic fragment, containing the beginnings of fourteen iambic lines written in a large and handsome uncial of the square sloping type characteristic of the third century; cf. **420**. On the *verso* is part of a document in cursive dating from the end of the century. A <term>paragraphus</term> <note>A horizontal line drawn in the margin to indicate a change of speaker or a new section</note> below line 9 marks a change of speaker. In lines 10-12 a marriage is being arranged, which may indicate that the conclusion of the play was not far off. A very deep margin at the top of the column is noticeable.

**430** consists of parts of eight lines in comic iambics from the top of a column, written on the *verso* of a second or early third century account. Marks of <term>elision</term> <note>The omission of a vowel at the end of a word when the next word begins with a vowel</note> and high stops <note>Punctuation marks placed at the top of the letter height</note> occur, but no breathings or accents. The writing on the *verso* is probably but little later than that on the *recto*.

**431** consists of parts of twelve lines of a dialogue in comic iambics, written in an uncial hand resembling the square sloping type, but more probably second century than third. Changes of speaker are indicated by <term>paragraphi</term> <note>Plural of paragraphus; marginal lines marking speaker changes</note> and, when in the middle of a line, by blank spaces.

**432** contains the beginnings of seventeen lines apparently from a comedy, written in a small uncial hand upon the *verso* of a second or early third century account. A correction in line 15 and marginal notes opposite lines 2 and 8 have been added in a more cursive hand, but probably by the original scribe. Changes of speaker are indicated by paragraphi and, when in the middle of a line, by double dots (cf. **409**). The marginal notes seem from their position to refer to the speakers, but the names (<margin>*The Rhetorician* <note>original: Ρ]ητορικ(ός)</note></margin> or <margin>*rhetorical* <note>original: ρ]ητορικ(ός)</note></margin> and <margin>*Ariphron* <note>original: Αριφ(ρων)</note></margin> or <margin>*Ariphrades* <note>original: Αριφ(ράδης)</note></margin>) are curious. The writing on the *verso* may be assigned to the third century. Between lines 13 and 14 is a blank space sufficient for two lines.

**433** contains the ends and beginnings of iambic lines from the upper parts of two columns. The manuscript seems to have been of a magical character, giving directions for a series of spells or incantations, the objects of which are indicated

# **435-444. PROSE FRAGMENTS.**

Under these numbers are included a variety of small prose fragments which we have not succeeded in identifying. Two (**435-6**) are historical, three (**437-9**) of a philosophical character, the remainder, with the possible exceptions of **441** and **444**, are oratorical <note>referring to speeches or the art of public speaking</note>.

**435** contains parts of two columns written in an informal uncial <note>a script written entirely in large, rounded capital letters</note> hand.

<summary>This page concludes a magical spell for causing loathing (misethron) and presents several highly damaged fragments, including a possible poetic piece mentioning nymphs and the Nile, and descriptions of unidentified prose fragments.</summary>

<page-num>77</page-num>
<header>435-444. NEW CLASSICAL FRAGMENTS</header>

...probably towards the close of the second or in the first half of the third century. The Corcyraeans <note>the people of the island of Corcyra, modern-day Corfu</note> are mentioned in connection with someone whose name began with Demo- <note>original: "Δημο"</note>, and who persuaded them to provide a talent <note>a large unit of weight or currency, usually of silver</note>; and there seems to have been some question of a marriage.

**436** is a third-century fragment from the bottom of a column, written in square sloping uncials <note>a formal style of ancient handwriting using large, rounded capital letters</note> (cf. **420** and **447**) of good size. The general sense of lines 5–10 is fairly clear, and the passage is evidently part of a description of some distinguished general, which might come either from a biographical monograph or from a more comprehensive historical work.

**437** comprises parts of fifteen lines from the bottom of a column, the subject of which seems to be the practice of surgery, though it is not clear whether the fragment belongs to some professedly medical treatise or to a philosophical work of a more general character. The hand is a medium-sized sloping uncial probably dating from the third century.

**438** consists of parts of twenty-three lines written upon the *back* <note>original: "verso"</note> of a second-century account in a semi-uncial hand <note>a script style intermediate between formal book-hand and everyday cursive</note>, also of the second century. The first line, which is shorter and apparently in a more cursive hand than the rest and has a space below it, is more likely to be a marginal note than the title of the work, which seems to have been of a philosophical character, the author using the first person very frequently.

**439** is written on the *back* <note>original: "verso"</note>, the *front* <note>original: "recto"</note> having only a diagonal stroke such as is found in accounts. Parts of fourteen lines are preserved, written in rather small third-century uncials of the usual type; cf. **420**. A breathing and elision mark <note>punctuation marks used in Greek to indicate breath sounds or omitted vowels</note> occur. The fragment comes from a philosophical writer, apparently not Plato.

**440.** Two fragments which were found together and are apparently in the same hand; but whether they belong to the same manuscript is doubtful, for the papyrus of (*b*) is somewhat thicker than that of (*a*), and (*b*) has on the *back* <note>original: "verso"</note> parts of six lines written in a good-sized uncial hand, while the *back* of (*a*) is blank. The writing on the *front* <note>original: "recto"</note> is a third-century uncial of a common type (cf. **447**). (*a*), which was a carefully punctuated papyrus, is probably a fragment of an orator.

**441** contains the ends and beginnings of lines from the upper parts of two consecutive columns, written in a small sloping hand probably of the third century. The use of the second person plural (line 16) and the occurrence of the name Philip <note>likely Philip II of Macedon</note> (line 20) suggest a rhetorical composition; but it might also be inferred from the short line at line 19 followed by a name in the genitive case <note>a grammatical form often used to denote authorship</note> that the manuscript comprised a collection of pithy sayings <note>original: "ἀποφθέγματα" (apophthegmata)</note> or anecdotes.

**442.** A long strip containing the latter halves of lines from one column and

## III. FRAGMENTS OF EXTANT CLASSICAL AUTHORS

### 445. HOMER, *Iliad, Book 6.*

->Height 30.5 centimeters. PLATE IV (Fragment *a*).<-

Of the numerous Homeric papyri from the Roman period that have been discovered, very few offer as many interesting and important details as the following fragments of the sixth book of the *Iliad*. It is written in a medium-sized <term>uncial <note>a formal script using large, rounded capital letters</note></term> hand with critical marks and occasional marginal notes. It contains parts of lines 128, 134-137, 148, 173-194, 199, and from line 445 to the end of the book. While the critical marks—which include the <term>diple <note>a mark shaped like a '>', used to draw attention to a specific line</note></term>, <term>antisigma <note>a mark shaped like a reversed 'C', used to indicate that lines were misplaced or out of order</note></term>, and <term>asterisk <note>a star symbol used to mark lines that appear correctly here but are also found elsewhere</note></term>—were all made by the original scribe, the marginal notes seem to have been written by two or three different people. However, because there is so little writing to compare, it is impossible to categorize these hands with total certainty. To the first corrector (whom we will call "A"), who used a small <term>semi-uncial <note>a script that combines capital and lowercase-style features</note></term> hand, we should attribute the notes on lines 128, 148, and 449, along with all the variant readings written above the lines. To the second corrector ("B"), who used a smaller and more cursive running hand, belongs the note on line 464. To a third ("C"), who wrote in a larger running hand, belongs the note on line 478. The figure at the end, which apparently gives the total number of lines in the book, is written in a running hand but seems to be by the original scribe. This question of who wrote what is not of great importance, however, as there is clearly no significant time difference between the writing of the main text and the addition of the <term>scholia <note>ancient explanatory notes or commentaries written in the margins of a manuscript</note></term> and the interlinear readings. A first-century date for the papyrus is out of the question; both the text and the notes suggest the second century or the beginning of the third. Breathings and accents are used occasionally, and marks indicating where a vowel was dropped (elision) are generally used. The punctuation is careful: a "high point" is usually used for a pause, except in lines 477 and 496, where a "middle point" occurs, indicating a shorter pause.

In its placement of critical marks, the papyrus generally agrees with the <note>Venetus A: A famous 10th-century manuscript of the Iliad (codex Marcianus Graecus 454) that preserves the most complete set of ancient scholarly markings</note> Venetus A, though there are some differences (see the notes on lines 183 and 189). The marginal notes, however, are very sparse compared to those in the Venetus A commentary, though the information they do provide is quite valuable since they all deal with different versions of the text. Most of these notes record differences between this papyrus and the <term>koine <note>original: "κοινή"; refers to the "common" or standard version of Homer's text that was most widely circulated in antiquity</note></term> (the generally accepted text). This "common text" is occasionally mentioned in other surviving Homeric commentaries, but never in connection with these specific passages. Besides the readings attributed to a specific source in the marginal...

The papyrus, which is remarkably free from errors and has more affinity with A <note>The "Townley Homer," a famous 11th-century manuscript noted for its scholarly marginalia</note> than with any other extant manuscript, presents in spite of its extremely mutilated condition a number of important readings which are either altogether new (see notes on lines 487, 494, and 523), or are known to have existed only from scholia <note>Ancient commentaries written in the margins of manuscripts</note> (line 187), or from quotations in other authors (line 493). Our collation is with the text of Ludwich <note>Arthur Ludwich, a 19th-century scholar whose edition of Homer was the standard reference at the time</note>.

**128.** The marginal note refers to the ancient variant reading *heaven* <note>original: "ouranon"</note> for the common reading *of heaven* <note>original: "ouranou"</note>. Scholion A <note>An ancient commentary found in the margins of medieval manuscripts</note> has (reading *of heaven* in the text): “Thus Aristarchus <note>A famous librarian and scholar in Alexandria</note> [read it], as if saying ‘you have come down from heaven’ <note>original: "katabibēkas ton ouranon"</note>. Therefore he writes it with the letter *n* <note>indicating the accusative case</note>, meaning ‘down from heaven’ <note>original: "kat' ouranon"</note>.” The reading of Aristarchus is found in several families of manuscripts; whether the text of the papyrus had *heaven* <note>original: "ouranon"</note> is uncertain.

**148.** The marginal note presents much difficulty. *Season* <note>original: "ōrē"</note> was according to Scholion A the reading of Aristophanes <note>Aristophanes of Byzantium, another major Alexandrian scholar</note>, while the nominative *season* <note>original: "ōrē"</note> is found in nearly all the manuscripts and is preferred by Ludwich <note>A 19th-century Homeric scholar</note>. The iota before the phrase *the ancient copies* <note>original: "hai arch(aiai)"</note> apparently belongs to the main text (which therefore agreed with Aristophanes), not to the note, and since *the ancient copies* would most naturally refer to the reading of Aristophanes, we should expect the authority for the other reading *season* to be given by the intervening word or words. But it is not easy to interpret the meaning of the abbreviation *o ēkou<sup>s</sup>*. The reading of the first letter is by no means certain, for the *o* is larger than the usual omicron of this scribe and might represent a *b*, and it is moreover placed underneath the *ch* of *ancient* <note>original: "arch(aiai)"</note>, which is above the line. But the following *ē* has been corrected from *o* apparently, so that what seems to have happened is that the scribe first wrote *ancient* <note>original: "arch..."</note> and then converted the *o* into *ē*, inserting *o* in the blank space underneath the *ch*. The obvious division is *the common reading omits [the iota]* <note>original: "hē ko(inē) h(ipo)s(tellei)"</note>, comparing the use of *omission* <note>original: "hypostolē"</note> in *Anecdota Bekkeri* II. p. 600 for the 'omission' of the letter iota. The scholium would then mean that the ancient copies read *to the season* <note>original: "ōrēi," with the iota subscript</note>, but the common reading was *season* <note>original: "ōrē"</note> with no iota. This gives very

...good sense, but the abbreviation *us* <note>original: "υ̅σ̅"</note> is hardly the kind of abbreviation of *withholds* <note>original: "hypostellei"</note> which would be expected on a papyrus of this period, and the construction of "which" <note>original: "ho"</note> (referring to the *iota* of *ōrēi* [in the season]) is somewhat difficult. *I heard* <note>original: "ēkouo( )"</note> written as one word, however, suggests nothing but the first aorist tense of the verb *to hear*, and though it is noteworthy that in Scholion A on this line the word *hears* <note>original: "akouei"</note> occurs (“Aristophanes writes *tēlethoōnta* [flourishing] and on the leaves *it hears* [akouei] and he writes *ōrēi* [in the season] with the *iota* according to the dative case”), the phrases *which he heard* <note>original: "ho ēkouse(n)"</note> or *which they heard* <note>original: "ho ēkouo(an)"</note> here make no sense, and for *as I heard* <note>original: "ho ēkousa(a)"</note>, there is no parallel in scholia of this character.

**174.** For the diple <note>A marginal mark (>) used by ancient editors to draw attention to a line.</note> before this line, compare Scholion A: “the diple [is used] because it refers back to the number nine.” The papyrus adds an antisigma <note>A mark like a reversed C or sigma (Ͻ), used to indicate lines that are out of order or repetitive.</note> as well; compare the explanation of this sign in a grammarian quoted by Dindorf: “the antisigma and the two dots [are used] when the same meaning is placed twice in succession.”

**176.** Scholion A has the diple against this line with comments upon *then he questioned him and [asked for] the token* <note>original: "tote min ereeine kai sēma"</note>.

**178.** Scholion A has a diple against this line, but no comment.

**181.** The diple before this line, like that before line 186, has a dot above it and possibly is meant for a *dotted diple* <note>original: "diplē periestigmenē"</note>, which should have a dot below as well. That sign was used to denote the readings or transpositions of Zenodotus, Crates, and Aristarchus <note>Famous ancient scholars who edited the text of Homer.</note>. But since Scholion A has an ordinary diple against line 181 with the remark *because the Chimera had one body* <note>original: "hoti hen sōma hē chimaira"</note>, and none at all against line 186, and since no variation of reading among the ancient critics is recorded in connection with those two lines, it is more probable that the diple with one dot has the same meaning as the plain diple, or at any rate means something different from the dotted diple.

**183.** Here the Venetus A manuscript has a diple with the remark *because it reveals nothing regarding the story of Pegasus* <note>original: "hoti ouden peri tēs kata ton Pēgason historias emphainei"</note>. Possibly the diple which is found in the papyrus before line 186, where the Venetus A has none, has been misplaced and should have preceded line 183. But there are several instances of divergence between the papyrus and Manuscript A with regard to the diple; see the note on line 189.

**187.** The reading of the first hand, *coming upon* <note>original: "eperchomenō"</note>, is ascribed to *others* <note>original: "alloi"</note> by Scholion A, but is not found in any manuscript. The reading of the corrector, *going away* <note>original: "aperchomenō"</note> (ascribed to Aristarchus by Scholion V), occurs in the Lipsiensis manuscript and apparently in Mr. Allen's L 20. It is curious that the papyrus seems to ignore *returning* <note>original: "anerchomenō"</note>, the ordinary reading and that ascribed to Aristarchus by Scholion A. It is now clear that the variant *coming upon* (which is not even mentioned by modern editors Ludwich or Monro and Allen) rested on considerable authority.

**189.** The papyrus has no diple before this line and line 191 where they are found in the Venetus A.

**194.** Compare Scholion A: “the diple [is used] because he derives the etymology of *temenos* [a sacred precinct] from *temein* [to cut] and *aphorisai* [to set apart].”

**199.** For the diple compare Manuscript A, which has a comment on the parentage of Sarpedon.

**449.** The scholiasts have no note on the reading *eummeliō* [of the spear-skilled] on this line, but compare Scholion A on Book 2, line 461 (“in the Asian meadow”): “An Ionic transformation; for the correct form is *Asiēō* like *Atreidēō*. Therefore it is without the *iota*.” Scholion T on the same line says: “...it should therefore be taken in the genitive case and without the *iota*, like *of the spear-skilled Priam* [*eummeliō Priamoio*], as Herodian [says] in the *General Prosody* and Ptolemy in his work *On Elision*.” And Scholion D on the same: “The word *Asiō* here is in the genitive case. Hence it does not have the *iota* ... like *eummelias, eummeliō* of Priam ... thus Horus in his *Orthography*.” The papyrus had *eummeliō* (genitive) in the text with most manuscripts. Mr. Allen informs us that besides Manuscript A, his D, V 16, and P, and probably a few more have *eummeliōi* <note>The dative form</note>, and this reading is indicated by the remark *dative with the iota* <note>original: "do(tikē) m(e)t(a) tou i"</note>. The papyrus seems unique in calling *eummeliō* a dative, perhaps from false analogy with *Asiōi* (mentioned above), which in spite of the ancient commentators is probably to be interpreted as a dative.

The dash after the letter *iota* is apparently a mark of punctuation. Whether *genitive* <note>original: "g(enikē)"</note> (if that be the right expansion of the abbreviation *g’* in the text) *eummeliōio* means that *eummeliō* is to be regarded as a genitive, equivalent to *eummeliou*, or that there was a variant *eummeliōio*, is not made...

clear. *with a good ashen spear* <note>original: "eummeliō"</note>, though it does not scan, is actually found in one manuscript; but the first hypothesis is more likely, though *of the one with a good ashen spear* <note>original: "eummeliou"</note> would be expected.

**456.** *Being in Argos* <note>original: "Argei eousa"</note> Ludwich <note>Arthur Ludwich, a 19th-century classical scholar known for his editions of Homer.</note>, the manuscripts being divided. *Towards* <note>original: "pros"</note> (Ludwich) is the reading of all the manuscripts except one at Vienna (W) in which *towards* <note>original: "pros"</note> is corrected to *before* <note>original: "pro"</note>, as here.

**464.** Over the *u* of *may it cover* <note>original: "kaluptoi"</note> is a circular mark resembling the sign for a short syllable.
The marginal note here is in a more cursive hand than that employed in the other cases. The <term>vulgate</term> <note>The "common" or standard version of a text accepted by tradition.</note> does in fact read *having died* <note>original: "tethneiōs"</note>; compare <term>Scholia A</term> <note>Ancient explanatory notes found in the margins of the Venetus A manuscript of the Iliad.</note> on Homeric lines 409, 633, 161, etc., from which it appears that Aristarchus read *dead* <note>original: "tethnōs"</note>. So far *others* <note>original: "alloi"</note> has been the only source assigned to the form *having died* <note>original: "tethneiōs"</note>, which is read in the majority of the manuscripts.

**475.** *they run* <note>original: "theousin"</note>: *to the gods* <note>original: "theoisi"</note> Ludwich.

**477.** Compare A, where *in* <note>original: "eni"</note> is superscribed above *unseemly* <note>original: "aprepea"</note>, the reading of other manuscripts and Ludwich.

**478.** After the <term>lacuna</term> <note>A gap or missing part in a manuscript.</note> following *might* <note>original: "biēn"</note> is a spot of ink at the top of the line, which we have considered to represent an <term>elision-mark</term> ’. If this is correct, the note probably refers to the alternative readings *good in his might* <note>original: "biēn t’ agathon"</note> (the best-supported reading, so Ludwich) and *good might* <note>original: "biēn agathon"</note> (so many manuscripts) or *and good in his might* <note>original: "biēn agathon te"</note> (ascribed to *others* by Scholia A). Of these *good might* <note>original: "biēn agathon"</note> is that most likely to have stood in the text of the papyrus, since *might [and]* <note>original: "biēn t’"</note> is recorded in the margin and the reading *and good in his might* <note>original: "biēn agathon te"</note> ignores the <term>digamma</term> <note>An archaic Greek letter (Ϝ) representing a 'w' sound, which disappeared from later Greek but remained functionally present in the rhythm of Homer's poetry.</note> before *Ilium* <note>original: "Ilion"</note>, whereas in line 493 the papyrus preserves a <term>digamma</term> which is ignored by the manuscripts. But it is possible that after *might* <note>original: "biēn"</note> there was no *and* <note>original: "t’"</note> and that the spot of ink represents a stop or is even accidental. Then the marginal note may refer either to *the battle-cry [and]* <note>original: "boēn t"</note> in the text or to *the battle-cry* <note>original: "boēn"</note> (or *the battle-cry [and]* <note>original: "boēn t"</note>), a reading found in manuscript D, two Vienna manuscripts, and Mr. Allen's N 4. The fact that the scholia do not mention "battle-cry" but comment on the position of "and" <note>original: "te"</note> is in favour of the view that the note here referred to a variation concerning "and," not "might."

**479.** *in two ways* <note>original: "dichōs"</note> over the line refers to the variants *this one* <note>original: "g’ hode"</note> (Aristarchus) and *but he* <note>original: "d’ ho ge"</note> (the reading of nearly all manuscripts). It is quite uncertain which of the two was found in the text of the papyrus.

**485.** Above the last two letters of *he called by name* <note>original: "onomaze"</note> are traces of ink which apparently indicate something superscribed. The only variant known is *he called by name [with final n]* <note>original: "onomazen"</note>, and the vestiges do not suggest either *n* or a horizontal stroke meaning *n*.

**487.** The *p* of *will send forth* <note>original: "proiapsei"</note> has been corrected from *a* (?). The variant *will attach to* <note>original: "protiapsei"</note> inserted above the line is not recorded in connexion with the present passage, but in Book 24, line 110, there was an ancient dispute whether *send forth* <note>original: "proiaptō"</note> or *attach to* <note>original: "protiaptō"</note> was to be read.

**490-2.** For the asterisks before these lines compare Scholia A on 490-3: “asterisks are placed beside four lines in succession because they are correctly placed here before the lines of the *slaying of the suitors* <note>original: "mnēstērophonias"</note> (Odyssey, book 21, line 350) but in the first book of the *Odyssey* (356-9) they are not.” The papyrus omits the asterisk before line 493.

**493.** *to all, but most of all to me, of those in Ilium* <note>original: "pasi malista d emoi toi Iliōi"</note>: this reading, which is superior to that of all the manuscripts (and Ludwich) *to all, but to me most of all, those in Ilium* <note>original: "pasin emoi de malista toi Iliōi"</note> because it preserves the <term>digamma</term> before *Ilium* <note>original: "Iliōi"</note>, is found in Epictetus, *Discourses* III. 22, 108, and had been restored in the present passage by Hoffmann and Bekker, comparing Odyssey books 1.359, 11.353, and 21.353. For another example of a conjecture in the text of Homer being confirmed by a papyrus see *P. Grenf. II.* p. 11, where in Iliad 23.198 Nauck's conjecture *and swift Iris* <note>original: "ōkea de Iris"</note> instead of the manuscript reading *and swift Iris [with elision]* <note>original: "ōkea d’ Iris"</note> is found in a third century B.C. papyrus. It is noticeable that there, as here, the papyrus preserves a <term>digamma</term> which had been ignored by the manuscripts.
*are born in* <note>original: "engegaasin"</note>: compare A, where too *n* is superscribed. *are born in* <note>original: "engegaasin"</note> Ludwich.

**494.** At the end of the line *illustrious Hector* <note>original: "phaidimos Hektōr"</note> is the reading of all the manuscripts and Ludwich. For the variant *with a stout hand* <note>original: "cheiri pacheiē"</note> compare Iliad 21.403, where *Pallas Athena* <note>original: "Pallas Athēnē"</note> is found in the Ambrosianus and a Vatican manuscript (compare Scholia A “in another [manuscript] *Pallas Athena*”) in place of the ordinary reading *with a stout hand*. *with a stout hand* <note>original: "cheiri pacheiē"</note> would suit just as well as *illustrious Hector* here, for *having spoken* <note>original: "phōnēsas"</note> could not refer to any one but Hector.

**507–9.** The Papyrus omits the asterisks which are found in Manuscript A <note>Venetus A, the most famous medieval manuscript of the Iliad</note> against these lines, but has the <term>diple</term> <note>A wedge-shaped mark (>) used by ancient editors to indicate a noteworthy passage or a variation in the text</note> against line 507, as in A.

**510.** *shoulders* <note>original: "ōm[ois"</note>: in the margin before this line is what looks like the top of a critical mark, of which the rest is lost. A has a <term>diple</term> against this line.

**518.** The smooth breathing mark above the initial *ê* <note>original: "η"</note> is uncertain, but the remains suit that better than a circumflex accent. There is a <term>diple</term> before this line in A.

**521.** The letters *d* and *m* of *to the divinity* <note>original: "daimoni ["</note> have possibly been corrected.

**523.** *but being silent* <note>original: "all' akeōn"</note>: the manuscripts usually read *but willing* <note>original: "alla ekōn"</note>. Compare Book 2, line 111, where the scholar Rhianus <note>A 3rd-century BC poet and grammarian</note> read *unwillingly* <note>aekonta</note> for *silently* <note>akeonta</note>. This error (mixing up "unwilling" for "silent") is not uncommon in manuscripts. *Being silent* <note>akeōn</note> makes good sense here.

**527.** The *o* of *among the heavenly ones* <note>original: "epouranioisi"</note> is corrected from *i*.

**529.** Below the <term>coronis</term> <note>An ornamental mark in the margin showing the end of a book or section</note> is a number, apparently referring to the lines in the book. If 525 is correct, Book VI in this papyrus was four lines shorter than in our standard texts. But in view of the carelessness of scribes in numbering successive hundreds of lines (compare fragment **223**), not much reliance can be placed on the figure here, though compare **448**. 302, note.

->18.4 x 4.3 cm. PLATE VI.<-

A narrow strip of papyrus containing parts of lines 58–99 of *Iliad* Book 13. The scribe was unusually careless, and the fragment has no critical value for determining the "correct" text of Homer; but <term>palaeographically</term> <note>relating to the study of ancient handwriting</note> it is interesting, since a portion of a cursive account on the <term>verso</term> <note>the back side of the papyrus</note> of the late second or third century supplies an approximate <term>latest possible date</term> <note>original: "terminus ad quem"</note> for the date of the literary text on the <term>recto</term> <note>the front side of the papyrus</note>. ### 447. HOMER, *Iliad XXIII*.

->7.3 x 4.2 cm. PLATE VI.<-

The following small fragment from the twenty-third Book of the *Iliad* has, like the preceding papyrus, a palaeographical <note>The study of ancient handwriting.</note> interest. The text on the *recto* <note>The front or "right" side of the papyrus leaf.</note>, written in square slightly sloping uncials <note>A style of large, rounded capital letters.</note>, represents a common type of literary hand; while on the *verso* <note>The back side of the papyrus leaf.</note> is part of an account in cursive handwriting which is not later than the beginning of the third century, and more probably belongs to the second. It is, therefore, not at all likely that the manuscript on the *recto* was written later than the latter part of the second century. A few accents etc. occur, apparently added by the original scribe.

### 448. **Homer, *Odyssey* XXII and XXIII.**

->Height of Column 29.6 *cm*.<-

The following fragments are from a roll comprising Books 22 and 23 of Homer’s *Odyssey*. Of the twenty-second Book portions of seven consecutive columns remain, covering with some intervals lines 31–317. Book 23 is represented only by two small pieces from a couple of columns, nine intermediate columns being wholly lost. The text is on the <term>verso</term> <note>the back side of the papyrus</note> of the papyrus, the <term>recto</term> <note>the front side of the papyrus</note> having been previously utilized for a prose literary work which has been carefully cleaned off—unfortunately so effectively that the writing is quite illegible. The letters here and there traceable are formal rather heavy upright <term>uncials</term> <note>a style of capital letters used in early Greek and Latin manuscripts</note> of good size, probably not earlier than the third century, to which the hand of the back side may also be attributed. This is also upright and rather large, but lighter and more ornate. Accents, breathings (usually acute-angled), marks of elision, etc., and high stops have been added with some frequency, mostly by a second hand, which has also introduced some corrections into the text; the marks of elision, however, seem to be mainly due to the original scribe. The system of accentuation is generally similar to that found in **223**, the long papyrus of *Iliad* Book 5; in <term>oxytone</term> <note>words with an accent on the last syllable</note> words, however, all the syllables except the last bear a grave accent (though not in Book 22, line 184: *broad old* <note>original: ευρύ γερον</note>), as in the *Bacchylides* papyrus, whereas in **223** only the penultimate syllable has the grave accent. As in **223**, <term>perispome</term> <note>words with a circumflex accent on the last syllable</note> words followed by <term>enclitics</term> <note>short words that "lean" on the preceding word for their accent</note> become oxytone. In the case of diphthongs the second vowel is usually accented, while in **223** the reverse is the case, but the writer was not very careful, and it is sometimes a matter of doubt for which letter an accent was intended. A peculiarity is the method of writing the accents, which are as a rule nearly, and sometimes quite, horizontal.

The papyrus shows on the whole a good text, which is of interest on account of some agreements with manuscript "X" <note>the Vindobonensis 133 manuscript, kept in Vienna</note>, or "U" <note>the Monacensis 519 B manuscript, kept in Munich</note>,

**Book 22, line 35.** The letter *u* of the word for *dogs* <note>original: "κυνες"</note> has been corrected; the scribe originally began to write a round letter.
**37-8.** These two lines are swapped in order in several **manuscripts**.
**37.** the word *and* <note>original: "τε"</note>: so Manuscript U and the commentator *Eustathius*; but the word *but* <note>original: "δέ"</note> is used by the editor *Ludwich* and other **manuscripts**.
**44.** The papyrus agrees with the majority of **manuscripts** (and *Ludwich*) in omitting the line: "Each man peered around to see where he might escape sheer destruction" <note>original: "πάπτηνεν δὲ ἕκαστος ὅπη φύγοι αἰπὺν ὄλεθρον"</note>, which is found in Manuscripts D, L, and W.
**87.** [to bo]th [of the]m <note>original: "α]μφ[οτεροι]σιν"</note>: common **manuscripts** and *Ludwich* use a shorter form of the word <note>original: "ἀμφοτέροισι"</note>.
**88.** The letters *us* of the word for *mist* <note>original: "αχλυς"</note> have been corrected by the original scribe from *eus*; that is, he began to write the word *Achilleus* by mistake.
**114.** The letters *au* of the word for *in this way* <note>original: "αυτως"</note> are written over an erasure of the letter *omega* by the first hand.
**119.** The correction was likely made by a second scribe.
**128.** "within are" <note>original: "εντος ε[ισαι"</note>: so Manuscripts X and U, and *Eustathius* notes either "within" or "inside are"; but other **manuscripts** and *Ludwich* read "well-fitted."
**129.** Read as *Odysseus*: compare lines 141 and 281. The letter *e* of the word [for] *dreadful* <note>original: "δε]ιον"</note> seems to have been deleted.
**130.** "standing" <note>original: "εστεωτ'"</note>: so *Ludwich* following Manuscript H and others; compare the scholar Aristarchus on the Iliad 24. 701. Other **manuscripts** vary between different Greek spellings of "standing" <note>original: "ἑσταῶτ', ἑστῶτ', ἑσταότ', and ἑστεότ'"</note>. The letter *r* (or *ph*) written instead of *t* by the original scribe was a simple mistake.
"near her" <note>original: "αγχου τη[ς"</note>: the word "near" <note>original: "ἀγχοῦ"</note> is not found here in any **manuscript**; "near herself" <note>original: "ἄγχ' αὐτῆς"</note> is the standard reading.
**141.** Read as *Odysseus*: compare lines 129 and 281.
**186.** "were loosened" <note>original: "δε λελυντο"</note>: The way the correction was made without an apostrophe indicates the corrector read it as two separate words <note>original: "δε λελυντο"</note> as in Manuscripts F and Z, rather than the combined form <note>original: "δ' ελελυντο"</note> found in other **manuscripts** and *Ludwich*; compare Book 23, line 192.
**192.** The omission of the line "the son of Laertes, the long-suffering noble Odysseus" <note>original: "υἱὸς Λαέρταο, πολύτλας δῖος 'Οδυσσεύς"</note> is in agreement with the majority of the **manuscripts** and *Ludwich*.
**233.** "stand" <note>original: "ιστα[σο"</note>: so Manuscripts F, D, U, L, W, and P; *Ludwich* reads "stand" in a different form <note>original: "ἵσταο"</note> following Manuscript H; compare the scholar *Didymus* on the Iliad 10. 291.
**245.** The corrector only crossed through the *e* of the word for *and* <note>original: "τε"</note>, but likely meant to include the *t*. The letter *e* in the word "they fought" <note>original: "εμαχοντο"</note> has been corrected.
**250.** The word "of what sort" <note>original: "οιοι"</note> apparently has a rough breathing mark <note>a mark indicating an 'h' sound</note>, as in Manuscripts F and H; read as "of what sort" <note>original: "οἷοι"</note>.
**251.** The word "but" <note>original: "δ'"</note> after "lest" is unique to this papyrus.
**252.** The letter *a* is a mistake for the word "to him" <note>original: "οἱ"</note>.
**254.** "might fall" <note>original: "πεσησι"</note>: *Ludwich* reads a slightly different spelling <note>original: "πέσῃσιν"</note>.
**255.** "he commanded" <note>original: "εκελευσε"</note>: so Manuscript X; other **manuscripts** and *Ludwich* use the imperfect tense "he was commanding" <note>original: "ἐκέλευεν"</note>.
**257-9.** *Ludwich* prints these lines in small type, noting that the commentator *Eustathius* said "some scholars marked these with an obelus <note>a symbol used by ancient critics to mark suspected or redundant lines</note> as being repetitive" <note>original: "τινὲς ὠβελισαν ὡς ταυτολογοῦντας"</note>.
**264.** "with evils" <note>original: "κακοισι"</note>: other **manuscripts** and *Ludwich* use a slightly longer spelling <note>original: "κακοῖσιν"</note>.
**274.** "[o]f [the]m but" <note>original: "[τω]ν δ"</note>: other **manuscripts** and *Ludwich* omit the "but"; compare line 251.
**275.** "[had thr]own" <note>original: "[βεβλ]ηκειν"</note>: so Manuscript U and the editor Bekker; *Ludwich* and other **manuscripts** read "had thrown" <note>original: "βεβλήκει"</note> in a different form.
**278.** "the tip" <note>original: "ακρην"</note>: so Manuscript U (first hand) and X; compare *Eustathius* who notes "the word for 'nose' is used as both feminine and masculine in the various copies." *Ludwich* and other **manuscripts** (and the scholar *Aristonicus* on the Iliad 16. 599) use the masculine form for "tip" <note>original: "ἄκρον"</note>.
