# 449. **Euripides**, *Andromache*.

->Largest fragment 9 x 7 cm.<-

These fragments of a single column from the beginning of Euripides’ *Andromache* provide what appears to be an early example of the use of the book form <term>codex: an early leaf-based book as opposed to a scroll</term> (compare **459**). The writing—a medium-sized, not very regular capital script <note>uncial</note>, probably from the first half of the third century—is on the back <note>verso</note> of the papyrus. On the front <note>recto</note> in the center of the page are the letters *re* <note>original: "ρη["</note> or *ri* <note>original: "ρι.["</note> with a short horizontal stroke above them and a gap <note>lacuna</note> large enough for another line below. These letters may represent a page number or perhaps a title, such as "Speech of Andromache" <note>original: "ῥῆ[σις ’Ανδρομάχης"</note>. Supposing this manuscript to have been a codex, the size of a page would have been about 28 x 14 cm. The text seems to have been a fairly good one. A version of the text <note>variant</note> not found elsewhere occurs in line 27.

. . . . . . .
**5** [Envied, at least in the time before, was I, Andromach]e <note>original: "[ζηλωτος εν γε τωι πριν Ανδρομαχ]η χρονωι"</note>
**6** n[ow, if there is any other most-unfortunate w]oman <note>original: "ν[ῦν δ ει τις αλλη δυστυχεστατη γ]υνη"</note>
. . . . . . .
**8** who [beholding] my hus[band Hector, by Achille]s <note>original: "ητις ποσ[ιν μεν Εκτορ εξ Αχιλλεω]ς"</note>
**9** dying, saw [my son whom I bore] to my husband <note>original: "θανοντ’ εσ[ειδον παιδα δ ον τικτ]ωι ποσει"</note>
**10** hurled from [the steep towers, Astyanax] <note>original: "ριφεντα π[υργων Αστυανακτ απ ορ]θιων"</note>
**11** since the [soil] of Tro[y was taken by] the Gree[ks] <note>original: "επει το Τροι[ας ειλον] Ελλ[ηνες πεδον"</note>
**12** and I my[self, now a slave], of most f[r]ee <note>original: "αυτη δ[ε δουλη νυν ε]λευθερω[τ]ατων"</note>
**13** houses [having been brought], I arrived in Greece <note>original: "οικων κ[ομισθεις] Ελλαδ’ εισαφεικομην"</note>
**14** to the islander [Neopt]olemus, given as a prize <note>original: "τωι νησιω[τηι Νεοπτ]ολεμωι δωρος γερας"</note>
**15** [as a] choice [gift] from the [Trojan spoi]ls; <note>original: "δοθεισα· λε[ιας Τρωι]κης εξαιρετον"</note>
**16** of Phthia [this land and] the city of Pharsalia <note>original: "Φθειας δε [τησδε και] πολεως Φαρσαλιας"</note>
**17** the borderi[ng lands I inhabit . . . . .] . . the sea-born <note>original: "σύγχορτ[α ναιω . . . . .] . ρ ιν ἡ θαλασσια"</note>

### 450. EURIPIDES, *Medea*.

->4.1 x 5.3 cm.<-

A fragment from the top of a column, containing parts of lines 710-5 of Euripides' *Medea*, written on the *verso* <note>the back side</note> of the papyrus. On the *recto* <note>the front side</note> are two or three mutilated lines of cursive writing, of the second or third century. The literary text on the *verso*, which is in a somewhat rapid, sloping <term>uncial|a style of handwriting using large, rounded capital letters</term> hand, may be assigned to the third century.

> 710 [By] your [knees] and [by your beard, I become your] suppliant
> [Pity,] pity me, [the] unfortunate [woman]
> [And] do [not] see [me] cast out [destitute]
> [But receive] me into [your] land and [as a guest] at your [hearth]
> [Thus] may [your] desire for [children] be [brought to fulfillment] by the gods
> 715 [And] may [you] yourself [die] happy
> .   .   .   .   .   .   .

713. **at the hearth** <note>original: δομοις</note>: the papyrus thus agrees with the manuscript reading; **of the houses** <note>original: δομων</note> Prinz-Wecklein edition.
714-5. These two lines were excised <note>removed from the text by a critic</note> by L. Dindorf and are bracketed by Prinz-Wecklein.
715. **and he himself** <note>original: και αυτ[ος</note>: the reading is fairly secure; read as **and he himself** <note>original: καὐτ[ός</note> <term>crasis|here, the contraction of "and" and "himself" into one word</term>.

<header>THE OXYRHYNCHUS PAPYRI</header>

...medium-sized <term>uncial|a style of writing characterized by rounded, capital letters used in ancient Greek manuscripts</term> hand from the middle or later part of the second century. Punctuation marks are occasionally found: a high point in lines 62 and 87, and a point level with the middle of the preceding letter in lines 50 and 118, though it is doubtful whether these were really intended to represent different lengths of pauses. There are a few corrections, sometimes written in a different hand. As the first papyrus of a portion of the *Gorgias* to be discovered, this fragment is of considerable interest, even though the text is not of the highest quality. There are numerous minor variations from the later <term>MSS|manuscripts</term>, but most of these are clearly errors; see the notes on lines 9, 18, 34, 40, 79, 105, and 116. It is worth noting, however, that in one passage (line 51) the papyrus agrees with the text of Iamblichus and Stobaeus <note>Ancient authors who quoted Plato in their own works</note> against the readings found in the standard manuscripts, and in another (lines 113-115) it resolves a slight difficulty where a textual error had already been suspected. It is also significant for the textual criticism of Plato that in two places (lines 48 and 105) the papyrus supports the *Vindobonensis* <note>A 14th-century manuscript from Vienna</note> against other manuscripts. The theories of various scholars regarding the sections covered by this fragment receive no support from it; even in a passage where the word **wretched** <note>original: ἄθλιοι</note> clearly seems to have dropped out of the text before or after the phrase **the wretched** <note>original: οἱ ἄθλιοι</note>, the papyrus follows the later manuscripts in omitting it; see the note for line 76.

We provide a comparison with the text published by Bekker (1826); however, for the specific readings of the manuscripts and those found in Iamblichus and Stobaeus, we are indebted to Professor J. Burnet, who kindly shared his research on this passage. B refers to the *Clarkianus* <note>An important 9th-century manuscript now in Oxford</note>, T refers to the *Venetus Marcianus* <note>A manuscript from the Library of St. Mark in Venice</note>, and F refers to the *Vindobonensis*.

## 455. PLATO, *Republic III*.

->9 x 6.6 *cm.* PLATE VI.<-

A fragment of the third book of Plato’s *Republic*, page 406, written in a not very regular <term>uncial</term> <note>a style of writing using large, rounded capital letters common in early Greek and Latin manuscripts</note> hand of medium size. On the back <note>original: "verso"</note> are parts of nine lines of a document in late third or fourth century <term>cursive</term> <note>a flowing style of handwriting used for everyday documents like letters or receipts</note>; the writing on the front <note>original: "recto"</note>, which is somewhat late in style, may accordingly be assigned to the middle or latter part of the third century. Changes of speaker are marked by the usual double dots (:). There are practically no variations from the standard text established by Bekker.

->20.5 X 14.3 cm.<-

5. O [men] <note>original: ὦ ἄνδρες (o andres)</note> : omitted by Blass, with the Zurich edition.
8. *from Amphipolis* <note>original: ἐξ Ἀμφιπόλεως (ex Amphipoleos)</note>, the alternative reading here, is found in all the manuscripts.
9. *to you* <note>original: ὑμῖν (hymin)</note> or *to us* <note>original: ἡμῖν (hemin)</note> is read in the manuscripts.
10. *without [but]* <note>original: ἄνευ δέ (aneu de)</note> : *for without* <note>original: ἄνευ γάρ (aneu gar)</note> Blass, with the manuscripts.
16. *the cause* <note>original: τὸ [α]ἴτιον (to aition)</note> : *the cause* <note>original: τἀΐτιον (taition)</note> Blass (using a combined form).
20. At the end of the line *to deliberate* <note>original: βουλεύσα[σθαι] (bouleusasthai)</note> was apparently written for *to deliberate*. The papyrus is rubbed, but there does not seem to be room for the letter 'n'. The manuscripts read *to deliberate/plan* <note>original: βουλεύεσθαι (bouleuesthai)</note>.
21. Considerations of space make it very improbable that the final 'a' of *at the same time* <note>original: ἅμα (hama)</note> was elided, as Blass suggests.
23. The numeral 16 in the margin marks the beginning of a new chapter or section; compare other Grenfell Papyri.
24. *and the* <note>original: καὶ τὰ (kai ta)</note> : omitted by the manuscripts and Blass.
26. *might be at odds* <note>original: στασιαζοις (stasiazois)</note> is a mistake for *might be at odds* <note>original: στασιαζοι (stasiazoi)</note>.
27. What was first written after *all things* <note>original: ἅπαντα (hapanta)</note> apparently makes no word; the scribe perhaps had *sending* <note>original: πέμπων (pempōn)</note> still in his mind.
29. *is* <note>original: ἐστιν (estin)</note> : omitted by Blass, with the manuscripts. The correction *since* <note>original: ἐπειδή (epeidē)</note> is in accordance with the usual reading; some manuscripts read *whenever* <note>original: ἐπειδάν (epeidan)</note>.
*he might have* <note>original: ἔχοι (echoi)</note> : so Blass, with most manuscripts; others read *he has* <note>original: ἔχει (echei)</note>; *he was having* <note>original: εἶχεν (eichen)</note>, which was first written here, is the reading of Wolf and Dindorf.
32. [*under him*]self <note>original: [ὑφ' ἑαυτ]ῷ (hyph' heautō)</note> : so some manuscripts; *of himself* <note>original: [ἑαυτο]ῦ (heautou)</note> (Blass, with the best manuscript) would not fill the gap, and the visible traces suit the 'o' ending better than 'u'.
40. *when* <note>original: ὅτε (hote)</note> : so the manuscripts; Blass omits *when*, following Dindorf.
41. *he took out* <note>original: ἐξεῖλ[ε (exeile)</note> : *he took out* <note>original: ἐξεῖλεν (exeilen)</note> (with the final 'n') Blass.
42. *say* <note>original: λέγε (lege)</note> : omitted by the manuscripts and Blass.
43. *this then* <note>original: [τοῦ]το τοίνυν (touto toinyn)</note> : *this* <note>original: τοῦτ' (tout')</note> Blass, omitting *then* with the manuscripts.
44. *you might be persuaded* <note>original: πεισθῆ[τε (peisthēte)</note> : so some manuscripts; Blass reads a different form of *you might be persuaded* <note>original: πειθῆσθε (peithēsthe)</note> with the primary manuscript.
*and that* <note>original: κἀκεῖνο (kakeino)</note>, which is all that intervenes in the manuscripts between "be persuaded" and "knowing," does not nearly fill the available space.
48-9. The manuscripts vary between the names *Philocrates* and *Iphicrates*, and all have "wherefore."

they say to the Lacedaemonians <note>original: φασὶ πρὸς Λακ.; referring to the Spartans</note>. It would be possible to read *Philo* at the end of line 48, but then the lacuna <note>A gap or missing part in a manuscript.</note> at the beginning of the following line is not satisfactorily filled, and the position of the overwritten *the* <note>original: τ]ον</note> is unaccounted for. Moreover the traces on the papyrus suit *they say* <note>original: φασὶ</note> much better; and we therefore suppose that this word was placed later in the sentence, its loss perhaps being compensated for by the insertion of *the* <note>original: τους</note> before *Lacedaemonians*, and that *Iphicrates son of Ephialtes* <note>original: Ιφικρατην Εφιαλτου; Iphicrates was a famous Athenian general</note> (which is preferable on account of the space to Philocrates) was originally written at the beginning of line 49, *Philocrates the* <note>original: Φιλοκρ. τον</note> being subsequently inserted above the line by the corrector.

53. *at least always* <note>original: γ' αει (g' aei)</note> which is inserted above the line is the reading of the manuscripts, which also omit *to do wrong* <note>original: ἀδικεῖν (adikein)</note> after *they will wish* <note>original: βουλήσονται</note>.
55. *if* <note>original: εαν (ean)</note>: *if* <note>original: ἄν (an)</note> in manuscript B.
56. *this man* <note>original: τουτον</note>: so manuscripts k, r, s, v; *this man* <note>original: τοῦτον (accented)</note> in manuscript B, with other manuscripts. At the end of the line *you might wish* <note>original: βουλησθε</note> seems to have been written for *you will wish* <note>original: βουλησεσθε</note>; there is not room for *you will wish* <note>original: βουλη[σεσ]θ</note>.
57. *what kind of man he would be if he ruled over all* <note>original: τινα αν ει πασης αρξειεν</note>: this is the usual reading; *what kind of man having ruled over all* <note>original: τίν' ἂν πάσης ἄρξας</note> in manuscript B (and manuscript S in the margin).
58. *of men* <note>original: ἀνθρώπων</note> is bracketed by Blass.
60. *gifts* <note>original: δωρεας</note>: *gifts* <note>original: δωρεάς (accented)</note> in manuscript B.
63-4. The words *and a friend* <note>original: και φιλον</note>, which have here been crossed through, are omitted in manuscript S. They are accepted by Blass.

### 463. Xenophon; *Anabasis VI.*

->Width of column 5 *cm.*<-

Part of Xenophon’s *Anabasis* Book VI, chapter vi, sections 9–24, written in narrow and rather short columns; the lower portions of seven columns are preserved. The handwriting is a good and apparently rather early specimen of the square sloping style, and may be assigned to the end of the second or the first half of the third century. The middle point <note>A punctuation mark used in ancient Greek manuscripts.</note> occurs irregularly and the common angular sign is used to fill up short lines. Our comparison is with the edition of Gemoll (Teubner, 1900), supplemented by that of Dindorf (Oxford edition, 1855); for some additional information concerning the readings of manuscript groups D and E, we are indebted to Mr. E. C. Marchant.

For purposes of textual criticism—the study of how ancient texts changed over time—this papyrus is of considerable interest. The manuscripts of the *Anabasis* fall into two well-defined divisions: a small group headed by the Parisinus (C) manuscript, and a more numerous group, generally recognized as inferior to the other but containing readings which all editors accept. The peculiarity of the papyrus lies in the fact that it combines readings characteristic of both groups...

Thus, while agreeing in several cases with the superior family against the inferior, it shows six instances of agreement with the inferior class against the superior where the latter is plainly wrong. The same characteristic of partial coincidence with both groups was traced by Dindorf (Preface to the Oxford edition of 1855, page 8) in the quotations from the *Anabasis* <note>Xenophon's famous account of the "March of the Ten Thousand" Greek mercenaries</note> in Athenaeus. This however is a debatable point and need not be insisted upon. In any case, the papyrus may be taken to represent not unfairly the tradition of the first few centuries of the Christian era; and it becomes very questionable whether modern critics have not carried their preference for one group of manuscripts somewhat too far. Gemoll, for instance, makes it the principle of his recent edition only to have recourse to other evidence where the reading of manuscript C is patently erroneous. This is no doubt a convenient and practical method; but its defects should not be lost sight of.

<meta>This page provides critical commentary on the papyrus fragments of Xenophon’s Anabasis (The Expedition of Cyrus) found on the previous page. It compares the papyrus text to several medieval manuscripts (represented by letters like A, B, C, D, E) to determine which version of the story is most accurate.</meta>

# THE OXYRHYNCHUS PAPYRI

**3–4.** <note>original: τὸ πρᾶγμα ἐδόκει</note> "the matter seemed" is the reading of manuscripts A, B, C, and E (as followed by the editor Gemoll), while the other manuscripts read <note>original: ἐδοκεῖ τὸ πρᾶγμα ἐκεῖνο</note> "that matter seemed." The papyrus thus follows the word order of the latter group, but agrees with the former in omitting the word <note>original: ἐκεῖνο</note> "that."

**5.** <note>original: Ελλησιν</note> "to the Greeks": The manuscripts and Gemoll’s edition use <note>original: Ἕλλησι</note> "to the Greeks" <note>This is a minor grammatical variation in how the word for 'Greeks' is spelled.</note>.

**15.** <note>original: φησίν</note> "he says": this matches manuscript D; the papyrus may of course have had the ungrammatical <note>original: φησὶν</note> found in manuscripts A, B, C, and E, but it is unlikely.

**16.** <note>original: τι</note> "something" or "anything": so found in B, C, E, and Gemoll; manuscript D and the <term>deteriores</term> <note>a Latin term used by scholars to refer to "inferior" or later manuscripts that are usually considered less reliable</note> read <note>original: τινός</note> "of something."

**18.** <note>original: εμαυ[του]</note> "of myself": found in manuscript E and the "inferior" manuscripts, as well as Gemoll; manuscripts A, B, and C read <note>original: ἑαυτοῦ</note> "of himself."

**24–25.** <note>original: ειπεν [Αγασ]ιας</note> "Agasias said": this is the word order found in manuscripts A, B, C, and E; the other manuscripts swap the order of the words.

**30.** <note>original: εκ]δωτε [με</note> "give [me] up": since a single letter after the word "give up" would make an unusually short line, it is probable that the papyrus read <note>original: με</note> "me," matching manuscripts A, B, C, and E. These manuscripts, however, use the spelling <note>original: ἐκδότε</note> (or <note>original: ἔκ δοτέ</note>) for "give up," while the papyrus correctly uses the spelling <note>original: ἐκδῶτέ</note> found in the "inferior" manuscripts. This is a good instance of the <term>eclectic character</term> <note>meaning the text of the papyrus does not strictly follow one family of manuscripts, but has a mix of readings from different sources</note> of this version. Gemoll also uses "give me up."

**35.** <note>original: οτι</note> "that" or "because": so found in manuscripts A, B, C, D, E, F, and H; other manuscripts use <note>original: ὅ</note> "which."

**38.** <note>original: [πολε]μειτε</note> "you make war": so in manuscripts A, B, C, and E; the "inferior" manuscripts use <note>original: πολεμῆτε</note>.

**39.** <note>original: σωζε[σθε</note> "save [yourselves]": the reading found in the "inferior" manuscripts; Gemoll and manuscripts A, B, and C use <note>original: σώζοισθε</note> "may you be saved."

**40.** <note>original: ποι</note> "to where": found as <note>original: ὅποι</note> in manuscripts D, F, H, I, K, T, and Z (and Gemoll); manuscripts A, B, C, and E read <note>original: ὅπου</note> "where," while other manuscripts read <note>original: ὅπῃ</note> "in what way."

**43.** The papyrus certainly agreed with manuscripts A, B, C, D, E, H, I, K, and L in reading <note>original: μοι</note> "to me," which other manuscripts omit.

**47.** <note>original: [κελευ]ουσι</note> "they order": manuscripts A, B, C, and E (and Gemoll) read <note>original: ἐκέλευσε</note> "he ordered"; the other manuscripts read "they order," or in the case of L, "they will order."
<note>original: ειτι</note> "if anything": Gemoll and the "inferior" manuscripts agree; A, B, C, and E read <note>original: εἴ τι</note>.

**50.** <note>original: εαν</note> "if": read as <note>original: ἄν</note> "if."

**52.** <note>original: και</note> "and": so in manuscript D; other manuscripts and Gemoll read <note>original: ἢ καί</note> "or also."

**57–58.** The papyrus has omitted the phrase <note>original: Δέξιππον δὲ οἶδα</note> "But I know Dexippus," which is found in all other manuscripts after the word "being" and is necessary for the sentence to make sense. The error was perhaps due to <term>homoioteleuton</term> <note>a scribe's error where their eye skips from one word to another with a similar ending; here, both words ended in "da" or "ta"</note> of the words "I know" and "being," assisted by the fact that the word "I know" had just appeared. It is noticeable that the omitted words are exactly the length of one line of text in this papyrus. We may then assume that the <term>archetype</term> <note>the original source manuscript from which these copies were made</note> followed the word order "I know chosen," as seen in A, B, C, and E, rather than "chosen I know" as seen in other manuscripts.

**61.** <note>original: ηιτησά[μεθα</note> "we requested": as in manuscripts A, C, and E.

**69–70.** <note>original: ηγες η αλλος τις</note> "you were leading or someone else": manuscript A has a corrupted reading; Gemoll and the "inferior" manuscripts agree with the papyrus's phrasing.

**71.** <note>original: και μη</note> "and not": so again the "inferior" manuscripts and Gemoll; manuscripts A, B, C, and E read <note>original: ἢ καί</note> "or also."

## IV. MISCELLANEOUS LITERARY FRAGMENTS

### 464. Astrological Epigrams.

->25.4 x 23.2 cm. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Late third century.<-

The following series of epigrams is written upon the *verso* <note>the back side of a papyrus sheet</note> of the papyrus, the *recto* <note>the front side</note> of which contains the fragment of a rhetorical treatise in Doric dialect (**410**). They are written in hexameters or elegiacs <note>standard forms of ancient Greek poetry</note> and are of varying length, with the longest preserved not exceeding six lines. Unfortunately, the papyrus is both broken and rubbed, and the difficulties of decipherment are increased by the character of the handwriting—an irregular, sloping <term>semi-uncial</term> <note>a style of script using rounded, simplified letterforms</note> from about the end of the third century—and by the poor quality of the Greek. Thus, only one of the epigrams (lines 12–16) is truly intelligible, and even that first requires some correction. Enough remains, however, to show that the collection, or at least this part of it, was primarily astrological in character; see, for example, lines 5, 13–16, 48, and 58. Prefixed to each epigram is a short heading giving the subject of what follows; the prevailing topic is the family—healthy or unhealthy children (lines 12–23), childlessness, and its opposite (lines 40–50, 57 and following). The literary merit of the composition is small. The several verses are often written continuously, and the lines are irregular in length. Marks of elision <note>symbols indicating a dropped vowel at the end of a word</note> are occasionally inserted, and a stop occurs at the end of line 46.

---

**4.** A letter may be lost before the fragment *om*, but this is unlikely.
**5.** The fragment *knon* is probably for **The Dog-star** <note>original: *Kyōn*, referring to Sirius</note>.
**12.** The word for **one about to live** <note>original: *zēsontos*</note> cannot be read; perhaps it is **about to be alive** <note>original: *zēn mellontos*</note>.
**15.** **Appearing** <note>original: *phailōn*</note>: **The Shining One** <note>original: *Phainōn*, a common name for the planet Saturn</note> was probably the word intended.
**16.** The latter part of the line appears to be corrupt. The fragment *phoi* is probably **he was** <note>original: *ephy*</note>, showing a common vowel swap in ancient Greek. The fragment *tothel* is more difficult; the sense requires something like **to die**, which may be supported by another case where the writer confused the letters 'l' and 'n' in line 15.
**18.** Read **those that rule** <note>original: *epikrateontes*</note>; compare Ptolemy’s *Centiloquium* <note>a collection of 100 astrological aphorisms</note>, which mentions a **ruling star**. The word **they honored** at the end of the line is quite doubtful, as the letter *m* looks too cramped. Moreover, something is wrong with the beginning of line 19, which does not follow the poetic meter.
**21.** The meaning of the horizontal stroke above the final *i* is obscure. It is unlikely that the letter *n* would be represented in this way in the middle of a line.
**26.** **Horus** <note>the Egyptian deity, often associated with specific astrological influences</note>: see line 37, where Horus apparently appears again; but the context is equally unclear.
**31.** **Phainon** <note>The Shining One</note> is very likely a proper name, specifically for the planet **Saturn**.
**38.** The word used for **youth** <note>original: *naiotēti*</note> is a spelling error for the standard Greek word for youth <note>original: *neotēti*</note>.
**50.** **Perceive** <note>original: *noei*</note>: see the note for line 6.
**58.** The letter *s* at the end of **witness** <note>original: *martys*</note> has been corrected from the letter *r*.

THE OXYRHYNCHUS PAPYRI

### 465. ASTROLOGICAL CALENDAR.

->Height 26.5 *cm.*          Late second century.<-

The *recto* <note>The front side of the papyrus, where the fibers run horizontally, usually used first.</note> of this long but imperfectly preserved papyrus contains a list of persons with their ages, written in second century cursive <note>A fast, flowing style of handwriting used for everyday business and letters.</note>. On the *verso* <note>The back side of the papyrus.</note> is an astrological calendar in an uncial <note>A formal style of handwriting using rounded capital letters, often used for literary works.</note> hand which we should also ascribe to the second century rather than to the third. There are parts of nine columns in all, but of these only the first is tolerably complete. We omit the second and ninth, and those parts of the other columns which are too fragmentary to yield any sense.

The scheme of the calendar is as follows. The year is divided into weeks of five days, instead of the more usual seven or ten. Each of these weeks of five days corresponds to the sixth part of one of the signs or constellations of the zodiac. Lines 10–44 refer to Pharmouthi 16–20 <note>Pharmouthi is the eighth month of the ancient Egyptian calendar, roughly April.</note>; the details concerning Pharmouthi 20–25 probably began in Column ii and were continued in one or more columns which may have been lost between Columns ii and iii. Lines 60–98 refer to Pharmouthi 26–30, lines 99–134 to Pachon 1–5 <note>Pachon is the ninth month of the ancient Egyptian calendar, roughly May.</note>. With line 135 begins the account of Pachon 6–10, as is indicated by the remaining letters **Pachon 6 to 10** <note>original: *Pa[chōn s heōs i*</note>; this continues up to line 196. The account of Pachon 11–15 occupies lines 197–212 and perhaps Column viii as well. The same formula is followed in the entries concerning each group of five days. First comes a brief astronomical statement of the relation between the part of the month under consideration and one of the signs or constellations of the zodiac, probably, as Mr. Smyly has suggested (line 11, note), the constellation which was rising just before dawn during that period. Next we have the name of the presiding deity who is sometimes male, sometimes female, and the interpretation of it, generally introduced by the phrase **it signifies, saying that** <note>original: *mēnyei legōn hoti*</note> (e.g. lines 13 and 200). This is succeeded by a detailed description of the **form** <note>original: *typos*</note> of the divinity, who is represented as a statue, partly human, partly animal. Then follows an elaborate account of the omens, signs, portents, and favourable and unfavourable influences, characteristic of the period presided over by the deity in question, which is introduced by the words **it shows, therefore** <note>original: *dēloi oun*</note>, and concludes with a statement of the particular form of **sickness** <note>original: *arrōstēma*</note> peculiar to the period. To this account of the presiding deity is in one place (lines 159 sqq.) added a description of her son, which proceeds on the same lines as that of the goddess herself, and ends with directions for making medical prescriptions (lines 190–6; cf. line 195, note).

The papyrus, which bears distinct marks of its Egyptian origin (cf. the local

references in lines 25 and 222), presents a striking resemblance to an astrological fragment from Egypt now at Munich, recently published with a commentary by Boll (*Archiv*, I. pages 492 and following). The Munich fragment, which is written on vellum <note>A fine parchment made from animal skin, typically more durable and expensive than papyrus.</note> and is several centuries later than the papyrus, also gives a list of deities with an account of the signs, events, and sicknesses associated with them, but is arranged on a somewhat different plan, the deities being connected not with particular groups of days, but with various stars or constellations, which are numbered so as to form a series. Both the Munich and Oxyrhynchus fragments recall in many details the technical phraseology of astrologers which is known from the *Tetrabiblos* <note>A famous four-volume work on astrology by the astronomer Claudius Ptolemy, written in the 2nd century AD.</note> of Ptolemy and the fragments of Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on religion and science in the 3rd century AD.</note>; compare the references given by Boll for the Munich fragment (*Archiv*, I. page 498) with the parallel passages in the papyrus, which supplies more astrological and less astronomical information. Dr. Boll, to whom we are indebted for several valuable suggestions and references, observing that the god of the 11th-15th degrees of Pisces is the second, not, as might be expected, the third (line 199), infers that a distinction is drawn in the papyrus between (1) the superior gods <note>original: θεοί (*theoi*)</note> who preside over each ten days, but more especially over the first five, and of whom the first mentioned in each month seems to be described as the god of the month (line 105), and (2) the inferior divinities called **mighty ones** (line 12) <note>original: κραταιοί (*krataioi*)</note> or **leaders** (line 20, note) <note>original: ἡγούμενοι (*hegoumenoi*)</note> who preside over the 6th-10th, 16th-20th, and 26th-30th days in each month. The superior deities he identifies with the Egyptian <term>decans</term> <note>Groups of stars in ancient Egyptian astronomy that divided the 360-day year into 36 "weeks" of ten days each.</note>, whose fantastic names, known from Egyptian inscriptions, Greek and Roman writers, and magical papyri, have a resemblance to those of the divinities mentioned in the papyrus (lines 13, 160, and 200), especially, as Mr. Smyly has pointed out (line 200, note), in one instance.

With regard to the **mighty ones** <note>original: κραταιοί (*krataioi*)</note> the only source of information hitherto known was a remark by Porphyry in the letter to Anebo (Eusebius, *Preparation for the Gospel* iii. 4), referring to Chaeremon (who wrote in the time of Nero): "For Chaeremon and the others do not suppose there is anything else prior to the visible worlds, placing at the level of first principles the Egyptian gods—none other than the so-called planets and those stars which fill the zodiac, and those which rise alongside them, the divisions into the <term>decans</term>, the horoscopes, and the so-called **mighty leaders** <note>original: κραταιοὺς ἡγεμόνας (*krataious hēgemonas*)</note> whose names are also found in the *Salmenichiaka*, as well as cures for illnesses, risings, settings, and signs of future events." <note>original: Χαιρήμων μὲν γὰρ καὶ οἱ ἄλλοι οὐδ' ἄλλο τι πρὸ τῶν ὁρωμένων κόσμων ἡγοῦνται... μελλόντων σημειώσεις.</note> This description of the *Salmenichiaka*, as Boll remarks, corresponds so clearly with the contents of the papyrus that the latter is to be regarded either as a fragment of the *Salmenichiaka* or as derived from it through an intermediary author. The text contains numerous errors, and the original manuscript <note>original: "archetype"</note> from which the scribe was copying seems to have been in parts illegible or imperfect, for he sometimes leaves blank spaces indicating a gap <note>original: "lacuna"</note>; cf. l. 24, note.

# THE OXYRHYNCHUS PAPYRI

for the following valuable note upon the passage. His explanation of the relation of the zodiac to the Egyptian year is not only new but serves to clear away many difficulties and apparent inconsistencies arising from the various references to it.

> 'It is clear from line 100 that Pisces began with Pachon 1; thus the compiler of the calendar identified the months of the Egyptian year with the signs or with the constellations of the zodiac: Thoth = Cancer, Phaophi = Leo, Athur = Virgo, Choiak = Libra, Tubi = Scorpio, Mecheir = Sagittarius, Phamenoth = Capricorn, Pharmouthi = Aquarius, Pachon = Pisces, Pauni = Aries, Epeiph = Taurus, Mesore = Gemini. At first sight this would seem to indicate a tropical solar year beginning with the summer solstice on Thoth 1, the months being determined by the signs of the zodiac through which the sun was passing. There is, however, very little evidence for an Egyptian year which began at the summer solstice and much for one beginning at the heliacal rising of Sirius <note>The first day Sirius is visible in the dawn sky after a period of invisibility</note>, and in the second century these dates differed by nearly a month, the solstice taking place on June 24 (Julian) and the rising of Sirius on July 20 (Julian). It is therefore much more probable that the year in question was a sidereal year <note>A year measured by the position of the stars rather than the sun's position relative to the equinoxes</note> regulated by the heliacal rising of Sirius (cf. the circumstance that in all the lists Sothis <note>The Egyptian name for the star Sirius</note> was the first decan of Cancer), and that the month in relation to the zodiac was determined not by the sign through which the sun was passing, but by the constellation which was the last to rise before dawn. The decans <term>decans: 36 groups of stars (constellations) used in Ancient Egyptian astronomy to divide the 360-degree zodiacal circle</term> would thus be **rising horoscopically** <note>original: hōroskopountes; meaning they were crossing the eastern horizon at a specific time</note> at the birth of the days over which they presided, and this suggestion is confirmed by the fact that in P. Brit. Mus. 98, 15 the decans are called **the thirty-six bright horoscopes** <note>original: hoi lamproi lz' hōroskopoi</note>. If the calendar refers to a year of this kind the five intercalary days <note>Extra days added to the 360-day calendar to align with the solar year</note> must have been taken into account, as well as a sixth intercalary day every fourth year; but these days were always regarded by the Egyptians as outside the year, and did not interfere with the convenient but inaccurate practice of dividing the ecliptic into 360 degrees, each of which corresponded to one day. Moreover the difficulty is considerably diminished if, as is probable, the decans are regarded not as fractions of the circle of the ecliptic, but as stars or groups of stars rising just before dawn. In this calendar the intercalary days would not have been under the presidency of any of the thirty-six decans or their **powerful ones** <note>original: krataioi; likely referring to the governing deities or planetary powers of the decans</note>, but each of them would have been dedicated to one of the five great gods of the Osirian circle, Osiris, Aroueris, Typhon, Isis and Nephthys, who were said to have been born on those days. It has long been a matter of dispute whether this year, supposing it to have existed, was divided into months bearing the same names as the months of the ordinary **wandering year** <note>original: annus vagus; the Egyptian civil year of 365 days which slowly rotated through the seasons because it lacked a leap year</note>. The papyrus seems to indicate that this was the case; but its late date prevents the evidence from being conclusive, for it may well have been drawn up by someone who was acquainted with the two traditions that the Egyptian year began with Cancer and also that it began with Thoth 1, and who combined his information by identifying the two years.
>
> It is just possible to explain the papyrus from the usual point of view that the month is determined by the sign of the zodiac through which the sun was passing, but this involves very great difficulties. In the *Pseudo-Gemini Calendar* (Wachsmuth's ed. of Lydus, p. 183) we find **"the sun passes through Aquarius in 30 days"** <note>original: ton de hydrochoon diaporeuetai ho hēlios en hēmerais l.</note>. These thirty days correspond to Jan. 23—Feb. 21 on the Julian calendar, and since Pharmouthi 16—20 on the same<gloss>1</gloss>

---

taining 30 degrees of the ecliptic; they are measured from the spring equinox, which is determined by the intersection of the equator and the ecliptic. The position of this point among the stars is not fixed, but slips slowly backward along the ecliptic; this is the **precession of the equinoxes**. With a most unfortunate lack of imagination astronomers since the time of Ptolemy have called these divisions by the same names as the constellations, which often gives rise to great confusion unless we know definitely which is referred to. Thus at present the vernal equinoctial point, though retaining the name "First point of Aries," is not in the constellation of Aries, but owing to the precession has shifted about 30° into the constellation Pisces. The constellations of the zodiac however (apart from variations in size) very nearly coincided with the signs in the second century of our era.'

> The thirty-fourth decan, the first of Pisces. >

He is naked, however having a cloak as if from the shoulders to the back, and in the right hand having a small water-jar, and in the left bringing the forefinger as if to the mouth, and having a crown upon the head. Engrave therefore etc.
>
> The thirty-sixth decan. This one has the name Syro; he is an invisible one called a coiled dragon, having a beard, and on the head a crown. Engrave therefore etc.

The name of the second decan in Pisces according to the papyrus is very likely connected with the name of the first decan according to Hermes, while the description bears great resemblance to that of the third. Similarly the name of the first decan of the papyrus (**<S>aphthun**?; compare the note on line 105) may well be connected with **Soaphi**, the second in Hermes' list.

# 466. Directions for Wrestling.

->13.5 x 18.3 cm. Second century.<-

This papyrus consists of a series of short sections giving directions for performing certain bodily gestures, and in each case ending with the verb **clinch** <note>original: "πλέξον" (plexon), which can mean weave, strike, or entwine</note>. As Mr. Smyly suggests, the purpose of these directions no doubt relates to the different grips in wrestling. That instructions in the <term>palaestra</term> <note>the ancient Greek wrestling school or gymnasium</note> were given in this way is shown by two curious passages: Lucian’s *The Ass*, sections 9-10, and the *Palatine Anthology*, book 12, poem 206. The word **himself** <note>original: "αὐτός"</note> in lines 25 and 30-1 means ‘your opponent,’ and **itself** <note>original: "αὐτή"</note> in line 19 probably refers to the hand.

The papyrus, which we should ascribe to the second century, is written in a good-sized <term>uncial</term> <note>a style of handwriting using large, rounded capital letters</note> hand with a tendency to link the letters together by short horizontal strokes. Parts of three columns are preserved, of which we print the first two, keeping the punctuation of the original.

## 469. Grammatical Rules.

->8.5 x 10.5 *cm.* Early third century.<-

This papyrus, which contained on its front <note>recto</note> official correspondence (in which the form **naubias** <note>a unit of measurement for earthwork or irrigation</note> occurs) written in a fine, almost uncial <note>a style of rounded capital letters</note> hand of the second century, had been cut down so as to form a long narrow strip before the back <note>verso</note> was used for writing a series of grammatical rules in several columns. The third conjugation of the circumflex <note>original: περισπωμένων; verbs with a specific accent on the final syllable</note> verbs is expressed in the present tense in the second <margin>15</margin> and third person through the **oi** <note>original: οι</note> diphthong, such as *chryso* <note>I gild; original: χρυσῶ</note>.

**1.** Over the **ai** <note>original: αι</note> there is a horizontal stroke; similarly in line 3 over the **i** <note>original: ι</note>, and so on. **1-2.** The Papyrus writes *diphthongou* <note>original: διφθογ'γου</note> with a mark; similarly in line 16. **6.** Read as *gelais* <note>you laugh</note> and *boais* <note>you shout</note>. **8.** The word *kata* <note>according to</note> is written over an erasure. **11.** The **el** <note>original: ελ</note> of *egelas* <note>you were laughing</note> was corrected from **g** <note>original: γ</note>. **13.** The **a** of *ka* <note>part of the word "according to"</note> was corrected.

> "The second conjugation of circumflex verbs in the present tense forms the second and third person by the diphthong **ai** <note>original: αι</note>, the **i** <note>original: ι</note> being adscribed <note>written next to the letter but not pronounced</note> but not pronounced together with the **a** <note>original: α</note>, as in *gelo* <note>I laugh</note>, *gelais*, *gelai*. The Aeolians <note>speakers of a specific ancient Greek dialect</note> however pronounce it *gelais* and *boais*. In the imperfect tense, the first person is formed by **on** <note>original: ων</note> and the second and third by **a** <note>original: α</note>, as in *egelon* <note>I was laughing</note>, *egelas*, *egela*.
> The third conjugation of circumflex verbs in the present tense forms the second and third person by the diphthong **oi** <note>original: οι</note>, as in *chryso* <note>I gild</note>, *chrysois*, *chrysoi*."

**5-6.** Compare the writings of Joannes Grammaticus (Meister, *Greek Dialects* volume 1, page 176): "In the second conjugation of circumflex verbs, the **i** <note>original: ι</note> in the second and third person, which is unpronounced in other dialects, is pronounced by them, such as *boais*, *boai*, *gelais*, *gelai*, *nikais*, *nikai* <note>shout, laugh, conquer</note>."

### 470. MATHEMATICAL TREATISE.

->16.7 x 19 *cm.* Third century.<-

A leaf, of which the top is lost, from a papyrus book written in double columns on a page, and containing apparently descriptions of astronomical instruments. The writing is a medium-sized semi-uncial <note>a script between formal capitals and cursive</note> of the third century. The high stop <note>a punctuation mark placed high in the line</note> is found, and a comma-shaped sign is used occasionally for filling up short lines. For the interpretation of this papyrus we are indebted to Mr. J. G. Smyly.

Lines 1-31 are the end of a description of a <term>petteuterion</term> <note>original: πεσσευτήριον; a board used for calculations or gaming</note>, of which instrument Eustathius (in his commentary *on the Odyssey*, page 1397) says: "And that Plato attributes the invention of the pebbles <note>pessi</note> to the Egyptians in the *Phaedrus*, saying they first discovered number and geometry and astronomy, and further, the game of pebbles <note>petteia</note> and dice-play <note>kybeia</note> and indeed letters; and that the commentaries on Plato say that it was not the Greek style of pebble-play meant by Plato, but that of the so-called <term>petteuterion</term>. For a certain small board <note>plinthion</note> is marked out, just as in the game of pebbles, through which the Egyptians work out the movements of the sun and the moon, and even the eclipses <note>original: τὰ ἐλλειπτικὰ</note>." The details are rather obscure; and the difficulties of the technical phraseology...

<header>THE OXYRHYNCHUS PAPYRI</header>

The difficulties of the text are increased by the inaccuracies of the papyrus, which throughout contains frequent errors especially with regard to numbers. These have strokes, either horizontal or slanting, over them, but no distinction is maintained between ordinary numerals and fractions. A mention of a <term>book</term> <note>original: βίβλος</note> occurs in line 24, which probably refers to the books of Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with wisdom, writing, and science</note> (compare the note for that location), perhaps the authority upon which the present treatise is based.

Lines 31 to the end are concerned with the construction of a <term>water-clock</term> <note>original: ὡρολόγιον; a device for measuring time by the flow of water</note> or time-piece, shaped something like a flower-pot. The figure, which in line 35 is called a <term>small mortar</term> <note>original: ὁλμίσκος</note>, appears to be a frustum of a right cone <note>the shape of a cone with the top portion cut off by a plane parallel to the base</note>, of which a vertical central section is a quadrilateral, having two sides horizontal and parallel, and the other two inclined at equal angles to the horizon. In the present case the length of the upper line is 24 <term>fingers</term> <note>original: δάκτυλοι; an ancient unit of measure</note>, that of the parallel lower line or <term>base</term> <note>original: πυθμήν</note> is 12, and the vertical depth is 18. The operations performed in lines 38-46 are:
1. add together the lengths of the top and base,
2. divide by 2,
3. multiply by 3, resulting in a value we will call *x*,
4. find one-third of *x*,
5. find one-fourth of *x*,
6. multiply the result of step 5 by the result of step 4, resulting in a value we will call *y* (for the nature of the last process, see the note for line 45).

The lines lost between lines 46 and 47 probably contained a statement that if a series of horizontal lines were drawn across the original figure at distances of 1 <term>finger</term> <note>original: δάκτυλος</note> from each other, there would be 19 such lines and 18 figures of the same kind as the original (since the height of the figure is 18 <term>fingers</term>). The lengths of the lines will form an arithmetical progression, each line being two-thirds of a <term>finger</term> shorter than the preceding; that is, they diminish <term>by two-thirds</term> <note>original: κατὰ δίμοιρον</note> (line 48). These quadrilateral figures are all subjected to the same process as the original, but the writer displays considerable ingenuity in varying his expressions. Probably the vessel was filled with water, and time was calculated by the nearly uniform descent of the surface caused by the water running through a small hole in the centre of the base.

**3-5.** The numbers are very unintelligible as they stand. If 60 be read for 6 in line 4 and 60 indeed for 64 in line 5, there may be some reference to the sixty dark nights and the sixty bright days in the space of two months. Compare the riddle <note>original: αἴνιγμα</note> of Cleobulus (recorded in Diogenes Laertius, Book 1, 90); it is said in the memoirs of Pamphila that he wrote a riddle like this:

> One is the father, twelve are the children, and to each of these
> belong children twice thirty, of two different aspects;
> some are white to behold, and others again are black;
> though they are immortal, they all waste away.

The answer is "the year" <note>original: ὁ ἐνιαυτός; the father is the year, the 12 children are months, and the 30 white and 30 black children are the days and nights</note>.

**5. the name of the dog:** <note>original: κυνὸς προσηγορίαν</note> there seems to have been a series of summations of consecutive numbers, of which a specimen is given in the following lines: $15 + 16 + 17 + \dots + 30 = 360$. In the Cizensis manuscript of Nicomachus of Gerasa, there is a series of arithmetic problems <note>original: προβλήματα ἀριθμητικά</note> of which the first is headed "of the dog" <note>original: τοῦ κυνός</note>. It asks: "Given any number of consecutive figures starting with unity to find their sum." This problem is generally assigned to Diogenes the Cynic <note>original: Cynicus (κυνός); 'Cynic' literally means 'dog-like'</note>. Perhaps arithmetical progressions went by this name.

**9-15.** "...up to the place in the gaming-board <note>original: πεσσεντήριον</note> which is called *Phoror*, which is the house of Horus, and extends for 30 complete regions <note>original: χῶραι</note>, making up the number of days from conjunction to conjunction." The real period from conjunction to conjunction <note>a new moon</note> is about 29 1/2 days. Without knowing more about the construction and use of the gaming-board it is difficult to say what "they do not move a counter" <note>original: οὐ μεταφέρουσιν ψῆφον</note> in line 17 means. The reason assigned in lines 18–20 is that on the day of conjunction the moon reflects no light from the sun. "House of Horus" <note>original: Ὥρου οἶκος</note> is a translation of *Phoror* which equals the Egyptian *Per-Hor* (house of Horus).

**24. book:** <note>original: βίβλος</note> the reference is very likely to the books of Hermes <note>Thoth</note>; compare Clement of Alexandria (*Miscellanies*, Book 6, 4): "After the singer, the observer of the hours <note>the astrologer</note> comes forward, having in his hand a sun-dial <note>original: ὡρολόγιόν</note> and a palm branch, the symbols of astrology. It is necessary that he always have in his mouth the four books of Hermes which treat of astrology, of which one is about the arrangement of the fixed stars that appear, another about the conjunctions and lightings of the sun and moon, and the remainder about their risings." 45. Line: it makes 18 times 13 1/2 [equals] 243. The last process consists of the multiplication of the two preceding figures (x/3 and x/4), though it is incorrectly performed here as in the corresponding passages of the various **graduations** <note>original: γραμμαί; the lines marked on the clock to indicate hours</note>. ->A geometric diagram of an inverted trapezoid. The longer top horizontal line is labeled A on the left and B on the right. The shorter bottom horizontal line is labeled C on the left and D on the right. A third horizontal line, EF, is drawn parallel to and halfway between the top and bottom lines, with E on the left diagonal side and F on the right.<-

The whole process may be explained in this way.
Let AB and CD be two successive **graduations**. Half of AB + CD is the length of EF drawn halfway between the two lines. This is multiplied by 3 **because of the circumference** (line 43): if the writer took the ratio of the circumference of a circle to its diameter to be 3 instead of π <note>The ancient writer uses a rough approximation of 3 for pi, which was common in some practical ancient traditions</note>, the result will be the circumference of the circle described on EF as diameter. This is divided by 3 (i.e. by π), giving the diameter again. The diameter is then multiplied by a quarter of the circumference (in modern language 2r × 2πr/4 = πr², where r is the radius), giving the area of the circle. If now the writer made the specious but incorrect assumption that the volume of the **frustum of the cone** <note>The section of a cone left after the top is cut off; the shape of the water-clock vessel</note> contained between the planes AB and CD was equal to that of the cylinder of equal height standing on the circle described on EF as diameter, then since the distance between AB and CD is 1 finger he would have regarded his result as the volume expressed in cubic fingers. The error arising from this assumption is comparatively small in the present case. If the instrument in question were a water-clock, a knowledge of this volume would be of great importance.

46. It makes thus 204: the meaning of this number, which corresponds to the revised totals in lines 66, 73, 79 and 85 after a certain deduction has been made from the totals obtained previously (compare line 45, note), is obscure.

48-57. 'The first line is therefore 24 fingers in length; twice this number is 48, subtract 2/3, the remainder is 47 1/3, half of this is 23 2/3, this multiplied by 3 makes 71, 1/3 of this is 23 2/3, and 1/4 is 17 3/4, total 420 1/2.' On the relation of this figure to the original one see introduction.

50. There is not room for "fingers" written out, but the word may have been abbreviated. The process of doubling the upper side and then subtracting 2/3 is equivalent to adding together the lengths of the two opposite sides; compare lines 38-40.

arithmetic in the parallel passages (cf. line 45, note) shows, is a mistake for **multiplied by 3** <note>original: ἐπὶ γ</note>, that is, multiplication by 3. This abnormal use of an arithmetical term is immediately followed by another, **second** <note>original: δεύτερον</note> instead of **two-thirds** <note>original: δίμοιρον</note> for 2/3, and the occurrence of these irregularities is traceable to the incorrect verbal interpretation of the figures **3** <note>original: γ</note> and **2** <note>original: β</note>. **57.** **312** <note>original: τιβ′</note>: read **420 1/12** <note>original: νκιβ′</note>, cf. line 45, note. The confusion of **u** <note>original: υ</note> and **t** <note>original: τ</note> is easy and the space left between **t** <note>original: τ</note> and **i** <note>original: ι</note> points to an omission.

**58—66.** ‘The second figure consists of 23 1/3 **fingers** <note>original: δάκτυλοι; an ancient unit of length</note>, twice this makes 46 2/3, subtract 2/3 for the **contraction** <note>original: συστολή; the narrowing of the vessel's diameter</note>, the remainder is 46, 1/2 is 23, 3 times this is 69, 1/3 of this is 23, 3/4 is 17 1/4, this multiplied by 23 makes 396 3/4, subtract 1/16, the remainder is 396 11/16.’

The process up to line 64 is the same as in the previous figure. The numbers in lines 64—7 are clearly very corrupt, but if **13** <note>original: ιγ</note> in line 64 be corrected to **23** <note>original: κγ</note> the result becomes intelligible. 17 1/4 × 23 gives 396 3/4, that is, **396 1/2 1/4** <note>original: τϟϛβ′ιβ′</note>, which has been corrupted to **315 1/2 1/15** <note>original: τιε (ἥμισυ) ι′ε′</note>; but after subtracting the last fraction the total in line 66 is nearly correct; cf. line 45, note.

**62.** **of the contraction** <note>original: [τῆς] συ[σ]τολῆς</note>: this means that 2/3 **finger** is subtracted because each **line** <note>original: γραμμή; a graduation mark on the clock</note> is both shorter than the one preceding and larger than the one following by 2/3 **finger**.

**69.** About eight lines are lost at the top of the column, which may be restored: **doubling it makes 45 1/3, take away 2/3, remaining is 44 2/3, of which half is 22 1/3, multiplied by 3 is 67, the 1/3 is 22 1/3, the 1/4 is 16 1/2 1/12, multiplied by 22 1/3 becomes 374 1/12. 4 [is] 22, doubling [is] 44, take away 2/3, remaining is 43 2/3, the half is 21 1/2** <note>original Greek: διπλώσον γίνεται μεγ′, ἄφελε β′, λοιπαὶ μδβ′, ὧν τὸ ἥμισυ κβγ′ ἐπὶ γ ξζ′, τὸ γ′ κβγ′, τὸ δ′ ιϛβ′ιβ′, ἐπὶ κβγ′ γίνεται τοδιβ′. δ κβ, διπλώσον μδ, ἄφελε β′, λοιπαὶ μγγ′, τὸ ἥμισυ καβ′</note> and so on.

**70—1.** The figures, as usual, are very corrupt; 16 1/2 × 21 2/3 = 357 1/2, instead of which the text has in line 71 **51 1/2**. The correct figure **352 1/12** <note>original: τνβιβ′</note> seems to have been transferred to line 70 and there to have been corrupted into the meaningless **taish** <note>original: ταισβ</note>. Though the final **2** <note>original: β</note> is not certain, **the equal things** <note>original: τὰ ἴσα</note> cannot be read, even if it made sense. The figures 4 1/12 in line 73 are a continuation of the original error 51 1/2 for 357 1/2; cf. note on line 45.

**73.** At this point the writer becomes more concise; **5** <note>original: ε</note> means the fifth **graduation line** <note>original: γραμμή</note>, which is 21 1/3 **fingers** in length. The usual operations are performed correctly as far as line 77. In line 78 **41** <note>original: μα</note> is an error for **21** <note>original: κα</note>, and 370 2/3 should be 330 2/3; cf. note on line 45.

The number at the end of line 79 should probably be 329 1/12.

**80—1.** ‘The sixth (**graduation line**) is 20 2/3 (**fingers**), which become 40 2/3 when the 2/3 has been subtracted.’ This is a short way of saying that when all the operations up to the subtraction of the 2/3 have been performed, the result is 40 2/3 (20 2/3 × 2 = 41 1/3; 41 1/3 - 2/3 = 40 2/3).

**82.** The superfluous **multiplied by** <note>original: ἐπὶ</note> before **20 1/3** <note>original: κγ′</note> is obviously due to the occurrence of **multiplied by 23** in the next line.

**84.** 15 1/2 × 20 2/3 = 310 1/12, for which the text has either 310 2/3 or 300 1/12; cf. line 45, note.

**85.** The seventh **graduation line** is 20 **fingers** long. **24** <note>original: κδ</note> is a corruption of **20** <note>original: κ</note> followed by **doubling** <note>original: διπλώσαν</note> or **having been doubled** <note>original: διπλασιασθέντος</note>.

**87.** **15** <note>original: ιε</note> is an error for **19** <note>original: ιθ</note>.

471. OFFICIAL

# V. SECOND CENTURY DOCUMENTS

## (a) OFFICIAL.

### 471. SPEECH OF AN ADVOCATE.

->30.5 x 46.5 cm. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Second century.<-

**THIS** long papyrus, written in a semi-uncial <note>a handwriting style using rounded, almost lowercase-like forms rather than formal block capitals</note> hand and elaborately punctuated like a literary work, contains part of a speech of an advocate directed against a person whose name is apparently Maximus. The precise point at issue is not clear. There are accusations concerning money-lending, and some question connected with the holding of the office of gymnasiarch <note>a high-ranking local official who oversaw the gymnasium and the education of young citizens</note> arises, but the greater part of the speech consists of an outspoken denunciation of the relations of Maximus to a certain boy. That Maximus was or had been a very high official is shown by several passages; see the references in line 54 to the regal state assumed by him, in lines 66-72 to the crowd of clients, in lines 95-7 to petitions made to him and his power to confiscate property, and in lines 124-30 to his journeys throughout Egypt. These allusions suit no one so well as the prefect <note>the Roman governor</note> himself, and the view that Maximus had been prefect of Egypt is supported by line 22, where **prefecture** <note>original: ε[π]αρχειας</note> is the most probable reading. On this hypothesis the **lord** <note>original: κύριος; referring to the sovereign</note> whose **fortune** <note>original: τύχη; the guiding spirit or "genius" of the ruler</note> is appealed to by witnesses in line 65 and before whom this speech was delivered, was more probably the reigning emperor (compare line 32, where **lord** <note>original: κύριος</note> means the emperor) than the prefect in office. Whether however this speech was really delivered or is a composition in the style for instance of document **33** may be doubted. It is difficult to imagine the circumstances under which such violent accusations would actually be made, and unfortunately the identity of Maximus is far from clear. The only second century prefect known to have borne that name is Vibius Maximus (A.D. 103-7), but the papyrus probably belongs to the age of Hadrian or the Antonines <note>the Roman dynasties ruling between 117 and 192 AD</note>.

Out of six columns the first (not printed) has only the ends of a few lines, while the sixth has lost the ends of lines, and the second and fifth are disfigured by considerable gaps. Two kinds of stops, the high and low point, are employed and one or two accents and breathings occur. The papyrus has been subjected to much revision, additions to or recastings of the main text being appended at the bottom of columns two through five by a different hand. The position at

2. The critical mark opposite this line perhaps indicates that the note at the bottom of the column was to be inserted at this point. 2–110. ‘I will add a fact, my lord, which will, I expect, excite your wonder and disbelief until we read the documents. The orator’s client was a woman called Hermione, against whom various charges of attempted poisoning, and fraud in connexion with a supposed mortgage, had been brought by a man whose name does not appear here, but was Sarapion, if, as is almost certain, **486** is concerned with the same dispute. An <term>epistrategus</term> <note>original: ἐπιστράτηγος; a high-ranking regional administrator in Roman Egypt who handled judicial and financial matters</note> is mentioned in the first column, and it is probable that the proceedings took place about A.D. 130 before Claudius Quintianus at the trial mentioned in **486**. 8 and 26, from which passages we learn that the <term>epistrategus</term> referred the case to the <term>praefect</term> <note>original: ἔπαρχος (eparchos); the Roman governor of Egypt, the highest judicial authority in the province</note>. The handwriting of the papyrus is very like that of the Petition of Dionysia (**237**), written in the reign of Commodus, and this copy of the speech may have been made some years after it was delivered.

### Col. ii.

...herself. For indeed he had gone out from his own house saying he had been poisoned, and when leaving Hermione's house he neither said to anyone that he felt anything, nor had he any suspicion at all; 
<margin>5</margin> but from the house of himself and of his son, who was to be the heir, he came forth saying he had been poisoned. Now, he had reasons for administering the poison to himself, which many others also have who prefer death to life, for he was being ruined by creditors and was destitute. But if indeed someone did plot against him, the son was the most suitable <note>in the sense of 'most likely' or 'best placed' to commit the crime</note> suspect. But why he brought the charge against this woman is clear. 
<margin>10</margin> For other things also might have been neglected during the time of his illness <note>original: προνοίας (pronoias); can mean 'forethought' or 'care/maintenance', here likely referring to the period of his alleged poisoning or medical care</note>, but the matter shows that he was also jealous of her because she did not acknowledge him <note>original: μὴ ἐπισταμένην (mē epistamenēn); literally 'not knowing' or 'not recognizing', suggesting she did not accept the relationship</note>, and he called himself her husband, but not being deemed worthy of this title by her, he both suffered the pains of love and did not want her to outlive him. <meta>This page continues the legal defense of Hermione against charges of poisoning and financial fraud. THE OXYRHYNCHUS PAPYRI

For it was from his own house that he emerged, claiming that he had been poisoned <note>original: πεφαρμακῶσθαι (pepharmakoshtai); to have been drugged or poisoned</note>. When he left Hermione's house, he did not tell anyone that he noticed anything unusual, nor did he show the slightest suspicion. Yet, it was from the house belonging to himself, his son, and his future heir that he came forth saying he had been poisoned. 

Indeed, he had reasons to administer poison to himself—reasons many others have shared when preferring death to life; he was ruined by creditors and was at his wit's end. But if anyone truly plotted against him, his son is the most likely suspect. Why he brought this accusation is now clear. He may have had other troubles during his time as a steward <note>original: προνοητής (pronoetes); an estate manager or financial administrator</note>, but the case reveals that he was jealous of her without her knowledge. He even called himself her husband, but since she never granted him that title, he suffered the pangs of a rejected lover and did not wish for her to outlive him.

If they claim that the slave Smaragdus has disappeared because he was accused of stealing a mortgage <note>original: ὑποθήκη (hypotheke); a legal document pledging property as security for a debt</note>, he is merely asserting that a mortgage existed so that he can claim it was stolen. It is impossible to steal something that never existed and could not exist. No such mortgage could have been drawn up, because neither the buyer [Hermione] nor the defendant knew how to write, nor does a stranger issue a deed of mortgage when another woman is already registered as the mortgagee. From whom could he claim to have received this mortgage? From whichever source he might claim, it would be invalid. Furthermore, if a slave runs away, this is not a valid argument against the master's character.

Moreover, the division of property helps prove that no such mortgage ever existed. Typically, those registered as mortgagees only have their names entered into the deeds and do not actually claim the property. However, the buyer here has clearly claimed the property and has enjoyed its fruits <note>the "fruits" refer to the income or harvests generated by the land</note> ever since she purchased it. Meanwhile, since the seller sold it, he has no longer enjoyed it, except when managing the mother's property as a steward and attacking my clients. 

If they argue that a joint agreement was made between the daughter and Hermione for 150 jars <note>original: κεραμίων (keramia); standard pottery vessels used to measure wine or oil</note> to be produced from these vineyards which Dionysia purchased, we assert that this has nothing to do with the plaintiff. If a daughter makes an agreement with her mother, it does not provide an excuse for these slanders <note>original: συκοφαντίαν (sycophantian); in this context, a malicious or false legal prosecution</note>. That agreement did not even happen at the same time, but nearly a whole year later. Furthermore, providing 150 jars is insufficient security for 4 talents <term>talent: a very large unit of currency; 4 talents represented a massive sum of money in the Roman era</term>, as that amount only covers the interest on a single talent. 

Again, if security had been given to the supposed seller, would the daughter have pledged herself to the State by another deed when she risked losing the property whenever he chose? The facts regarding the provision are as follows: Hermione had three children: Aphro... and Dionysia... Dionysia entreated her mother not to leave her with only what had already been spent, but to give her something since she relied on a single resource. Consequently, Hermione paid her one and a half talents. But so that her mother would not be deprived of that capital during her lifetime, Dionysia pays this annual provision in place of interest.

### 473. DECREE IN HONOUR OF A GYMNASIARCH.

->21.4 X 29.6 cm.  A.D. 138–160.<-

This document is a resolution dated to the reign of Emperor Antoninus Pius. It was issued by the magistrates and the people of Oxyrhynchus, alongside the resident Roman and Alexandrian citizens, to honor a <term>gymnasiarch|a prestigious civic official responsible for the gymnasium and the funding of public games</term>. The honor includes the setting up of a statue, a full-length portrait, and three honorary shields. Because the first 30 to 40 letters of each line are missing, we do not know the name of this individual. The list of his public services mentions his "unstinted provision of unguents" <note>oils used by citizens in the public gymnasium</note>, his contributions to theatrical displays, and his restoration of the public baths and "greater thermal baths" <note>large, heated bath complexes</note>. This resembles other historical letters regarding the heavy financial burdens taken on by gymnasiarchs. 
The handwriting is a large, handsome formal style, though the scribe appears to have made several mistakes.

1 <margin>1</margin> [In the year of Emperor Caesar] Titus Aelius Hadrianus [A]nto-
[n]inus Augustus Pius, in the month of Kaisareios, on the twenty-seventh day,
2 <margin>2</margin> [it was resolved by the magistrates of the most illustrious city of the Oxyrhynch]ites and the people, [and the] Romans and Alexandrians residing here: since 
3 <margin>3</margin> [having given himself] to a voluntary <term>gymnasiarchy|the office of managing and funding the gymnasium</term>... he showed himself even more eager in the unstinted supply of unguents...

### 474. CIRCULAR TO OFFICIALS.

->34.6 x 18.5 cm. A.D. 184?<-

This papyrus contains copies of three letters written by a high-ranking official, **Plautius Italus**, to various subordinates. The first (lines 1-8) is addressed to the **district governors** <note>original: "strategi"</note> and the **royal scribes** <note>original: "basilico-grammateis", the chief financial and record-keeping officers of a district</note> of several **districts** <note>original: "nomes"</note>, which were apparently listed in lines 8-9. This letter directs their attention to the following letter (lines 10-30) from Italus to the governor of the **Tanite district**, in which he reprimands him and the royal scribe for **peculations** <note>the embezzlement or theft of public funds</note>. This is followed (lines 31-41) by another letter to the same set of officials as the first, forbidding in more general and forceful terms the practice of diverting **imperial revenues** <note>tax money intended for the Emperor's treasury</note> to pay the **salaries** of the principal revenue officers of the districts. While the third letter is complete, a large portion of the first two is impossible to read due to staining on the papyrus. The circulars were issued on December 16.

### 474. OFFICIAL 157

This document dates to the 25th year of an unnamed emperor, who must however be Commodus or Caracalla, since none of the others reigned so long. The handwriting, which suggests the second century rather than the third, is in favor of the earlier date. What position Plautius Italus held is not certain. If the reigning emperor was Commodus, it is possible that he was the prefect in A.D. 184, but this is not very likely, since Longaeus Rufus was prefect in May 185 (**237.** vi. 15, compare P. Amh. 107), and Veturius Macrinus in July 181 (De Ricci, *Proceedings of the Society of Biblical Archaeology* 1902, p. 67) and *perhaps* in May 183 (B. G. U. 847). December 16, 216, falls in the prefecture of Valerius Datus (De Ricci, [in the place cited] <note>original: "l. c." (loco citato)</note> p. 100). It is more probable that Plautius Italus was a **Chief Administrator** <note>original: "διοικητής" (dioiketes), a high-ranking financial officer in Roman Egypt</note> or perhaps the **Manager of the Special Account** <note>original: "ἴδιος λόγος" (idios logos), the official responsible for the Emperor's private revenues and ownerless property</note>. Since his letters are addressed to officials of **nomes** <note>original: "nomoi", the administrative districts of Egypt</note> in the Delta as well as of, presumably, the Oxyrhynchite nome, it is hardly possible that he was a **Regional Governor** <note>original: "epistrategus", a high official overseeing several nomes</note>.

"That person" in line 22 and "his" in line 24 refer presumably to the royal scribe, who is also the subject of "withheld." After "to you" in line 22, three or four letters may be lost. **31-41.** “(Copy) of another (letter). Plautius Italus to the district governors and royal scribes of the hereinafter-mentioned administrative districts, greeting. On examining the accounts of the money revenue I discovered that certain of the district governors and royal scribes had paid themselves salaries for some period on their own responsibility, in defiance rather than obedience to the proclamations. Thereupon I sent them a suitable admonition, and I now make this second order applying to all that the imperial moneys are not to be touched without leave.”

**41.** **Imperial funds** <note>original: "κυριακοῦ χρήματος" (kyriakou chrematos)</note>: that is, the revenue of the **Imperial Account** <note>original: "κυριακὸς λόγος" (kyriakos logos)</note>, on which see P. Meyer in *Festschrift for O. Hirschfeld* page 139. His view that the **Imperial Account** is the same as the **Treasury** <note>original: "fiscus (διοίκησις)"</note> as opposed to the **Special Account** <note>original: "ἴδιος λόγος" (idios logos)</note> is true in most instances, but a notable exception occurs in *P. Catt. v. 17* (compare *Archiv*, III. 1), where the **ownerless property** <note>original: "bona vacantia"</note> of a soldier who had died without heirs are appropriated by the manager of the special account, Julianus, for the **Imperial Account**.

### 478. SELECTION OF BOYS <note>original: "ἐπίκρισις" (epikrisis). An official process to determine eligibility for the privileged class of residents who paid a reduced poll-tax.</note>

->26 x 6.1 cm. A.D. 132.<-

An application addressed, as usual at Oxyrhynchus in such cases, to the <term>registrars of the archives</term> <note>original: "βιβλιοφύλακες" (bibliophylakes)</note>, by Dionysous, a freedwoman, requesting that her son, who had reached the age of 13, might be placed on the list of privileged persons who paid a poll-tax of only 12 <term>drachmae</term> <note>original: "δραχμαί". The standard silver currency of Roman Egypt.</note>, and stating the grounds of the claim. The evidence of this papyrus was utilized by us in a discussion of the whole question of *status examination* <note>original: "ἐπίκρισις"</note> in P. Oxy. II. pages 217 and following, to which the reader is referred. Since the publication of that volume the subject has been treated at length by P. Meyer (*Military System of the Ptolemies and Romans*, pages 109 and following), who however had not the Oxyrhynchus documents before him, and could only refer to them in an appendix (*work cited* pages 219 and following), and by Wessely (*Proceedings of the Academy of Sciences in Vienna*, Volume CXLII. ix), who gives an elaborate recapitulation of the evidence in the light of the Oxyrhynchus papyri. A formal inquiry into an individual's status, usually for tax or military purposes.</note> is ‘examination,’ ‘decision,’ requires no special demonstration, and the term of course is, as we remarked (P. Oxy. II. p. 220), a relative one. But in connexion with the <term>poll-tax</term> <note>original: "laographia." A head tax imposed by the Roman administration on adult males; certain social classes were eligible for reduced rates.</note> *examination* and its cognates acquired a technical signification, being used of the process by which persons of a certain status were partially or wholly relieved of liability to that impost. P. Meyer however goes much too far in asserting that <term>having been examined</term> <note>original: "ἐπικεκριμένος" (epikekrimenos). A status designation indicating one has passed the official screening.</note> implies total exemption from the poll-tax, a view which he somewhat perversely tries to maintain (*op. cit.* p. 231) in the face of our statement of the evidence derived from the present text. It is abundantly clear from lines 9–10 and 31 below, that persons who enjoyed the privilege of paying less than the regular amount of the tax went through a process of *examination*, and were just as much *examined* as those who were entirely exempt.

"To Hadrion and Zoïlus, keepers of the archives, from Dionysous, freedwoman of Dionysia daughter of Dionysius also called Chresimus son of Dionysius, of Oxyrhynchus, with her guardian Eudaemon son of Menoetes, of the same city. A technical term for a verified or consistent tax register.</note> of the 13th year of Hadrianus Caesar the lord at the said quarter, and is now dead, and that the father of my aforesaid patroness Dionysia <gloss>he does not agree</gloss>, Dionysius also called Chresimus son of Dionysius, of the same city, was similarly rated at 12 drachmae by the selection of the 7th year of the deified Trajan in the Lycians' Camp quarter, and died at an advanced age; and I swear by the Emperor Caesar Trajanus Hadrianus Augustus that the foregoing statement is correct. The 17th year of the Emperor Caesar Trajanus Hadrianus Augustus, Tubi 13.
