**10-2.** It is noticeable that the further qualification specified in the parallel passage of **258**, "seven (?) years in the same quarter" <note>original: "ἐ(π)τὰ (?) [ἔ]τη ἐπὶ τοῦ αὐτοῦ ἀμφόδου"</note>, is here omitted. But not improbably the interlinear notes on lines 15 and 28 have some reference to such a restriction.

**15.** The addition added below this line by a different hand is a note by an official remarking some inconsistency between this statement of the <term>district</term> <note>original: "amphodon." A neighborhood or administrative quarter of the city.</note> in which Ptollis lived and his own assertions. The question had an important bearing on the consideration of the claims for exemption, for it appears from **258. 9** that a certain permanence of residence was required; compare the previous note. A similar interlinear insertion occurs in line 28 in connection with the evidence on the mother's side.

**22. Through a uniform poll-tax list:** <note>original: "di' homologou laographias."</note> the meaning of this is obscure. So far as the present passage goes, <term>uniform</term> <note>original: "homologos."</note> might here have its ordinary sense of "corresponding," the meaning being that the poll-tax list of the year referred to corresponded with the statement in the text that the father of Ptollis was a <term>twelve-drachmae metropolitan</term> <note>original: "metropolites dodekadrachmos." A citizen of the metropolis eligible for the reduced tax rate.</note>. But this interpretation is not satisfactory in another case of the use of the phrase in *B. G. U. 618. 13*: "from (?) the uniform poll-tax list, 4 men" <note>original: "ἐκ (?) μὲν ὁμολ(όγου) λαογρ(αφίας) ἄνδρες δ"</note>—for so no doubt the passage should be read on the analogy of the present papyrus—which occurs in a list of individuals who were responsible for work on the embankments. The term <term>uniform</term> is also applied to persons, when it perhaps has a technical signification:—e.g. *B. G. U. 560. 20*: "uniform men engaged in farming," *P. Brit. Mus. 259. 190-1*: "to the same... of whom 600 (?) are uniform men," *P. Brit. Mus. 260. 142-3*: "and in the 1st year of Vespasian from among the strangers... together with their fathers included among the uniform residents," and "being in the uniform poll-tax" in a Vienna papyrus described by Wessely. Wilcken, who quotes the *Theodosian Code* (11. 24. 6. § 3): "those who, having deserted the villages to which they were registered and who are called 'uniform' <note>original: "homologi"</note> by native custom, have moved to other villages or to other masters" <note>original: "qui vicis quibus adscripti sunt derelictis et qui homologi more gentilicio nuncupantur ad alios seu vicos seu dominos transierunt"</note>, supposes that <term>uniform residents</term> were a particular class of cultivators; but though that explanation would suit *B. G. U. 560. 20* it clearly cannot be brought into harmony with the passages in which "uniform" is connected with the <term>poll-tax</term> <note>original: "laographia."</note>. There is more to be said for Wessely's view, who supposes these people to be domiciled strangers subjected to the poll-tax, and refers in support of his theory to—

This explanation would well accord with British Museum Papyrus 260. 142-3 and the Vienna papyrus, in which Jews are concerned. But how is it to be applied to the <term>consistent poll-tax register</term> <note>original: "homologos laographia"</note> here, in which <term>metropolis residents rated at twelve drachmae</term> <note>original: "metropolitai dodekadrachmoi." These were privileged citizens in district capitals who paid a reduced tax rate compared to rural villagers.</note> figure? A better interpretation of <term>consistent</term> <note>original: "homologos"</note> in all these passages has been suggested to us by Mr. Smyly, who would translate it "assessed at the same rate," i.e., in the present case at 12 drachmae. This explanation would account for the variations in the use of the term, the meaning of which is relative to the context in each instance.

Lines 26 and following: This passage combines with B. G. U. 324 to show that slaves were placed on the same footing with regard to liability to the poll-tax as their masters; and we here learn that liberated slaves at least could even transmit their privileges to their children.

Line 28: For the insertion above the line see the note on line 15.

Line 35: <term>among the over-age</term> <note>original: "en hyperetesin"</note>: i.e., above the age of 60, when men ceased to be liable to the poll-tax. The word <term>over-age</term> <note>original: "hyperetes"</note> appears to be not otherwise known.

3. <term>Priest of Zeus and Hera and . . .</term> : It is very likely these deities are a Greek-style rendering of the triad commonly worshipped at Oxyrhynchus: Sarapis, Isis, and Thoëris. Sarapis and Zeus were often identified together, and Isis might well be identified with Hera, whose specific worship is rarely mentioned in Egypt. Thoëris was perhaps identified here with Athena.

<meta>This page continues the scholarly commentary on document 483, specifically discussing the historical naming conventions of military allotments and the significance of "Imperial Days" in the Egyptian calendar. It then begins a new section of petitions, starting with document 484.</meta>

5. **Of Zenodorus... allotment <note>original: "klērou"</note>**: compare **47**. 18. Our contention (P. Oxy. I. p. 102) that the persons who gave their names to **allotments** <note>original: "klēroi," land grants originally given to soldier-settlers</note> were the original grantees has recently been disputed by P. Meyer (*Military Affairs* <note>original: "Heerwesen"</note>, p. 107), who wishes to make them the owners immediately preceding the actual ones. This view—that for example **from the allotment of Menoetius** (**45**. 10) means no more than **the property formerly belonging to Menoetius** <note>original: "tas proteron Menoitiou"</note>—is not only very unlikely in itself and ignores the preposition **from** <note>original: "ek"</note> which indicates that the **Menoetius allotment** was larger than the area in question, but it altogether fails to account for the following facts: (1) the uniformly Greek character of the names, (2) the absence of women, (3) the frequent insertion of nationalities (e.g., **Demetrius of Miletus 270**. 17, **...the Lydian 265**. 40; cf. **506**. 24 **Ptolemy the Persian, of the cavalry allotment** <note>original: "Ptolemaiou Persou hippikou klērou"</note>), (4) the common occurrence of the same **allotments**, e.g. that of Drimacus (**250, 265, 344**). On the other hand, all these facts point to the Ptolemaic origin of the persons who give their names to **allotments**, which, seeing that the Ptolemaic organization of <term>catoecic land</term> <note>land reserved for "katoikoi," or privileged Greek military settlers</note> still survived to some extent (cf. **482**. 18, note), is in no way surprising.

30. **Phamenoth, on the Imperial Day <note>original: "Sevastē"</note>**: probably the 29th; cf. line 37, which was most likely written on the same day, and **289**. i. 2. On **Imperial Days** <note>original: "hēmerai Sevastai," monthly days of celebration dedicated to the Roman Emperor</note> see P. Oxy. II. p. 284.

### [Summary Translation]
To Apolinarius, <term>strategus</term> <note>a high-ranking local administrative official</note>, from Pausiris son of Petsiris, from the village of Sephtha, living at Nemera. Since Didymus son of Amois has delivered to me an accusation charging me with defrauding his son Didymus in connection with some wheat, I request that a copy of this memorandum be served upon his aforesaid son Didymus in order that he may have a written notice and appear wherever his highness the <term>praefect</term> <note>the Roman governor</note> Avidius Heliodorus holds his auspicious court for the <term>nome</term> or administers justice, and that he may attend until the trial takes place so that the facts may be proved. The 22nd year of the Emperor Caesar Trajanus Hadrianus Augustus, <term>Mecheir</term> 3. I, Pausiris son of Petsiris, have presented this memorandum.

---

**484.** The earliest mention of Avidius Heliodorus as <term>praefect</term> has previously been found in records from March 139 AD, and the previous year has generally been assigned to Valerius Eudaemon, who was <term>praefect</term> about the end of Hadrian’s reign or early in that of Antoninus. Document **484** now shows that Avidius Heliodorus was already <term>praefect</term> on January 28, 138 AD. Consequently, it is no longer possible to suppose that the date in document **237**, column 7, line 7—recorded as <note>original: "(etous) kb theou Adrianou Mecheir k," meaning "Year 22 of the deified Hadrian, Mecheir 20" (February 14, 138 AD)</note>—refers to a proclamation by Eudaemon. 

This being the case, it becomes practically certain that the date in document **237**, column 8, line 18—recorded as <note>original: "(etous) e theou Ailiou Antōninou Epeiph kd," meaning "Year 5 of the deified Aelius Antoninus, Epeiph 24"</note>—does indeed refer to the proclamation of Eudaemon, who was therefore <term>praefect</term> on July 18, 142 AD. This conclusion creates a conflict with another record (B. G. U. 113. 9), where, if the editor’s reading is correct, Avidius Heliodorus is still listed as <term>praefect</term> in the 6th year, <term>Pachon</term> 21 (May 16, 143 AD). However, the reading of the specific number in that document is doubtful; if the number "3" is substituted for "6," the whole difficulty is removed. Valerius Eudaemon would then take his place between Avidius Heliodorus (138–141 AD) and Valerius Proculus (145–147 AD).

## 485. NOTIFICATION TO THE STRATEGUS.

30.5 x 12 *cm.*                                     A.D. 178.

Copy of a notification addressed to the <term>strategus</term> <note>a high-ranking local administrative official</note> by Serenus, a freedman <note>a formerly enslaved person who has been granted legal freedom</note>, of the fact that he had brought before the <term>archidicastes</term> <note>a high-ranking judicial official based in Alexandria</note> a claim for the recovery of a debt, and that official had authorized the strategus to forward this claim, of which a copy is added, to the alleged debtor—a proceeding equivalent to a summons to appear for the trial of the case. Appended at the foot are the authorization of the strategus that the claim should be duly forwarded as desired, and a corresponding acknowledgement of receipt on the part of the defendant. Similar documents are B. G. U. 578 and 614, the legal aspects of which have been discussed by Mitteis (*Hermes*, xxxii. pp. 644 sqq.), and Gradenwitz (*Introduction to Papyrus Study*, pp. 35 sqq.), and especially 888, the text of which admits of several improvements (see the notes below). The dispute in the present instance was concerned with a loan of 900 <term>drachmae</term> <note>the standard silver currency of the time</note> on the security of a female slave from Serenus to Sarapias, a woman living at Psobthis which we learn from this papyrus was the name of the metropolis <note>administrative capital</note> of the Small Oasis <note>the modern Bahariya Oasis</note>. Cf. **592**.

### 485. PETITIONS

From Serenus, freedman of Apollonianus Sarapion, of the city of Oxyrhynchus. I lent, according to a public contract drawn up through the record-office <note>original: "mnēmoneion", a local archive where legal documents were registered</note> in the same city of Oxyrhynchus in the past 18th year, on the 11th of the month Sebastos <note>the first month of the Egyptian year, roughly September</note>, to Sarapias, daughter of Podon, son of Horus, her mother being Thaesis, from Psobthis of the Small Oasis, the principal sum of nine hundred silver <term>drachmae</term> <note>the standard silver currency of Roman Egypt</note> at the interest of one drachma for each <term>mina</term> <note>a unit of value equal to 100 drachmae; this rate equals 12% annual interest</note> per month. The principal was due on the 30th of the month Kaisareios <note>the final month of the year, roughly August</note> of the same past 18th year. It was stated that if she did not repay it by the deadline, the possession and ownership of the slave belonging to her, also named Sarapias—then about 25 years old—should remain with me and those who succeed me, in place of the principal and any interest that might not be repaid. This is according to the other terms the loan contains and the provisions recorded therein for my security regarding the escape or death of the slave.

Since the deadline has passed and the repayment to me has not occurred, I request you to order a copy of this to be given to the <term>strategus</term> <note>the chief administrative and police official of the district</note> of the Oxyrhynchite nome to serve to Sarapias,
->if she survives; if not, to her<-
adult heirs, or if they are minors, to their legal guardians whose names shall be declared on the spot, so that they may know and make the repayment to me, or else know that I shall employ the appropriate legal measures for taking possession <note>original: "embadeia", a legal process for a creditor to enter and seize mortgaged property</note> as is fitting.

Year 19 of Aurelius Antoninus and Commodus the lords Augusti, Phaophi [day unknown]... the strategus having ordered the delivery [of this notice] to Sarapias as is fitting.

Year 19 of the Emperors Caesars Marcus Aurelius Antoninus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus Augusti, Armeniacus, Medicus, Parthicus, Germanicus, Sarmaticus, Maximus <note>these are victory titles celebrating the emperors' military successes</note>, Hathyr 19.

### 485. PETITIONS

...and if they are minors, to their lawful guardians, whose names will be ascertained on the spot, in order that they may be informed and may make repayment to me or else may know that I shall take the proper proceedings to which I am entitled for entry upon possession <note>original: "embadeia", a legal term for a creditor taking possession of mortgaged property</note>, as is right. (Signed) 'I, Sarapias, daughter of Podon, received a copy of this petition.' Date. 'I, Musaeus also called Pausirion, son of . . ., am registered as her guardian having been (appointed) by the <term>strategus</term>, and wrote for her as she was illiterate. I, Syrion, assistant, served the petition upon Sarapias, as aforesaid.' Date.

3. **I did not provide, etc.** <note>original: "ou eporisa k.t.l."</note> : in B. G. U. 578 and 614 <note>B.G.U. refers to the Berlin Greek Papyri collection</note> the formula used is **I did not bring from the account of publication** <note>original: "ou parekomisa apo dialogēs dēmosiōseōs"</note>. In connection with "registration" <note>original: "katalogi(u)"</note> here it may be noted that in B. G. U. 614 the copy of the petition to the <term>archidicastes</term> <note>the chief judge of Roman Egypt, based in Alexandria</note> is headed **record of the registry** <note>original: "graphē katalogeiou"</note>, indicating the office where it was originally drawn up. In the present case the reply of the <term>archidicastes</term> to the petitioner seems to have been issued through the same medium.

7. The letter of the <term>archidicastes</term> is in B. G. U. 578 signed, as here, by two persons whose titles are not given; cf. B. G. U. 888. 4, where the corresponding signatory is the **registrar of the market** <note>original: "nomographos agoras"</note>.

28. **not having occurred** <note>original: "mē genomenēs"</note> : so no doubt B. G. U. 888. 18.

29. **a copy of this** <note>original: "toutou antigr(aphon)"</note> : the present papyrus is the actual copy made in accordance with this request, as is shown by the fact that the docket of the <term>strategus</term> (lines 34-5) is in the same hand as the body of the text, as well as by the frequent abbreviations (cf. especially line 1).

31. **it shall be made clear on the spot** <note>original: "epi tōn [to]pōn dēlōthēsetai"</note> : "shall be made clear" <note>original: "dēlōth[ēs]eta[i"</note> is similarly to be read after **the spots** <note>original: "topōn"</note> in B. G. U. 888. 21. In line 8 of the same papyrus we should suggest ] . . os son of Mystes. **of the things owed** <note>original: "opheilomenōn"</note>, in line 13 **upon or because of mortgages** <note>original: "epi or eph' hypallagmasi"</note> (cf. B. G. U. 86. 12, etc.), and in line 26 **to the Augustus** <note>original: "seb(astō)"</note> for **I have signed** <note>original: "ses(ēmeiōmai)"</note>.

33. **entry upon possession** <note>original: "embadeias"</note> : cf. B. G. U. 101. 15-6 **it is not permitted for me to redeem nor to enter upon possession** <note>original: "mē exeinai moi lytrōsai mēde embadeuein"</note>, and the Etymologicum Magnum <note>a Byzantine Greek dictionary</note> p. 334. 35: **to enter and entry; this is what is now called "embadia" with a "d", the act of the lender entering and going into the property of the debtor as a pledge for the loan.** <note>original: "embateusai kai embateia; estin hē nyni legomenē dia tou d embadia, to ton daneistēn embateusai kai eiselthein eis ta ktēmata tou hypochreou enechyriazonta to daneion"</note>.

34-5. In B. G. U. 578. I the corresponding formula is [**Ammonius, strategus**] **of the Arsinoite nome, Heraclides division, to Heron, assistant. Deliver notice in person as is fitting according to the orders.** <note>original: "[Ammōnios str(atēgos)] Arsi(noitou) [Hēr]akleidou merid(os) Hērōni hypēretē. metad(os) enōpi(on) hōs kathēk(ei) tois prostetagm(enois) akolou[thōs]"</note>. The present passage is more compressed, probably because the document as far as line 41 is a copy of the original; cf. note line 29. The word after **having ordered** <note>original: "s[u]ntaxantos"</note> is perhaps **to make** <note>original: "poi[eisthai]"</note> and "enes" suggests **current** <note>original: "enestōsē"</note>, but the reading is very doubtful.

44-7. The **guardian** <note>original: "kyrios"</note> here associated with Sarapias is different from the person who acted in that capacity when the loan was contracted; cf. lines 52 sqq. This circumstance explains the statement in lines 46-7 that the second **guardian** was assigned **by the strategus**. For the competence of the <term>strategus</term> in the appointment of guardians cf. *ibid.* 13-5, and the Geneva papyrus discussed by Erman in *Zeitschr. d. Sav. Stift.* xv. 241 sqq. For some reason—whether from death or other cause—the original guardian of Sarapias was not available, and a new one therefore became necessary.

## 486. PETITIONS TO THE EPISTRATEGUS AND PRAEFECT.

->34.5 x 26.7 cm. A.D. 131.<-

This petition to the <term>epistrategus</term> <note>a high-ranking Roman official overseeing a large administrative district known as a "Heptanomia"</note>, enclosing a petition to the <term>praefect</term> <note>the Roman governor of Egypt</note> with his answer, is concerned with the same subject as **472**. Dionysia and Sarapion had had a dispute concerning the ownership of some land which Dionysia claimed to have bought from Sarapion’s father, while Sarapion asserted that she held it only on mortgage, combining his claim with a charge of poisoning against Dionysia’s mother, Hermione. The matter came before the <term>epistrategus</term> Claudius Quintianus, who referred it to the <term>praefect</term> and ordered the rival suitors to proceed to Alexandria. Dionysia complied with his instructions, but not Sarapion; and after waiting some time in vain, she petitioned the <term>praefect</term> Flavius Titianus to give her permission to return home (ll. 18–36). To this the <term>praefect</term> replied by referring her back to the <term>epistrategus</term>, who by this time was Julius Varianus (ll. 37–8). Accordingly Dionysia wrote to him re-stating her case, and enclosing her previous petition and the answer to it; and reiterated her request for leave to return to Oxyrhynchus and for the case to be decided there. On the *verso* <note>the back side of the papyrus</note> in a small cursive hand is the rough draft of another petition of Dionysia on the same subject, but too much obliterated for continuous decipherment.

Since therefore news has reached me while staying here that all my property has been lost through the <margin>33</margin> excessive rise of the most sacred Nile <note>original: *hyperbarous anabaseos tou hierotatou Neilou*. The "most sacred" Nile's flood was the lifeblood of Egypt, but an "excessive" flood (hyperbarous) destroyed the very infrastructure it was meant to nourish.</note>, including farm buildings, lands, and dykes, I entreat you, my lord <term>Prefect</term>, in the continued absence of my opponent, to permit me to sail back in order that I may obtain justice there and that I may <margin>35</margin> not, in addition to the loss of my property, also perish of hunger, that I may obtain redress. Farewell. 

The 16th year of Hadrianus Caesar, <term>Phaophi</term> 12. <note>October 9, 131 AD. Phaophi was the second month of the Egyptian calendar.</note>

## 488. PETITION TO THE EPISTRATEGUS.

->26.5 x 15.5 cm. Late second or third century.<-

The scribe of the local <term>komogrammateus</term> <note>A "village scribe," the official responsible for local land surveys and tax records.</note>, the official specially concerned with the land-survey, had entered her purchase in the survey-lists at more than an <term>aroura</term> <note>A unit of area used in Egypt, roughly 0.6 of an acre.</note> in excess of the correct amount, and the petitioner appealed to the <term>epistrategus</term> to set matters right. The petition has been gummed on to another document on each side; the beginnings of a few lines of the right-hand one are preserved.

**Notes on the Greek text:**
1. Julius Julianus is written as *Iuliō Iulianō* in the Papyrus.
3. The second 'a' of the word for "registration" (*paragraphe*) was corrected from 's'.
4. The name *Psaitos* appears in the Papyrus with the 'a' corrected.
32. The first 'e' of "falsely registered" (*paregrapsen*) was corrected from 'a'.
43. The word "not" (*mē*) was corrected by the scribe.

### Commentary

**16.** After the word for "falsely registered" <note>original: *paregrapsen*</note>, the scribe began to write a word starting with the letters "em," perhaps meaning "to us" <note>original: *hēmin*</note> or "half" <note>original: *hēmisy*</note>, but changed it to "me" <note>original: *me*</note> without erasing the initial "h."

**17.** The phrase "one and more" <note>original: *miā kai pros*</note> is a common formula in land documents of this period to indicate a fraction beyond a whole unit.

**22.** The text is damaged here. Neither the word for "land," "house," nor "property" perfectly fits the surviving traces of ink and the available space.

**37.** We would expect the name of a specific official to follow the phrase "into the hands of," but the scribe left it blank or nothing further was written.

**43.** The relationship of this line to the rest of the summary is unclear. Above the first letter of "nothing" <note>original: *mēdenos*</note> is a small mark like an 'o', suggesting the scribe started writing a different abbreviation. The word "withheld" <note>original: *epechomenou*</note> is also difficult to read; it might instead mean "if no one objects" <note>original: *eperchomenou*</note>.

## 489. WILL OF DIONYSIUS.

->35.5 × 24.2 cm. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; A.D. 117.<-

Will of Dionysius son of Harpocration. The testator bequeaths to his wife Diogenis an apartment rent-free in a house belonging to him, together with the furniture of the whole house and his slaves. After the death of Diogenis the whole property is vested in their son, who presumably was to inherit during his mother’s lifetime whatever was not expressly reserved for her, though this is not definitely stated. The papyrus is dated in the reign of Trajan, and the number of the year, which is lost, can be fixed by the occurrence of the title Parthicus <note>A victory title meaning "Conqueror of the Parthians," which Emperor Trajan adopted in 116 A.D.</note>, which was assumed by that emperor in his 20th year. On Aug. 27, when the papyrus was written, Trajan had, as a matter of fact, been dead about three weeks <note>News of the Emperor's death in Cilicia had not yet reached this part of Egypt.</note>. This and the following wills, except **494**, are written across the fibres of the papyrus; cf. **583**, **634**, and **646–52**. The seals of the testator and witnesses were attached to the outside of the roll, but these have not been preserved; cf. P. Tebt. I. 104 introd.

[In the 20th year of the Emperor] Caesar Nerva Trajan the Best Augustus Germanicus Dacicus Parthicus, in the month of Caesareus <note>This was the Egyptian month Mesore, renamed in honor of the Emperor (Caesar).</note>, the 4th intercalary day, on the holiday of the Empress <note>original: *Sebastē* — a day of monthly celebration for the Imperial family.</note>,
[in the city of Oxyrhynchus in the Thebaid], <note>The Thebaid refers to the region of Upper Egypt.</note> for good fortune.
[This is the will, made while sound] in mind and [judgment], by Dionysius, son of Harpocration, grandson of Sarapion,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;whose mother is Esorsis, from the city of Oxyrhynchus, made in the street <note>A legal term indicating the will was recorded publicly by a notary.</note>.
<margin>5</margin> [For as long as I survive], I [remain the master] of my own property, [to use and] manage as I wish, and to change this will in whatever way I choose.
[But after my death], I grant to my wife who lives with me,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Diogenis, daughter of Ptolemy, from the same city, for as long as [she]
[survives, the right to live in and] use, rent-free, one room of her choosing
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;from the [stone house] I own in the North Quay quarter <note>original: *Krēpeidos* — a district in Oxyrhynchus near the river embankments.</note>,
[with its entrance and] exit; she shall also have use, for as long as she
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;survives, of the [belongings and furniture] left by me in the
[same room and in the house], and the service and
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;earnings <note>original: *apophoras* — the daily or monthly payments a slave working abroad would pay to their owner.</note> of my slave Hilarous and her offspring.

### 491. WILL OF EUDAEMON.

->22.7 x 39 cm. A.D. 126.<-

Will of Eudaemon, son of Thonasuchis, bequeathing his property to his three sons. Two of the sons, who were at the date of the will not yet 20 years old, are placed under tutelage <note>A legal arrangement where a guardian manages the affairs of a minor.</note> until they attained that age, and are also prohibited from disposing in any way of their inheritance before reaching 25 years.

**1** In the tenth year of the Emperor Caesar Trajan Hadrian Augustus, on the 5th of the intercalary days <note>These were five "extra" days added to the end of the Egyptian calendar to complete the 365-day year.</note> of the month of Caesareus, in the city of Oxyrhynchus in the Thebaid <note>A region in Upper Egypt.</note>, with good fortune <note>original: "ἀγαθῇ τύχῃ" (agathē tychē). A standard formula for auspicious beginnings.</note>.
**2** Eudaemon, son of Thonasuchis, grandson of Thonis, his mother being Thaesis, from the city of Oxyrhynchus, has made this will. He is a <term>pastophoros</term> <note>A "shrine-bearer," a lower-ranking priest responsible for carrying the sacred images or shrines of the gods during processions.</note> of the goddess Thoeris <note>The hippopotamus goddess, the patron deity of Oxyrhynchus.</note>, the greatest goddess, and of Isis <unclear>and the other gods</unclear> of the
**3** temple located in the village of Mouchinor, in the street. As long as I survive, I am to have power over my own property to perform whatever I wish, and to change my will or void this testament <note>This clause ensures that the will only takes effect upon death and remains revocable during the testator's lifetime.</note>;
**4** and whatever I perform shall be valid. But if I should die with this will still in effect, I leave as heirs my three sons, Thonis, Horus, and Eudaemon, whose mother is Ta... [daughter of Harpaesis] also called
**5** Horus, in equal shares to each of them if they survive; if not, to their children. These heirs shall receive the building sites, lands, and <term>slave bodies</term> <note>original: "δουλικῶν σωμάτων" (doulikōn sōmatōn). A standard legal term for enslaved people considered as property.</note> which I may leave behind. However, Thonis alone [shall have the right] to choose [from my possessions] ... of all 
**6** kinds, on the condition that the same Thonis shall pay whatever debts I am shown to owe, and shall give to his brothers Horus and Eudaemon—if they have already reached twenty years of age at the time of my death—one year
**7** after my death; but if they are not yet of that age, then to each of them as they complete their twentieth year, five hundred drachmae, so that there are one thousand drachmae for both. It is not permitted [for the same Horus and]
**8** Eudaemon, nor for any of them, to sell or mortgage or otherwise dispose of the property that comes to them from my name until each of them completes twenty-five years [of age. If...]

2. "and of Sarapis" <note>original: "καὶ Σαράπιδος"</note> would be expected after "of Isis" <note>original: "Ἴσιδος"</note> (cf. **48**. 8-9, &c.), and "of Sarapis" <note>original: "Σαράπι[δος"</note> might indeed be read, but there is then no room for "and" <note>original: "καὶ"</note>.

This difficulty might be evaded by supposing that "but until then" <note>original: "μέχρι δὲ τότε"</note> refers back to "20 years" <note>original: "ἐτῶν κ"</note> in line 14, but that is certainly not the natural interpretation. Possibly therefore "twenty (five)" <note>original: "εἴκοσι (πέντε)"</note> should be read throughout. 20 is the age when the period of tutelage terminated in another case (**495**. 10), but in **487**. 5 we find a guardian being appointed for youths of 25.

->23.8 x 38.5 cm. A.D. 130.<-

In this will Thatres daughter of Ammonius leaves as her heirs two half-brothers, whose relationship, if any, to herself, is not stated. The father of one of the brothers is expressly excluded from a house which formed the principal item in the property.

**3** Heraclous, daughter of Sarapion, granddaughter of Sarapion, her mother being Tauseiris also called Sarapous, [the guardian being] the son of Horion also called Theon, grandson of Sarapion, son of [ . . . ] of the inhabitants of Ibion Ammonius in the same lower district, [executed] in the street <term>in the street: indicates the document was drawn up publicly by a notary</term>.

### 493. WILL OF PASION AND BERENICE.

->11.3 x 25.9 cm. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; Early second century.<-

The following will is peculiar in being a joint deed by a husband and wife, who both have property to dispose of. The beginning is lost, but the remaining clauses suffice to show that the survivor of the two was constituted the heir of the other, with power to divide the whole property among the four children of the marriage; but the wife is, in the event of her outliving her husband, expressly authorized to retain the ownership if she chose to do so. The papyrus was probably written in the reign of Trajan or Hadrian <note>Roman Emperors ruling from 98–117 AD and 117–138 AD, respectively</note>.

### 494. WILL OF ACUSILAUS.

->39 × 23.2 *cm.* A.D. 156.<-

This long papyrus, which is in an excellent state of preservation, gives a copy of an elaborate and more than usually interesting will. The testator, Acusilaus, after conferring freedom upon five of his slaves, ‘in consequence of their goodwill and affection,’ leaves his son Dius heir to his property, subject to a life-interest reserved for Aristous, the wife of Acusilaus. The document is not the original will, but an official copy made at a later date; compare line 25, note.

A noticeable palaeographical <note>palaeography: the study of ancient writing systems and the deciphering of manuscripts</note> peculiarity in this papyrus is the **sigma**, which is of a square shape, consisting of two horizontal strokes joined by an upright one with a slight inward curve to the right.

<summary>This page concludes the joint will of Pasion and Berenice, detailing the penalties for violating its terms and listing the witnesses. It also introduces the will of Acusilaus, which features the manumission of slaves and the designation of his son as heir.</summary>

5–6. "By Zeus, Earth, and Sun" <note>original: ὑπὸ Δία Γῆν Ἥλιον</note>: compare document **48**. 6 and **49**. 8; another instance of the manumission <note>The formal act of freeing a slave.</note> of a slave by will is found in B. G. U. 326. 17.

21. The word after "own" <note>original: ἴδιον</note> could not be read as "debt" <note>original: χρ[έ]ος</note>, even if this were otherwise suitable. "Apart from" <note>original: χωρ[ί]ς</note> would be possible, though not very satisfactory.

25. "Under the official copy" <note>original: ὑπὸ τὸ ἐκδόσιμον</note>: <term>Official copies<note>original: ἐκδόσιμα</note></term> are mentioned in **34**. ii. 6, where the keeper of the ‘Nanaeum’ <note>A temple in Oxyrhynchus used to house public archives.</note> is ordered not to give them without authorization from the Library of Hadrian: — "the overseer of the Nanaeum shall neither give the official copies nor permit inspection nor manage anything else until he is instructed," <note>original: ὁ ἐπιτηρητὴ[ς] τοῦ Ναναίου μήτ[ε τὰ ἐκδόσιμα διδότω μήτε ἐπ[ι]σκέψασθαι ἐπ[ι]τρεπέτω μήτ[ε ἄ]λλο τι οἰκονομείτω πρὶν αὐτῷ ἐπιστέλλῃ[τ]αι κ.τ.λ.</note> etc. There the official copies appear to be official versions of the deeds deposited in the archives; and in the present passage (compare also **495**. 15) the word has the same meaning, as is indicated by the contrast drawn between the "official copy" and the "actual will" <note>original: διαθήκη</note>. It is indeed most probable that this papyrus was itself an official copy, for it is stated to be a copy and yet is signed by witnesses, who state that they had recognized the seals which they had affixed to the original document. We must then suppose that testators were permitted to use such official copies of their wills for the purpose of adding codicils <note>Legal supplements or additions to a will.</note> without being put to the trouble of withdrawing and cancelling the original deeds. This however was of course sometimes done; compare **106–7**, which refer to the absolute revocation of wills.

27. "as in the" or "as in the same" <note>original: ὡς ἐν τῇ or ὡς ἐν αὐτῇ τῇ</note> would be expected but was certainly not written. The phrase recurs in **495**. 16, but in a mutilated form.

31. Thonis <note>original: Θώνιος</note>: the mythical guard of the Canopic branch of the Nile; compare Herodotus i. 114–5. Probably "In the Canopic" <note>original: Ἐνκανώπου</note> in **634** refers to him.

38. "City of the Oxyrhynchites" <note>original: Ὀξυρυγχιτῶν πόλις</note>: this is an early example of this specific form of the city's name, which is not found in common use before the third century. **473**. 2 is in fact the only other instance in this volume.

44. The word "published" <note>original: προετέθη</note>, if correct, presumably refers to the publication of the contents of the will after the testator's death; but the note may merely record the date at which the present copy was made. Perhaps "deposited" <note>original: παρετέθη</note> should be read.

### 495. WILL OF PETOSORAPIS.

->9.7 x 34 cm. A.D. 181–189.<-

This will is much mutilated, but possesses an interest as a specimen from a somewhat later period than that to which the preceding group belongs; and its general tenour remains fairly clear. The testator Petosorapis leaves as his heir in the first instance his son Epinicus, a minor; and appoints his sister Apollonous to administer the estate, and take charge of Epinicus until he reached the age of 20 years. It may be inferred that the mother of the boy was either dead or had separated from her husband. A certain part of the property is appropriated to Apollonous herself, who was to pay the testator's debts; and the stipulation is made that she should not be asked to render an account of her trusteeship. A minor legacy was apparently made to a nephew of Petosorapis.

1 [In the ... and] twentieth year of the Emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Commodus Antoninus Augustus, Conqueror of the Armenians, the Medes, the Parthians, the Sarmatians, the Germans, Greatest, on the 2nd of the month Epeiph <note>A month in the Egyptian calendar, roughly June–July.</note>, in the city of Oxyrhynchus in the Thebaid <note>A region in Upper Egypt.</note>; with good fortune <note>original: ἀγαθῇ τύχῃ — a traditional invocation for a successful outcome.</note>.

2 [The following disposition was made, being] sane and of sound mind, by Petosorapis son of Petosorapis, grandson of Epinicus, his mother being Sarapias, of the city of Oxyrhynchus, in the street. So long as I survive, I am to have power over my own property to do whatever I wish

3 [with it,] and to revoke or cancel this will without hindrance; and whatever I may perform shall be valid. But if I die with this will still in force, without having made any other [disposition],

4 I leave as my [heir] my son Epinicus, whose mother is ...us, [from] the same city, [if he survives]; and if not, then such [children] as he may have, and any other children that may be born to me, or if no other children are born to me

5 [ ... ] all [ ... ] of the property belonging to me, formerly that of Hermias, acting under the name of his mother Isais [ ... ] opposite the village of Pela <note>A village in the Oxyrhynchite nome.</note> from the

6 [ ... ] to the future [ ... ] descendants and whatever I may leave in [furniture], utensils, household goods, and debts [owed to me]

### (e) CONTRACTS.

## 496. MARRIAGE CONTRACT.

->21 x 75.5 cm. 127 AD.<-

A contract of marriage between Sarapion, son of Eudaemon, and Thais, daughter of Sarapion. It is written on the front side (*recto*) of **34**, an important decree issued by Flavius Titianus <note>Flavius Titianus was the Prefect of Egypt between 126 and 133 AD; his edicts regulated how public records were managed.</note> concerning the archives. The ends of the lines, which are exceptionally long, are missing throughout the papyrus, which has also suffered significantly from rot and discoloration. However, the gaps can almost always be restored by comparing it with documents **265**, **497**, and similar marriage contracts from the Fayûm region now held in Vienna and Berlin; thus, the meaning is rarely in doubt. The result is a nearly complete example of a marriage contract from Oxyrhynchus from this period. The provisions generally resemble those found in similar documents from the Fayûm, but there are distinct differences in the specific legal formulas used. The main clauses include: (1) a detailed list of (*a*) the dowry of Thais, which includes various pieces of jewelry, clothing, 1,800 silver drachmae <note>The drachma was the standard unit of currency in Roman Egypt.</note> provided by her father, and a female slave presented by her grandmother (lines 2–6); (*b*) the property brought into the household by Sarapion (lines 7–8); (2) the legal conditions for a divorce (lines 8–10); and (3) provisions for the distribution of property in the event of the death of either spouse (lines 10–16). See also documents **603–7**.

1 The eleventh year of the Emperor Caesar Trajan Hadrian Augustus, the 24th of the month Pharmouthi <note>original: Φαρμοῦθι κδ — This corresponds to April 19, 127 AD.</note>, in the city of Oxyrhynchus in the Thebaid <note>A region in Upper Egypt.</note>. With good fortune; [this contract was executed] in the street of Julia Augusta.

2 Sarapion, son of Sarapion, grandson of Sarapion, great-grandson of Sarapion, his mother being Thais, daughter of Sarapion, from the city of Oxyrhynchus, has given away in marriage his own daughter Thais (whose mother is <unclear>...</unclear>) to Sarapion, son of Eudaemon, grandson of Theon, his mother being Heras, daughter of <unclear>...</unclear> and granddaughter of Didous. The groom has received from Sarapion, the father

3 and giver of the bride, <unclear>...</unclear> a pair of <term>earrings</term> <note>original: τ̣ιων — likely "enotia," the standard term for earrings.</note> weighing three <term>mnaeia</term> <note>A unit of weight; in Oxyrhynchus, a mnaeion was a standard measurement for gold and silver.</note> and fourteen and a half <term>tetartae</term> <note>A "quarter" weight; usually a quarter of a stater.</note>; a small brooch weighing eight <term>tetartae</term>; a <unclear>...</unclear> weighing six <term>tetartae</term>; a small chain having green <unclear>...</unclear> stones, the gold of which weighs <unclear>...</unclear> and a half; making the total weight of the gold according to the Oxyrhynchite standard five <term>mnaeia</term> and <unclear>...</unclear> <term>tetartae</term>.

are accounted for by the articles of dress and 1800 were paid in money, leaving 1680 to be accounted for by the value of the jewelry. Since a **mnaion** <term>mnaion|A unit of weight used for precious metals, roughly equivalent to 1 pound or 100 drachmae in weight</term> contained 16 **tetartai** <term>tetartai|A small unit of weight, literally meaning 'quarters'</term> (<note>original: 9. verso 16</note>), the items in line 3 make 4 **mnaia** and 13 **tetartai** plus the number of **tetartai** in the little chain. A **mnaion** of gold is converted into 288 silver drachmae in the document *C. P. R. 12*, and at the same rate 1680 drachmae would represent 5 5/6 **mnaia**. If the figure lost in line 3 before **half** <note>original: ἥμισυ</note> was ten (no higher figure is possible), the total weight of the jewelry was 5 7/8 **mnaiai**. The difference is due to variation either in the rate of exchange or in the weights.

6\. **the service** <note>original: τὴν 〈δὲ〉 δουλείαν</note>: in the translation we have supposed that the possessive names Callityche, etc., depend on a word like **ownership** <note>original: κυρείαν</note> lost at the end of line 5, but **the service** (of the slave) may be the word on which they depend (cf. **489**. 8), in which case a relative pronoun (who or which) must be supplied in the gap <note>original: lacuna</note> before the word **will maintain** in line 6.

**brought as dowry** <note>original: προσφερόμ[ενον</note>: this is the word commonly used for property brought to the husband by the bride, for example, in a first-century fragment of a marriage-contract, "the dowry being brought" <note>original: τὴν φερνὴν προσφερομένην</note>.

7\. For the suggested completion at the end of the line, see for example **491**. 8.
9\. For the completion at the end see **497**. 16.
10\. Some such word as **should happen** <note>original: συμβῇ</note> is required before **any**; see **497**. 11.
12\. **let her be alone, etc.** <note>original: ἔστω μόνη κ.τ.λ.</note>: see **265**. 29.
13\. **the items in the dowry** <note>original: τὰ ἐν φερνῇ</note>: see line 15. Or **brought in** <note>original: ἐ[νεχθέντα</note> may be read; see *C. P. R. 27. 18*.
15\. **legal claims** <note>original: διαστολῶν</note>: used here for the recovery of the dowry; see **497**. 18. See for the completion *C. P. R. 22. 23, 27. 19*.
16\. **identifier** <term>identifier|known as a gnostēr (γνωστήρ), this was a person who officially vouched for someone's identity in legal proceedings</term>: compare a Vienna papyrus cited by Hartel in *Greek Papyri from the Archduke Rainer Collection*, page 66: "to the councilman of Antinoopolis <note>original: Ἀντινοέων</note> who acted as my **identifier** during the examination," and *B. G. U. 581. 13* (a deed of surety): "the aforementioned person... is identified by Lucius Octanius Longus, discharged from military service." The **identifier** of a person was a witness of his or her identity.

### 497. MARRIAGE-CONTRACT.

->11.5 x 14.1 cm. Early second century.<-

Contract of marriage between Theon and Ammonous, written in very long lines across the fibers of the papyrus <note>Writing across the fibers means the text runs perpendicular to the natural grain of the reed paper</note>, probably in the reign of Trajan or Hadrian. Though a mere fragment of the whole contract, the sense and construction are intelligible throughout, for the missing portions at the beginnings of the lines can be largely restored from the other Oxyrhynchus marriage-contracts of this period (**265** and **496**), and the Ptolemaic marriage-contracts from the Fayum (*P. Tebt. 104* and *Archive*, Volume I, page 484). At the end are the signatures of the bridegroom and the bride’s father, and of a third person who seems to have been concerned in receiving the dowry, but whose relation to the contracting parties is obscure.

### 498. CONTRACT WITH STONE-CUTTERS.
->17.8 x 8.7 cm. Second century.<-

A contract by which two stone-cutters agree to supply the stone required for building a house at Oxyrhynchus at different prices according to the size and nature of the stones. Food was to be provided for them while they were engaged upon the work, and wages were guaranteed to them if their services were required by the builders, but the ornamentation of the stone is excluded from their duties. The stone was to be brought from the ‘northern quarry,’ which is still a noticeable feature a little way to the north of the site on the edge of the desert. The papyrus supplies several new technical terms connected with stone-cutting.

<summary>This page concludes a 2nd-century marriage contract detailing the recovery of a dowry and introduces a new labor contract with stone-cutters for a building project.</summary>

### Editor's Translation and Commentary

> Copy. To Antonia Asclepias, also known as Kyria, acting through her guardian Apollonius, from Asclas, son of Alexandrus, and Apollonius, son of Amois (whose mother is Tauris), both of Oxyrhynchus. We undertake to cut the squared building stones—sized for transport by camel—from the northern quarry required for your house, Antonia, in the quarter of Pammenes’ Garden. The wage for stone-cutting is: for the outer squared camel-load stones, 4 drachmae for every 16 stones; for the inner ones, 4 drachmae for every 30; for <term>filling-stones</term> <note>original: ἀντιβλήματα (antiblamata). Stones used to fill the interior of a wall between two finished faces.</note>, 3 drachmae for every 100 squared camel-load stones. For oblong cornerstones, 8 drachmae for every 16 outer stones and 8 drachmae for 30 inner stones. For chipped squared camel-load stones, 4 drachmae for 50, and for chipped oblong cornerstones, 8 drachmae for 50. We will cut all the aforementioned stones, but no decorative carving shall be required of us. Each of us shall receive for each day worked both a loaf of bread and relish. If the builders require our assistance in stone-cutting, we (or one of us) will provide it, each receiving a daily wage of 4 drachmae plus a loaf and relish. Until the 22nd of the present month, Epeiph, you have the right to transfer this contract to other laborers for the cutting of the aforementioned stones from the northern quarry...

8. **camel-load**: The adjective <note>original: καμηλικῶν (kamelikon)</note> is previously unrecorded in Greek texts of this period. It indicates that the stones were standardized to a weight and size manageable for a camel to transport.
16. **filling-stones**: These stones, being the least expensive, were likely the smallest fragments used to fill empty spaces between the larger, more expensive blocks.

# VOCABULARY

**Oxyrhynchus**: An ancient city in Egypt where thousands of papyri were discovered.
**Papyrus**: The ancient equivalent of paper, made from the pith of the papyrus plant.
**Antonia Asclepias (Cyria)**: The wealthy female employer named in the contract.
**Stone-cutting**: The primary labor being contracted here.
**Wages**: Paid in both currency (drachmae) and food rations.
**Drachmae**: The standard silver currency in Roman Egypt.
**Epeiph**: An Egyptian month (June/July).
**Camel-load**: A specific unit of measurement for stone size.
**Filling-stones**: Rubble or small stones used for wall interiors.

The text highlights the use of camels as the primary means of transporting standardized construction materials.</summary>

The 15th year of the Emperor Caesar Trajan Hadrian Augustus, Phaophi 5 <note>Roughly October 2nd.</note>. We, Horus son of Psenomoithas and Nekpheros son of Thaisous, of the village of Sinekthoieku in the eastern part of the Thostian district, have leased the aforesaid 20¼ <term>arourae</term> <note>A unit of land area, approximately 0.6 acres.</note> of public land near Tetaphou at 2 <term>artabae</term> <note>A measure of volume for grain, roughly 40 liters.</note> of wheat and for the addition upon the whole land 5 <term>artabae</term> of wheat, and near Psenarsiësis 1 <term>aroura</term> likewise of public land at 3 <term>artabae</term> of wheat, and we will measure . . .’

11-2. The genitives <note>Grammatical cases indicating possession.</note> in these lines probably refer to the previous lessees; cf. **279**. 8. <note>original: "α[.] ι]ουδαίω[ν" (a[.] i]oudaiōn)</note> —of the Jews— seems to be the termination of a compound word expressing a particular class of Jews. There is room for one or two more letters in the lacuna <note>A gap or missing part in the manuscript.</note> before <note>original: "εἰρημ[ε]νων" (eirēmenōn)</note> —aforementioned—, but the writer frequently leaves spaces between words. In l. 12 the termination -ιτων <note>original: "-itōn"</note> of <note>original: "]ηρονομων" (hēronomōn)</note> —heirs— suggests a place-name.

13. **Public land** <note>original: "δημοσί(ας) γῆς" (dēmosias gēs)</note>: in *Ostraka* volume I, page 646, Wilcken adopts the explanation of ‘public land’ proposed by Viereck (*Hermes*, volume xxx, page 119) that it means land belonging to the commune (‘communal land’) as opposed to **royal land** <note>original: "βασιλικὴ γῆ" (basilikē gē)</note> or ‘domain land’; but in *Archiv*, volume I, page 157 he speaks of *P. Brit. Mus. 335*, which is an application for a sub-lease of **public land**, as if that papyrus referred to ‘Crown land,’ i.e., as if **public land** were the same as **royal land**. There is, we think, no doubt that the first theory is incorrect. The use of **public** <note>original: "δημόσιος" (dēmosios)</note> in papyri in connection with **account** <note>original: "λόγος" (logos)</note>, **bank** <note>original: "τράπεζα" (trapeza)</note>, and **farmer** <note>original: "γεωργός" (georgos)</note>, where it corresponds in the first case to **Caesar's** or **lordly** <note>original: "Καίσαρος" (Kaisaros) or "κυριακός" (kyriakos)</note> (cf. *Ost.* I. p. 645) and in the other two to **royal** <note>original: "βασιλικός" (basilikos)</note>, renders such a contrast between **public** and **royal** as is required by Viereck’s theory very improbable. When we hear of land belonging to a ‘Commune,’ as for example in *P. Gen. 16*, *C. P. R. 39* and *41*, it is never called **public**, but land **from the city account** <note>original: "ἀπὸ τοῦ πολιτικοῦ λόγου" (apo tou politikou logou)</note> or **of the village** <note>original: "τῆς κώμης" (tēs kōmēs)</note>. These instances all belong to the third or fourth century, and it is not at all likely that there were enough ‘Communes’ previously to account for the frequent mention of **public land** before the reign of Septimius Severus. It is far more probable that **public** in the phrase **public land** has the same meaning as in the phrase **public farmer** (cf. *P. Brit. Mus. 256 (e) 1-2*: —to public farmers for the land they cultivate, whether royal or sacred or other land—) and, that **public land** included **royal land**, without however superseding the older term in the manner in which the Roman **public bank** superseded the **royal bank** of the Ptolemies. The evidence on which attempts have been made to draw a real distinction between **public** and **royal land** is extremely slender. In *B. G. U. 560. 21* **public** and **estate land** <note>original: "οὐσιακὴ γῆ" (ousiakē gē)</note> are coupled together, but there **public** in the sense of the Crown lands of the Ptolemaic kings makes a better contrast with estates acquired by the Emperors from private persons than **public** in the sense of ‘communal land’; and it is quite uncertain that the **royal land** mentioned two lines later is intended to be distinguished from the previously mentioned **public land**. *B. G. U. 188. 23*, where the editors read —53rd allotment of royal public land—, if **public** is right (which is extremely doubtful; ‘of public taxes’ is preferable), would rather tend to show that **public land** coincided with **royal land** than that it was something different. In *B. G. U. 285* where **arourae of public land** are distinguished from **arourae of royal land**, it is not certain that land at the same village is meant, nor is it at all clear that ‘public’ is there feminine, as would seem to be the view of the maker of the index to *B. G. U.* Under these circumstances we abandon the view expressed in the introduction to *P. Fay. Towns 88*, since there is no reason for departing from the natural meaning of **public** at this period or for regarding **public land** as anything but a general term for land belonging to the State, i.e., the imperial domains $^1$.

---

$^1$ Cf. also the recent discussion of **public land** in *Festschr. zu O. Hirschfeld* <note>A commemorative publication for scholar Otto Hirschfeld.</note>, p. 140, by P. Meyer, who comes to the same conclusion as that expressed here.

### 504. Sale of Catoecic Land.

->33.2 X 13.5 cm. Early second century A.D.<-

Contract for the sale of 6 2/3 <term>arourae</term> <note>An aroura was a standard unit of land area in Roman Egypt, approximately 2,756 square meters or about two-thirds of an acre.</note> of <term>catoecic land</term> <note>original: "κατοικικῆς γῆς" (katoikikēs gēs) — land originally granted by the Ptolemaic kings to Greek military settlers, which carried specific tax privileges and was registered in a special office.</note> in the Oxyrhynchite nome for 1000+ drachmae, the seller being Aphroditous, a freedwoman, acting with her husband Adrastus as <term>kyrios</term> <note>original: "κύριος" (kyrios) — a male legal guardian. Under the law of the time, women required a guardian to formalize legal contracts.</note>, and the buyer being Flavius Apion. The adoptive mother of the seller, Thaisous, who seems to have had some rights of ownership over the land, appends her consent. The formula of the papyrus differs somewhat from that found in similar contracts from the Arsinoite and Heracleopolite nomes. The contract is dated in the third year of an emperor who was probably Trajan or Hadrian, and is written in a small cursive hand with several mistakes of spelling and grammar. Cf. **633**.

R.* I. 1. 11: **"[to have] completed [for] Ptolemaïs the [transactions] through the [land-registry of the military settlers] regarding the three [conceded arourae]."** <note>original: "[ἐπιτετε]λε[κέναι τὴν] Πτολεμαίδα τὰς εἰς τὸν Μάρωνα [διὰ τ]οῦ κατοικικοῦ λογιστηρίου τῶν παρα[κε]χωρημένων ἀρουρῶν τριῶν οἰκονομίας."</note>

**12. Of the addition:** <note>original: "προσθέματος"</note> the technical meaning of this variant for the usual word **allotment** <note>original: "κλήρου"</note> is obscure. **And** <note>original: "καί"</note> cannot be read after **the** <note>original: "τοῦ"</note> in l. 44.

### 506. LOAN OF MONEY ON SECURITY.

->(*a*) 16 x 17.7 *cm.*, (*b*) 10.7 x 14.2 *cm.* A. D. 143.<-

Contract for the loan of 1000 drachmae for two years and nine months at 6 per cent per annum, from Sarapion to two sisters called Thatres and Teteorion, and their mother Demas, upon a mortgage of 1 49/64 arourae <note>An aroura was a standard Egyptian measure of land, roughly 0.66 acres; 1 49/64 arourae is approximately 1.15 acres.</note> of land belonging to the sisters. The document being a copy of the original deed, the signatures are omitted. For other examples of loans upon security cf. **507**, P. Brit. Mus. 311, and the Florence papyrus cited on p. 172. The papyrus is in two pieces of which the exact relation to each other is uncertain, besides a small detached scrap.

(*a*) Copy <note>original: "Antigraphon"</note>. In the seventh year of the Emperor Caesar Titus Aelius

The 7th year of the Emperor Caesar Titus Aelius Hadrianus Antoninus Augustus Pius <note>The Roman Emperor known as Antoninus Pius; the 7th year of his reign corresponds to 143–144 AD.</note>, the [blank] of the month Hadrianus, at Oxyrhynchus in the Thebaid. Sarapion son of Herodes son of Exacon, of Oxyrhynchus, his mother being Caecilia Polla, has lent to Thatres and Teteorion, both daughters of Apollonius son of ..., and to their mother Demas daughter of Apollonius son of Panechotes, her mother being Philotera, all three Persians <note>In Roman Egypt, "Persian" was often a legal status designating a specific class of debtors or settlers, rather than a literal ethnic description.</note> from the village of Pela, each with her guardian <note>Under Roman and Egyptian law, women typically required a male relative or husband to act as a legal guardian in formal contracts.</note>, of Thatres her husband Peteuris son of Ammonas son of Sagathes, his mother being Panechotis, of Oxyrhynchus, of Teteorion her maternal uncle Panechotes son of Apollonius and Philotera, of the aforesaid Pela, and of Demas her paternal uncle Hatres son of Panechotes son of Apollonius, of the said Pela, in the street, a sum of 1000 **drachmae** <term>drachma</term> <note>The standard silver currency of the time.</note> of Imperial silver coin, to which nothing has been added, at the interest of 3 **obols** <term>obol</term> <note>A smaller unit of currency; 6 obols made one drachma.</note> for each **mina** <term>mina</term> <note>A unit of weight and value equal to 100 drachmae; an interest rate of 3 obols per mina per month equals 6% per year.</note> per month dating from the present month Hadrianus. The borrowers shall pay to the lender the interest at the conclusion of each twelvemonth, the lender having security for everything for which they do not produce his written receipt, and the principal on the 30th of the month Caesareus of the 9th year of Antoninus Caesar the lord together with the interest for the remaining 9 months without any delay. If they fail, Thatres and Teteorion concede that the borrower and his assigns in place of the principal and of all interest which he may not receive shall from the time when the payment falls due have the possession and ownership for ever out of the land owned by them in equal shares near the said Pela in the **cavalry-soldier’s holding** <term>kleros</term> <note>A "kleros" was a plot of land originally assigned to military settlers.</note> of Diocles and Ptolemaeus, Persian, namely the third portion of what was previously a vineyard but is now dry vine-land, in the most northerly portion of the said third part 1 4 4/64 **arourae** <term>aroura</term> <note>An Egyptian unit of land area, roughly equivalent to 0.6 acres.</note> with all their contents, of which the adjacent areas are, on the south the land of Stephanus ... and Thatres the aforesaid, daughter of Apollonius, on the north ..., on the east a canal ... and the land of Stephanus, on the west ...; and (the borrowers) are compelled to deliver this land to the lender or his assigns guaranteed for all time against all risks with every guarantee and free from obligation to cultivate Crown land or Imperial estates and from all kinds of imposts and all State requisitions and taxes dating from previous times up to the period of Sarapion’s ownership. And until the borrowers repay to the lender the principal and the interest, Thatres and Teteorion have no right to sell this land or mortgage it or dispose of it in any other way or register any one as owning it, while the lender has the right at the expiration of the term of the loan, if he fails to recover it, to assume the ownership of this land in place of both the principal and whatever interest at 6 per cent. he may fail to recover and interest for overtime at the equal rate of 6 per cent., and to make an execution upon the borrowers who are security to each other for payment and upon whichever of them he chooses and upon all the aforementioned land and upon the rest of their property as if in accordance with a legal decision, the lender having the right whenever he chooses to register his mortgage at the property record-office ..., and the said lender shall incur no loss in his right of execution for the other sums which Thatres and Teteorion owe him in respect of another loan drawn up through the said registry-office in the present month Hadrianus for which their mother is security upon the mortgage of the aforesaid 14 3/4 arourae of wheat-bearing land, namely a principal sum of 1 talent 600 drachmae and interest, but all the provisions of that deed are valid. This contract is valid.’

24. **Persian cavalry-soldier’s holding** <note>original: "Persou hippikou klērou"</note>: compare the notes on documents **482**, line 18 and **483**, line 5.

37. **Far]min[g of royal] and [estat]e land** <note>original: "ge]ōrgi[as basilikēs] kai [ousi]akēs gēs"</note>: see *The Amherst Papyri* 95, line 4, where the word "royal" alone is found in a similar context. We previously suggested that either the word "land" or "farming" should be filled in there. Wilcken (*Archiv*, volume 2, page 132), comparing *Corpus Papyrorum Raineri* 6, line 16 where "land" is used, decided in favor of the first option. However, this text proves that while "royal" refers to "land," the word "farming" is meant to be understood even if it is not explicitly written; see also documents **577** and **633**.

## 509. MODIFICATION OF AN AGREEMENT.

->19.7 x 8.7 cm. Late second century.<-

This draft agreement, in which the names of the principal parties are not given, is a modification of a previous contract by which the writer had appointed a representative to collect a debt owed to him at Alexandria. The debt having been paid in the meantime, the writer now limits the duty of his representative to issuing a receipt for it. For contracts appointing representatives, compare documents **94, 97,** and **261.** The document is written on the back <note>original: "verso"</note> of document **507.**

[Someone] to [someone], greetings. On the present day I appointed you by a public deed drawn up through the archive here as my representative to collect from Gaius Memmius Cor-
<margin>5</margin> nutus, also called Polydeuces, who is in Alexandria, my half share of the sums owed by him to the heir of my same father, his nephew Heraclides also called Amoitas, 
<margin>10</margin> but it happens that I have been fully satisfied regarding the debts owed to me. I acknowledge that the contract of representation has been made for you for the sole purpose of the receipt 
<margin>15</margin> being issued by you to the public officials without receiving anything, and to release the mortgage, because I, as aforesaid, have already received the money according to the autograph 
<margin>20</margin> receipts I issued, and I make no claim about anything whatsoever.

4. Gaius <note>original: "γάϊον"</note> in the papyrus. 12. "to have been made" <note>original: "πεπυῆσθαί"</note>; read "to have been made" <note>original: "πεποιῆσθαι"</note> in standard Greek. 13. The final "n" <note>original: "ν"</note> of "only" <note>original: "μονον"</note> was corrected from "s" <note>original: "ς"</note>.

> ‘A to B, greeting. To-day I appointed you by a public deed drawn up through the record-office here as my representative to collect from Gaius Memmius Cornutus also called Polydeuces, who is at Alexandria, my share of the sums owed by him to my said father’s heir, his nephew Heraclides also called Amoitas, but it happens that I have been paid the debt in full. I acknowledge that the contract of representation has been made with you for the sole purpose of your issuing a receipt to the officials without receiving anything, and for cancelling the mortgage, because I have, as aforesaid, already received the money as stated in the autograph receipts <note>An "autograph" in this context refers to a document written in the party's own hand, serving as a personal guarantee of the transaction.</note> which I have issued, and I make no claim on any matter whatever.’

**7-9.** The relationship of the different persons mentioned in this contract is rather difficult to make out, especially owing to the omission of the names of the principals. Apparently the father of the man who speaks in the first person had bequeathed certain sums owing to himself at his death to his nephew Heraclides with the stipulation that half of them was to be paid to his son. "Of the same" <note>original: "τοῦ αὐτοῦ"</note> in line 8 refers to the father (of "the sender"), whose name would be given in the actual contract. "His" <note>original: "αὐτοῦ"</note> in line 9 also refers to the father.

### Technical Vocabulary
<term>Contract of representation</term> — A legal appointment (systatikon) allowing one person to act on behalf of another in financial or legal matters.
<term>Autograph receipts</term> — Private, handwritten acknowledgments of payment that were legally binding even if not initially filed in a public archive.
<term>Archive/Record-office</term> — The "archeion," a local government office where contracts were registered to make them "public" and enforceable.

<summary>This document is a formal notification where a creditor admits a debt has already been paid privately and authorizes a representative to perform the legal formalities of canceling the mortgage and notifying officials.</summary>

### 511. ACKNOWLEDGEMENT OF LOAN.

-> 13.3 X 7 cm. A. D. 103. <-

A receipt for 16 drachmae lent by Didymus to Harmiusis to enable the latter to pay the amount of the tax upon a mortgage. The loan was only a temporary accommodation, to be returned immediately. The writing is across the fibers of the papyrus.

2. The 'o' of 'public' <note>original: δημοσιω</note> is written above the line. 4. Read 'remainder' <note>original: λοιπόν</note> for the original spelling 'lypon'. 5. The 'k' of 'mortgage' <note>original: υποθηκ(η)s</note> is written above the line.

> ‘Harmiusis also called Heraclas to Didymus son of Sarapion, keeper of a public temple of Aphrodite <note>original: ἀφροδίσιον</note>, greeting. I have received from you the remainder of the tax upon a mortgage of the 3rd year of Trajanus Caesar the lord, namely 16 drachmae of silver, total 16 drachmae, which I will repay to you when I arrive on the spot without delay. The 7th year of the Emperor Caesar Nerva Trajanus Augustus Germanicus Dacicus, Thoth 6.’

2–3. **public official of the temple of Aphrodite** <note>original: δημοσίῳ ἀφροδ(ισιαστῇ ?)</note>: the papyrus is rubbed and the reading somewhat uncertain, but though the specific term for an 'attendant of Aphrodite' <note>original: ἀφροδισιαστής</note> does not seem to occur elsewhere, it is a likely enough word. On the temples or establishments of Aphrodite <note>original: ἀφροδίσια</note> of the Ptolemaic period, compare *P. Tebt. I. 6. 29*, note. The present passage supports the view that the supply of female companions <note>original: ἑταῖραι</note> in Roman times was a monopoly of the government; compare *P. Grenf. II. 41* and *Fayum Towns*, pages 149 and following.

4–5. **tax on the mortgage** <note>original: τέλος ὑποθήκ(η)ς</note>: compare entries **348** and **510**. 20. The amount of the tax upon mortgages, which is also known by the more general term *enkyklion* <term>enkyklion: A general tax on transactions and property transfers, usually set at a percentage of the value.</term>, is shown by document **243** to have been 2 per cent, payable by the mortgagee <term>mortgagee: The lender who holds the security interest in the property.</term>.

6. **3rd year** <note>original: γ (ἔτους)</note>: the receipt being dated in the 7th year, Harmiusis’ payment was four years in arrears. This seems a remarkably long period, but the figure before "year" <note>original: (ἔτους)</note>, though rubbed, is certainly '3' and not '6'.

<summary>A receipt for sixteen drachmae paid as a mortgage tax (enkyklion) during the reign of Trajan, notable for its reference to a public official associated with the temple of Aphrodite and a four-year delay in payment.</summary>

# THE OXYRHYNCHUS PAPYRI

### 512. PAYMENT FOR FODDER.

->11.5 x 10.3 cm. 173 AD.<-

An acknowledgement to Apion, a former <term>gymnasiarch: A prestigious official responsible for the city gymnasium and often for funding public festivals.</term>, from Dorion, a former <term>exegetes: A high-ranking municipal magistrate who oversaw various administrative and religious functions.</term>, that he had bought green-fodder produced by Apion for 1720 drachmae. Of this sum, 600 drachmae were paid directly to Apion, and the rest was to be paid to the agents of the heirs of Aurelius Antiochus, who were no doubt Apion’s landlords and thus received approximately two-thirds of the value of the crop as rent.

Dorion, former exegetes and however I am styled <note>original: καὶ ὡς χρηματίζω; a legal formula used to cover any other official titles the individual might hold.</note>, to Apion also called Dionysius, former gymnasiarch and however you are styled, greeting. I have bought from you the green-fodder <note>original: χλωρά</note> which you hold on lease within the surrounding-dyke known as Sampsouchinus for 1720 drachmae; of which sum I have paid to you 600 drachmae, and the remaining 1120 drachmae I will pay to the agents of the heirs of Aurelius Antiochus in accordance with the terms of your lease, and I will deliver the receipt for these to you. The 13th year of Aurelius Antoninus Caesar the lord, Phamenoth 12 <note>Phamenoth 12: March 8, 173 AD.</note>.

---

4. The 'u' of 'from you' <note>original: σου</note> was corrected from an 'i'.

---

> ‘Dorion, former exegetes and however he is styled, to Apion also called Dionysius, former gymnasiarch and however he is styled, greeting. I have bought from you the green-stuffs of the land which you have on lease within the surrounding-dyke called that of Sampsouchinus for 1720 drachmae; of which sum I have paid you 600 drachmae and will pay the remaining 1120 drachmae to the agents of the heirs of Aurelius Antiochus in accordance with the terms of your lease, and I will deliver to you the receipt for them. The 13th year of Aurelius Antoninus Caesar the lord, Phamenoth 12.’

<note>This document illustrates the complex nature of agricultural sub-leasing in Roman Egypt. Even high-status former officials like Dorion and Apion were deeply involved in the management and sale of crops like fodder.</note>

<summary>A financial contract from 173 AD where Dorion (a former magistrate) acknowledges purchasing fodder from Apion (a former official), involving a split payment to satisfy Apion's rent to his landlords.</summary>

### 513. Receipt for Sale of Confiscated Property.

->34.2 X 11.7 cm. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; A. D. 184.<-

An acknowledgement from Diogenes to Serenus of the receipt of 705 drachmae 3 obols 3 chalci <term>chalcus: The smallest unit of copper currency; eight chalci made up one obol, and six obols made up one drachma.</term>. This sum had been paid by Diogenes to the State in A.D. 181 as the price (including extra payments) of some confiscated house-property, which had been sold to him by the strategus <term>strategus: The chief administrative official of the district (nome), responsible for civil and financial governance.</term> at an auction. Two years later however a much higher bid for the property, amounting to three times that of Diogenes, was made by Serenus, to whom it was assigned by the dioecetes <term>dioecetes: A high-ranking financial administrator in Roman Egypt who oversaw state revenues and property.</term>, the arrangement of the strategus being thus overridden. In the present document Diogenes acknowledges that he has been repaid by Serenus the sum which he had expended on the purchase. The papyrus throws some interesting light upon the methods of the government in dealing with confiscated property, and incidentally provides important information with regard to the banks at this period; cf. notes on ll. 7 and 37.

[Diogenes also called Dionysius], son of Sarapion, grandson of Hermias, of the [Phylaxithalassian] tribe and [Althaean] deme <note>Phylaxithalassian and Althaean: These are names of specific "tribes" and "demes" (political subdivisions) belonging to the city of Alexandria; their use here indicates Diogenes held Alexandrian citizenship.</note>, to Serenus, son of Philiscus, grandson of [Sarapion], mother being Helene, from the city of Oxyrhynchus, greeting. 

Since I was confirmed in ownership by Nemesianus, the former <margin>5</margin> strategus of the district, in the twenty-second year of Aurelius Commodus Antoninus Caesar the lord, in the month of Hadrianus <note>original: Αδριανοῦ; this refers to the Egyptian month of Choiak, roughly November/December.</note>, from the unsold property of the administration, of a house, an open-air court, and a yard, with all fixtures, located in the Lycians’ <margin>10</margin> Quarter <note>original: Λυκίων Παρεμβολῆς; a neighborhood in the city of Oxyrhynchus.</note>, which formerly belonged to Sarapion, son of [unclear]... for the [appraised] sum of six hundred drachmae and the associated costs; and these [charges] were registered against me by the Royal <margin>15</margin> Scribe <term>Royal Scribe: A high-level official (basilikos grammateus) in charge of land records and taxation data in the district.</term> of the district, Pericles, including the extra payments <term>extra payments: Surcharges (prodiagraphomena) added to the base price of government-sold property.</term>, amounting to six hundred thirty-seven drachmae and three obols; and likewise for interest for the twenty-second year, thirty-nine drachmae, three and a half obols, and three chalci; and for the twenty-third year, twenty-eight drachmae, two and a half obols...

<summary>A legal receipt where a man named Diogenes acknowledges being reimbursed by Serenus for a house originally bought from the state, after the state accepted Serenus's much higher subsequent bid. It illustrates the precarious nature of buying confiscated property from the Roman government.</summary>
