...a total of 705 drachmae <note>drachma: A silver coin that served as the standard unit of currency in Roman Egypt.</note>, 3 obols <note>obol: A smaller unit of currency; six obols usually equaled one drachma.</note>, and 3 chalci <note>chalcus: A tiny copper coin; the smallest denomination, with 8 chalci making up one obol.</note>, and that **I** neither have nor will have any claim against you with regard to this or any other matter whatever up to the present day, and if any action is brought against you or your assigns with regard to this, **I** will take the responsibility upon myself. My father Sarapion son of Hermias son of Hermias, of the Sosicosmian tribe and Althaean deme <note>deme: A local administrative district within a city, similar to a ward or precinct.</note>, being present consents to the aforesaid. This receipt is valid. The 24th year of the Emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Commodus Antoninus Augustus Pius Armeniacus Medicus Parthicus Sarmaticus Germanicus Maximus . . . I, Diogenes also called Dionysius, son of Sarapion, of the Phylaxithalassian tribe and Althaean deme, have received from Serenus the aforesaid total of 705 drachmae 3 obols 3 chalci in full, and I have no claim against him with regard to this or any other matter whatever, as aforesaid, and if any action is brought against him or his in connexion with this, I will take the responsibility upon myself. I, Serenus son of Philiscus son of Sarapion, my mother being Helene, consent to the aforesaid provisions and have received the receipts with your signature as aforesaid. I, Sarapion son of Hermias son of Hermias, of the Sosicosmian tribe and Althaean deme, consent to all the aforesaid provisions. Epeiph 4 <note>Epeiph: An Egyptian month roughly corresponding to late June and July.</note>, executed . . .'

---

1. <term>Phylaxithalassian also called Althaean</term> <note>original: "Φυλαξιθαλάσσειος ὁ καὶ ᾿Αλθαιεύς"</note>: compare line 52 and document **477**, lines 7-8. It is curious that the father of Diogenes belonged to a different tribe; see line 48, which mentions the <term>Sosicosmian also called Althaean</term> <note>original: "Σωσικόσμιος ὁ καὶ ᾿Αλθαιεύς"</note>. Since the Phylaxithalassian was in all probability an Alexandrian tribe (as noted by Kenyon in *Archiv*, II. p. 78), it is most likely that the Sosicosmian was also an Alexandrian tribe.

7. <term>unsold property of the administration</term> <note>original: "ἀπράτων τῆς διοικήσεως"</note>: the present passage serves to explain a document in the Berlin collection (B. G. U. 18) which caused the scholar Wilcken some difficulty. The <term>assets among the unsold property</term> <note>original: "ἐν ἀπράτοις ὑπάρχοντα"</note> mentioned there were undoubtedly, as they are here, confiscated land and houses. The commission appointed by the "basilico-grammateus" <note>A royal scribe or chief administrative official.</note> was limited to the <term>appraisal</term> <note>original: "συντιμήσασθαι"</note> of this particular kind of property and does not refer to a general valuation of all private property. The <term>appraisal</term> <note>original: "συντίμησις"</note> was a kind of reserve price serving as a basis for higher offers; note the distinction drawn in document **500**, lines 13-14, between the regular rent of <term>public land</term> <note>original: "δημοσία γῆ"</note> and the <term>increase</term> <note>original: "ἐπίθεμα"</note> or surcharge.

11. The traces of the first word would fit the term for a <term>chief farmer</term> <note>original: "ἀρχυγεωργοῦ"</note>; compare document **477**, line 4. However, we hesitate to introduce that rare and curious title here, especially as the term <term>fourth</term> <note>original: "τεταρτ["</note> is quite obscure.

12. For <term>incidental charges</term> <note>original: "ἑπομένων"</note> in connection with the purchase of confiscated property, compare the Amherst Papyri, document 97.

14. We previously explained the <term>incidental charges</term> <note>original: "ἑπόμενα"</note> there as referring to the <term>annual revenue</term> <note>original: "πρόσοδος"</note> or yearly payment to the State mentioned in the British Museum Papyri. However, it would also be possible to refer these charges to the <term>extra payments</term> <note>original: "προσδιαγραφόμενα"</note> and <term>interest</term> <note>original: "τόκοι"</note> which are added here in lines 14 and following to the original 600 drachmae of the <term>appraisal</term> <note>original: "συντίμησις"</note>. The extra payments here amount to 6 1/4 percent on the 600 drachmae.

16. <term>interest</term> <note>original: "τόκου"</note>: though Diogenes bought the property in the month of Hadrianus (also called Choiak) in the 22nd year, he seems not to have paid the purchase price until towards the middle of the 23rd year. This explains the necessity for interest.

37. <term>one who has contracted for the tax-farm of the . . . bank</term> <note>original: "ἀσχολουμένου ὠνὴν τῆς . . . τραπέζης"</note>: this passage, which clearly indicates that the bank at the Serapeum <note>Serapeum: A temple dedicated to the god Serapis, which often housed administrative offices or archives.</note> was farmed out by the government, throws a new light upon the relationship between the State and banks in Roman Egypt. From the *Revenue Laws* it was known that under the Ptolemaic kings, banks other than the <term>royal banks</term> <note>original: "βασιλικαὶ τράπεζαι"</note> were farmed out by the government. But in the absence of evidence from the Roman period, it was previously supposed that private banks were entirely independent. It is now clear that for this bank at least, the privilege of managing it had to be purchased from the state.

<summary>This page concludes a receipt for the sale of confiscated property and provides detailed scholarly notes on the administrative and banking systems of Roman Egypt. It highlights how the state auctioned off seized assets and managed local banks through a system of government contracts or tax-farming.</summary>

# 514. RECEIPTS

...be bought from the government; and it is noticeable that in document **91**, lines 8 and following, written four years later than **513**, overseers <note>original: "ἐπιτηρηταί" (epitēretētai)</note> of the bank at the Serapeum <note>Serapeum: A temple dedicated to the syncretic god Serapis; these temples often housed public administrative offices and banks.</note> are mentioned, and the Epimachus who issues the promise <note>original: "ὑπόσχεσις" (hypothesis)</note> (**91**, line 11) is probably identical with the Epimachus mentioned here. Since overseers are commonly found in connection with tax-farming contracts <note>original: "ὠναί" (ōnai)</note> (as noted in the previous volume), the two papyri point to the same conclusion, and raise the problem of how far the banks which are simply called by the name of an individual were truly private. The bank at the Serapeum is mentioned in previous reigns (compare **98**, line 8 and **264**, line 7) under the names of different persons, and more probably they were either the officials <note>original: "ἀσχολούμενοι" (ascholoumenoi)</note> or the overseers of it rather than the owners. If this be granted, the persons who elsewhere give their names to banks may well be to a large extent, if not wholly, in the same position, and the condition of the banking business in the Roman period would not differ very much from that in the Ptolemaic <note>Ptolemaic: The period of Greek rule in Egypt (305–30 BC) before the Roman conquest.</note>. One change however can be traced; the public bank <note>original: "δημοσία τράπεζα" (dēmosia trapeza)</note> plays a less important role in Roman times than the royal bank <note>original: "βασιλικὴ τράπεζα" (basilikē trapeza)</note> had done previously, for most private transactions were in the Roman period conducted through the private banks <note>original: "ἰδιωτικαὶ τράπεζαι" (idiōtikai trapezai)</note> (compare document **505**), whereas under the Ptolemies the existence of banks other than royal ones is only known from the Revenue Papyrus. A tax called "banking fee" <note>original: "τραπ(εζιτικόν ?)" (trapezitikon)</note> occurs in document **574**, being perhaps a charge for the maintenance of the official banks.

### 516. ORDER FOR PAYMENT IN KIND.

->18.3 x 9.1 cm. A. D. 160.<-

Authorization addressed to the grain collectors <note>original: "sitologi"</note> by Dionysius, a victor in the games and late municipal director <note>original: "exegetes" — a high-ranking magistrate in Egyptian cities</note>, for the payment to Apion of a quantity of wheat. **619-82** are a series of similar notices to the grain collectors, another specimen of which is **88**. These <term>delivery orders</term> <note>original: "διαστολικά" (diastolika)</note> appear to be, so far, peculiar to Oxyrhynchus; and clearly indicate that the grain collectors, besides receiving dues to the government, undertook the storage of grain for private individuals, the public granaries thus presenting the closest analogy to the public banks. The correlatives of these orders on the grain collectors are found in the receipts issued by them stating that a certain payment had been made, e.g **517-8**. Those two documents are clearly concerned with private transactions, notwithstanding the opening formula <term>measured into the public treasury</term> <note>original: "μεμέτρη(νται) εἰς τὸ δημόσιον" (memetrēntai eis to dēmosion)</note>; and they show that caution must be exercised in the explanation of other grain collector receipts from the Fayûm and elsewhere, which need not refer to payments to the government of rent or taxes in the absence of an express statement to that effect. Cf. also **501**. 18, 24, 26, and **533**. 24.

> <term>and former municipal directors of the city of the Oxyrhynchites</term> <note>original: "καὶ ἐξηγητευκότ(ων) τῆς Ὀξυρύγχων πόλεως"</note>

Measured into the public granary <note>original: "demosion"</note> from the wheat produce of the past 19th year of the Aurelii Antoninus and Commodus Caesars, the lords, through the grain collectors <note>original: "sitologoi," local officials responsible for the management of public grain stores</note> of the western toparchy <note>An administrative subdivision of an Egyptian district</note> in the district of Epi...

### (g) ACCOUNTS

### 519. ACCOUNT OF PUBLIC GAMES

->(a) 8.9 × 6 cm., (b) 11.1 × 6.6 cm. Second century.<-

Two fragments, apparently in the same hand, though the writing is a little larger in one case than in the other, from accounts of receipts and expenditure in connection with the public games at Oxyrhynchus. Fragment *(a)* gives a list of payments on Mecheir 23 <note>A month in the Egyptian calendar, roughly equivalent to late January to February</note> for a theatrical entertainment, including the high sums of 496 drachmae to an actor, and 448 drachmae to a Homeric rhapsodist <note>A professional performer who specialized in reciting the epic poetry of Homer</note>, besides payments for music and dancing. The other fragment *(b)* contains the end of a list of receipts which amounted to 500 drachmae 1 obol <note>The obol was a small unit of currency; six obols typically equaled one drachma</note> in all, the exegetes and cosmetes <note>High-ranking civic officials in charge of municipal administration and the supervision of the youth and festivals</note> contributing 95 drachmae 1 obol. There follows (lines 4–13) a list of payments in connection with a religious procession <note>original: "komasia"</note>, which amounted to 124 drachmae 96 obols, the silver and copper being, as often, added up separately, and then (lines 14–16) another list of payments to gymnastic performers.

### 520. ACCOUNT OF A SALE.

->22.4 x 17 cm. A. D. 143.<-

Report of a sale of articles from a general store <note>original: "pantopolion," a shop selling a wide variety of miscellaneous goods</note> belonging—or lately belonging—to a man called Chares. 2. The mutilated word at the end of the line is not "so-called" <note>original: "legomenou"</note>.
6. Double jars <note>original: "diplon"</note>: compare text **141.5** (from the Byzantine period), where the "double" is a measure of wine. 6. *xylouaiskion* <note>meaning a wooden tool or vessel</note> is a new compound word.
11. 25 artabae <note>An artaba is a dry measure of volume, roughly 30 to 50 liters</note> seems rather an incongruous item, but we can find no alternative reading.
13. *badillos* occurs in the Suidas <note>a massive 10th-century Greek encyclopedia</note>, but the meaning was unknown. L. Dindorf remarks (in the *Thesaurus Graecae Linguae*) <note>original Latin: "nisi potius nomen est proprium factum a badios . . . corruptum videri potest ex badimos"</note> "unless it is rather a proper name made from *badios*... it can be seen to be corrupted from *badimos*." The present passage disposes of this criticism by showing conclusively that *badillos* means a vessel or instrument of some kind, in this case made of iron, and Mr. Smyly is no doubt right in identifying it with the Latin *batillum* or *batillus*, meaning a 'shovel'; compare the mention of 'tongs' (*karkinos*) in line 14.
18. *hydren* is a shortened form of *hydreion* <note>a water-pot or vessel</note>.
22. *galakto[* is probably a compound word meaning a receptacle for milk; it recurs in line 24.

### 522. ACCOUNT OF CORN-TRANSPORT.

->30.8 x 18 cm. Second century.<-

An account, probably rendered by an official to his superior, of expenses connected with the dispatch of several boat-loads of corn by river, no doubt to Alexandria <note>Egypt was the "breadbasket" of the Roman Empire, and grain was shipped down the Nile to Alexandria before being sent to Rome</note>. The papyrus is written in a large cursive hand, resembling that of document 520.

Account of the dispatch of Triadelphus:
(Of wheat) 3,400 artabae at 21 drachmae [per hundred] makes 712 drachmae.
To the same, for 1,000 artabae at 4 drachmae [per thousand] makes 12 drachmae.
For transport of 171 artabae of wheat carried for the discharging and drying of the grain <note>original: "psygmou," the process of airing out grain to prevent rot or overheating during transport</note>,
5 at the rate of 4 drachmae per 100 artabae, makes 6 drachmae.
For the price of a jar <note>original: "keramion"</note> sent to the assistants and a soldier, 8 drachmae 1 obol.
To the elders of Ophis <note>a village in the Oxyrhynchite nome</note> for the wages of 11 laborers loading the grain, 6 drachmae 2 obols.

to the assistants and the soldier 8 drachmae 1 obol. Price of 2 more jars sent to the sailors 16 drachmae 2 obols. Price of vegetables for the same, without bread, 4 obols. 1. Triadelphus, like Horion son of Ammonius and Pausiris, was probably the owner of a <term>shipping permit</term> <note>original: "apostolon", a document authorizing the dispatch of a ship or cargo</note>. The payments in lines 2 and 14, which are at the rate of slightly more than 1 obol per artaba, seem to be the charge for transport to the vessel's destination, probably Alexandria. Why in the first case there was an extra payment (line 3) of 4 drachmae per 1000 is obscure. The calculation of the 712 and 12 drachmae is not quite accurate. The correct figures would be 714 and 13¾.
4. **forced out** <note>original: "exosei"</note>: if this word is not corrupt, it would seem to be a technical term connected with the fuller's <note>A person who treats and cleans cloth</note> trade.
6. **soldier** <note>original: "str(atiote)"</note>: for soldiers accompanying the corn-vessels as <term>guards on board</term> <note>original: "epiplooi", officials tasked with preventing the theft of state grain</note> cf. **276**. 9.
11. The figure after **of which the half** <note>original: "hon to (hemisy)"</note> has not been filled in; cf. lines 23–25.
15. **sailor's fee** <note>original: "nautik(ou)"</note>: this if correct means a payment to a <term>sailor</term> <note>original: "nautes"</note>. Perhaps **to a sailor** <note>original: "nautik(oi)", the masculine form</note> should be read. Horion 'the pilot' is probably different from the Horion in line 12.
18. **loaves of bread?** <note>original: "art(on?)"</note>: cf. **498**. 31, etc.
21. **aside from the half-artaba** <note>original: "para to (hemisy) (artabes)"</note> is very obscure. The order is in favor of constructing it closely with <term>serving</term> <note>original: "hyper(e)tount(i)"</note>, and against making it mean 'in addition to the ½ artaba received by the workman.'

### 525. LETTER.

->14.6 × 10.7 cm. Early second century.<-

7. small libation fee <note>original: "σπο[ν]δάριον"</note>: compare with **610** and **101**. 19, where in a lease 12 drachmae of libation <note>original: "σπονδῆς"</note> are an item in the rent. An additional payment of some kind is there meant, but the precise significance of the word is not clear. In **653** libation <note>original: "σπονδή"</note> is coupled with portion-tax <note>original: "ἀπόμοιρα"</note> and acreage-tax <note>original: "ἐπαρούριον"</note>, which suggests that the charge ‘for a libation’ was primarily imposed upon vine-land (compare with Revenue Laws xxxvi. 19, where the sixth part <note>original: "ἕκτη"</note>, that is, the portion-tax <note>original: "ἀπόμοιρα"</note>, is devoted for the sacrifice and the libation <note>original: "εἰ[ς] τ[ήν] θυσίαν κα[ὶ] τὴν σπ[ο]ν- δ[ήν]"</note>), though, as **101** shows, its application became extended.
10. There would perhaps be room for the <note>original: "τῆς"</note> in the lacuna <note>A gap or missing section in the manuscript</note> before Isis.

->9. Read: I am going up. 10. Read: he were going up. 12. Read: I was breaking.<- <note>The editor notes that Cyrillus made several spelling and grammatical errors in his original Greek, common for those with less formal education</note>

> ‘Greeting, Calocaerus: I, Cyrillus, address you. I was not so unfeeling as to leave you without reason; for though a man gets his interest in <term>Tubi</term> <note>The fifth month of the Egyptian calendar, roughly January to February</note> tenfold, he still does not recover his capital. I am going up with the dancer; even if he were not going I should not have broken my word. Farewell. (Addressed) Deliver to Calocaerus.’

5-8. The meaning is that no amount of interest will satisfy a man who desires the repayment of the capital sum.
9. dancer <note>original: "ὀρ]χηστῇ"</note>: compare with **519.** (*a*) 6.

### 528. Letter of Serenus to Isidora.

->13.3 x 10.4 *cm.* Second or third century.<-

A highly emotional letter from Serenus to his "sister" Isidora. In the context of Roman Egypt, "sister" was often a term of endearment for a wife. The letter is written in a somewhat unrefined hand with many phonetic spellings, reflecting the spoken Greek of the era. Serenus describes his deep depression since Isidora's departure and defends himself against rumors spread by a man named Kolobos.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;before Thoeris <note>The hippopotamus goddess, the patron deity of the city of Oxyrhynchus, often invoked for protection</note> who loves you. I want
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;you to know that since you left me
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;I have been in mourning, weeping by night
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;and grieving by day. Since the 12th of Phaophi <note>An Egyptian month roughly corresponding to October</note>, since
10 I last bathed with you, I have not bathed
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;nor anointed myself <note>In the ancient world, refraining from the public baths and the use of olive oil was a standard physical sign of deep grief or extreme distress</note> until the 12th of Hathyr <note>The following Egyptian month, roughly November</note>; and you
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;sent me letters that could move a stone <note>An ancient idiom indicating that her words were incredibly powerful, heartbreaking, or persuasive</note>,

On the back <note>original: "verso"</note>

### 530. Letter of Dionysius.

->19.8 x 12.2 cm. Second century.<-

A letter from Dionysius to his mother Tetheus, chiefly concerned with money matters. The writer states that he has paid certain taxes, while some others for which his mother was being troubled had been omitted by an oversight; and he announces the dispatch of 112 <term>drachmae</term> <note>The standard silver currency of the time; for context, a laborer might earn roughly one drachma per day</note>, 108 of which were to be devoted to the redemption of his wardrobe from the pawnbroker. The letter is written in a well-formed uncial hand with occasional lapses into cursive. An example of the letter <term>Xi</term> <note>original: "Ξ"</note> formed with three distinct strokes occurs in line 13.

Dionysius to Tetheus his mother, greetings.
I have received all the letters you wrote to me. Regarding the <term>wheat</term> <note>original: "πυρῶν" (pyron)</note> 
which the <term>tax-collectors</term> <note>original: "πράκτορες" (praktores)</note> demanded from you, they are <term>acknowledged</term> <note>original: "ὁμόλογοί" (homologoi) — likely referring to a settled tax status or recognized category</note>;
<margin>5</margin>it had escaped my notice to remit something, but the <term>naubion</term> <note>original: "ναύβιον" — a tax paid by landowners in lieu of the manual labor required to maintain dikes and canals</note> 
and all the other fees I have paid in full. 
Regarding the little matter I wrote to Theon about, 
do not let it be a concern to you if it has not been finished; for in vain 
I have been waiting on Pausirion’s man for so much 
<margin>10</margin>time <unclear>...</unclear> was <unclear>...</unclear>. Receive 
from Chaeremon, the one bringing this little 
letter to you, one hundred and twelve silver drachmae, 
from which you will give to Sarapion the friend 
of Apeis, in order to <term>redeem my clothes</term> <note>original: "λυτρώσασά μου τὰ ἱμάτια" — in Roman Egypt, clothing was valuable enough to be used as collateral for loans, and pawning items was a common way to manage cash flow</note>,

### 531. LETTER OF CORNELIUS.

->21.5 x 11.7 cm. Second century.<-

A letter from a father to his son, giving him good advice, and announcing the dispatch of clothes and money.

Cornelius to Hierax, his most sweet son,
->greetings.<-

<margin>5</margin>write to me, do not pay him any mind <note>original: "μηδὲν προσποιηθῇς" (mēden prospoiēthēs) — literally "pretend nothing," here meaning to ignore or show no interest in the person's provocations</note> until I come to you for your own good, together with Westinus and the donkeys. Regarding the man about whom you write to me so often, do not pay him any mind until I come to you for your own good in company with Westinus and the donkeys. I shall send you by Anoubas both the money and the monthly supplies and the other pair of scarlet cloaks. You won me over by the dainties, and I will send you the price of these too by Anoubas; until however Anoubas arrives, you must pay for the provisions of yourself and your household out of your own money, until I send you some. For the month of <term>Tubi</term> there is for yourself what you like, for Phronimus 16 <term>drachmae</term> <note>The standard silver coin of the era</note>, for Abascantus and his companions and Myron 9 drachmae, for Secundus 12 drachmae. Send Phronimus to Asclepiades in my name, and let him obtain from him an answer to the letter which I wrote to him, and send it. Let me know what you want. Good-bye, my son. <term>Tubi</term> 15. (Addressed) To my son Hierax from his father Cornelius.

15. <term>myrtle-colored</term> <note>original: "μουρσίνων" (moursinon)</note>: "Myrtle-colored" seems to be intended, though a word meaning "mulberry-colored" occurs in other records and might be the word meant here.
18. The punctuation and meaning of this line are a little difficult. Of the known meanings of <term>exallassein</term> <note>original: "ἐξαλλάσσειν"</note>, that of "to amuse" or "to win over" seems to be the most suitable. This refers to the "dainties" or snacks mentioned earlier.
19. A grammatical note regarding the word <term>mentoi-ge</term> <note>original: "μέντοιγε" — meaning "however" or "nevertheless"</note> being used at the start of a sentence.

### DOCUMENTS

**574.** 3.9 x 13.2 cm. On the **recto** <term>recto: the front side of a papyrus sheet, where the fibers usually run horizontally</term> part of a list of payments for taxes, etc., mentioning: "for five grades, 11 **drachmae** <term>drachma: a silver coin and unit of currency</term> and 4 **obols** <term>obol: a small unit of currency; six obols made one drachma</term>; for the prison-guard tax, 1 obol and 2 **chalci** <term>chalcus: the smallest copper coin, worth 1/8 of an obol</term>; Total: 11 drachmae, 5 obols, [2 chalci]. For the assessment of brick-making <note>original Greek: plintheuomenês</note> for the 15th year, for the Pammenes Quarter, Paradise district, 1st grade; for the Hermaeum district, 1st grade; for the Square of Thoeris . . . ; for the bank tax (?) of the 15th year, in the month of Phaophi, 2 obols; . . . for the pig-tax of Sarapas, slave of Apollonius Claudius Demetrius, registered at the Square of Thoeris, 1 drachma, 4 1/2 obols; additional charges, 1 obol." For "brick-making," here connected with the term "grade" <note>original Greek: bathmou</note>, see the note on document **502**. 43. The "bank tax" <note>original Greek: trapezitikon</note> is also new, and is perhaps a tax for the maintenance of the official bank; compare document **513**. 37, note. For the prison-guard tax <note>original Greek: desmophylakia</note> compare *Fayûm Towns and Their Papyri* 53 introduction, and for the pig-tax see document **288**. Second century. 8 nearly complete lines. On the **verso** <term>verso: the back side of a papyrus sheet</term> an extract from a narrative regarding the rescue of Eurypylus by Patroclus (compare Homer's *Iliad* book 11, lines 575 and following). The text reads: "Patroclus [was sent] to find out who it was; he, having recognized [him] and being released from the battle line, meets Eurypylus, whom he leads away to his tent since he was suffering from a wound." <note>original Greek: Patroklon mathêsomenon tis eiê... epignous... sunanta... eis tên ekeinou skênên elatai</note>. The phrase "of the 8th [book?]. Achilles sent" <note>original Greek: tês ê. Achilleus epempsen</note> is to be supplied at the beginning, probably from a previous column. Second century, written in a semi-uncial hand. 5 lines.

Dated in the fourteenth year of Trajan, in the month of Phaophi (October/November, A.D. 110). Written in very corrupt Greek upon the **verso**, the **recto** containing only the title. Practically complete. 19 lines in all.

**576.** 30.1 x 8.6 cm. On the **recto** a lease dated in the tenth year of Trajan (A.D. 106–107), incomplete and much obliterated. Lease of 2 <term>arourae: about 1.3 acres</term> at the <term>Settlement: original "epoikion," a small rural hamlet</term> of Nicostratus, from the <term>allotment: original "klērou," land originally granted to Greek soldier-settlers</term> of Ptolemaeus and Philiscus, from Thrasyllous to Sarapion for four years and four <term>inundations: original "brochai," the annual flooding of the Nile</term> at an annual rent of 8 <term>artabae: a dry measure of roughly 30-40 liters</term> of wheat and 32 <term>drachmae: silver coins</term>, the land to be cultivated with any crop "except for woad and fodder" <note>original: "chōris isateōs kai ochomeneiou"; woad was used for blue dye, and ochomenion is a specific, unidentified fodder plant</note> (compare **101. 12**). Title on the back. Written in the thirteenth year of Aurelius Antoninus (A.D. 172–3). Incomplete, the end being lost. 29 lines.

**594.** 7.2 x 15.3 cm. Conclusion of a petition mentioning the <term>prefect: the Roman governor of Egypt</term> Sempronius Liberalis <note>original: "Libelarios"</note>. Dated in the twenty-second year (of Antoninus), in the month of Tybi (A.D. 159). 6 incomplete lines.

**595.** 5.3 x 11.6 cm. Beginning of a monthly <term>grain return: original "mêniaios sitikôn"</term> of receipts by the <term>grain collectors: original "sitologoi," officials who managed the state granaries</term> of the middle <term>district: original "toparchia," an administrative subdivision of the nome</term>, in the areas of Petne. Written in the nineteenth year of Antoninus (A.D. 156). 4 lines.

**596.** 6.3 x 12.9 cm. Horoscopes of two persons. The first was born in the thirteenth year of Antoninus, in the month of Mecheir, on the night between the 8th and 9th at the 5th hour; the sun, Mercury, and Venus were in Capricorn, the moon in Pisces, Saturn and Jupiter in Aries, Mars in Sagittarius, and the <term>Ascendant: original "hōroskopos," the point of the zodiac rising on the horizon</term> in Libra. The second was born in the second year of Antoninus, in the month of Phamenoth, on the night between the 30th and 1st at the 4th hour, the sun being in Pisces, the moon in Gemini, Saturn and Mercury in Aquarius, Mars and Venus in Taurus. Written about A.D. 150. Nearly complete. 17 lines.

**597.** 12.8 x 6 cm. Letter to Macer, <term>strategus</term> of the division of Heraclides in the Arsinoite <term>nome: an administrative district of Egypt</term>, from a <term>tax-collector: original "praktōr argyrikōn," an official collecting money taxes rather than grain</term> of [certain] villages, continuing: "from the... for the [account] of Phamenoth, [collected from the?] Romans and the <term>unexamined: original "anepichritōn," individuals whose status had not yet been verified for tax purposes</term>... I declare those of the <term>examinations: original "epikriseōn," status checks for tax exemptions or social standing</term>..." from 6,000 (?) drachmae... 19th year <note>original: "L," the symbol for "year"</note> likewise... 10 lines, of which the beginnings are lost.

**598.** 9.4 x 14.2 cm. Beginning of a letter, which was left unfinished, from Andronicus to his father Statilius Phanias. Second century, written in irregular uncials <note>a style of handwriting using large, rounded capital letters</note>. 5 lines.

# VII. DESCRIPTIONS OF SECOND CENTURY DOCUMENTS

**599.** 5.1 x 13.4 cm. A short letter written across the fibres:—"To Ptolemaeus the Canopite, my friend. Say nothing about the small account for the <term>strainers: original "hylistriōn," likely tools used for filtering wine or oil</term> which you owe me until you give it <note>The original Greek uses "him" but the editor notes it should likely be "it," referring to the account.</note>." <note>original Greek: "Πτολεμαίωι τῶι Κανοπίτηι τῶι φίλωι. μηδὲν λέγε περὶ οὗ ὀφείλεις μου λογαριδίου τῶν ὑλιστρίων ἕως δώσης αὐτῶι (l. αὐτό)."</note> Late first or second century. Complete. 3 lines.

**600.** 22.2 x 14.5. Cairo Papyrus 10004. On the <term>front: original "recto," the side where the papyrus fibers run horizontally</term> are parts of two columns giving measurements of land and buildings. Early second century. Incomplete and much effaced. On the <term>back: original "verso," the side where the fibers run vertically</term> is a similar document. Dated in the sixteenth year of Hadrian (A.D. 132). Complete. 18 lines, partly obliterated.

**601.** 17.7 x 11.8. Cairo Papyrus 10005. Letter addressed to the <term>agoranomi: original "agoranomois," public officials who served as notaries and market overseers</term> of Oxyrhynchus by an official (compare with documents **106-7**), stating that Harpocras had received back from the public archives the will which he had made four years before. Dated in the nineteenth year of Trajan, in the month of Epeiph (A.D. 117). Nearly complete, but broken at the top. 13 lines.

**602.** 22.8 x 13.9. Cairo Papyrus 10010. Letter from Dionysius to Heraclides, <term>scribe of the district governor: original "γραμματεὺς στρατηγοῦ" (grammateus strategou)</term> of the Oasis of the Thebaid, stating that he would procure a <term>boat: original "ploion"</term>, and inviting him to come and stay until the <term>small boat: original "ploiaridion"</term> was found. Address on the back. Second century. Complete. 11 lines.

**603.** 18.5 x 18.5 cm. Marriage contract, in which the husband (who speaks in the first person) acknowledges the receipt of the dowry and <term>personal belongings: original "parapherna," items brought into the marriage by the bride that remained her property</term>, and promises not to sell or transfer his house property without his wife's consent (compare with **496. 7-8**). In the event of a divorce, the personal belongings were to be repaid immediately and the dowry in sixty days, with an extra allowance if the wife was <term>pregnant: original "enkyos"</term> (compare with **496. 10**). Written in a semi-<term>uncial: a formal script with rounded capital letters</term> hand in the sole reign of Marcus Aurelius (A.D. 169-176). Incomplete, the earlier portions of lines being lost throughout, besides other gaps in the text. 39 lines.

**604.** 8.1 x 13.7 cm. Parts of 13 lines from the beginning of a marriage contract, written (across the fibres) <term>under Julia Augusta: original "epi Ioulias Sebastēs"</term>. Early second century.

**605.** 17 x 9.8 cm. Part of the conclusion of a marriage contract with the signatures. Late first or early second century. 21 incomplete lines.

**606.** Height 3.5 cm. Parts of 8 lines from a marriage contract, written across the fibres. On the back are parts of 2 lines of the title. Late first or early second century.

**607.** 16.8 x 9 cm. Parts of 11 lines from the conclusion of a marriage contract, another column having probably preceded. Written in a good-sized round uncial hand in the fourteenth year of an emperor, probably Trajan (i.e. A.D. 110-1).

**608.** 23 x 11.8 cm. Letter from Horion to his sister Taëoukon (?) Address on the back. Second century. Nearly complete, but much obliterated in parts. 25 lines.

### VII. DESCRIPTIONS OF SECOND CENTURY DOCUMENTS

Sarapas, leaving his property to his two sons Sarapas and Petosarapis who have to make a payment to Zoilus. The seal of one of the witnesses is of **Athena**. Early second century. 27 lines, written across the fibres.

**650.** 7.7 x 13.6 cm. Parts of 11 lines from the beginning of a will of a woman, written in a small semi-uncial hand across the fibres in the late first or early second century.

**651.** 12 x 12.2 cm. Beginnings of 13 lines of the will of Amois, dated in the eleventh year of Hadrian (A. D. 126-7). The testator leaves his property to his children, a guardian being appointed for them, if minors, until they reached <term>the age prescribed by law</term> <note>original: τῆς κατὰ νόμους ἡλικίας</note> (i. e. twenty-five years probably; cf. note on **491. 6**). Written across the fibres.

**652.** 7 x 12.5 cm. Ends of 12 lines from the will of a woman, written across the fibres. Early second century.

**653.** Height 22.7 cm. Two fragments of a long roll, the first (*a*) containing two columns of a list of payments for <term>the tax on garden land</term> <note>original: ἀπόμοι(ρα)</note>, <term>acreage tax</term> <note>original: ἐπαρού(ριον)</note>, <term>freight charges</term> <note>original: ναῦ(λον?)</note>, <term>cargo tax</term> <note>original: φο(ρτίων?)</note>, and <term>libation tax</term> <note>original: σπονδ(ή)</note> (cf. **525. 7**, note), by various persons for different years ranging from the twenty-first (of Antoninus) to the third of Marcus Aurelius and Verus (A. D. 162-3). 46 lines. Fr. (*b*) contains the ends of 16 lines of another column of the same taxing-list, and on another <term>selis: a sheet of papyrus glued to others to form a roll</term> in a different hand an account of a trial held before the praefect Lucius Volusius Maecianus. The surface of this sheet is much damaged and much of the writing of the upper portion has been obliterated. The dispute arose in connection with a mortgage upon the property of Voltimus which had been seized by the creditor, Sempronius Orestinus. The advocates Isidorus and Crepinus (likely Crispinus) appear for Orestinus and Voltimus respectively, and a previous trial before the <term>chiliarch: a military commander of a thousand men</term> Honoratus is mentioned. 

Lines 1-2: "From the minutes of Lucius Volusius Maecianus, [in the ... year] of Antoninus Caesar the lord... In line 14 "Julius Fidus, scribe" occurs. 

Lines 18 and following: "...Orestinus saying that he had used legal means, Maecianus said: '...it is usually said to you, concerning the debt it is established as the chiliarch decided... <meta>This page continues the catalog of second-century legal and administrative documents from Oxyrhynchus. While the previous page focused on wills and tax lists (649-653), this page provides a transcript of a judicial proceeding involving the Prefect of Egypt, Lucius Volusius Maecianus.</meta>

->### THE OXYRHYNCHUS PAPYRI<-

->**290**<-

"...he ordered them to be sold." Maecianus said: "You take the <term>loan</term> <note>original: δάνιον</note> and do not worry about the rest." Isidorus said: "Let him also pay back the interest." Maecianus said: "[You] enjoy the <term>profits</term> <note>original: καρποῦ — this refers to the 'usufruct' or the right to enjoy the income generated by the property</note> of these." When Isidorus said that he had not received any profit, Maecianus said: "You took possession. Therefore, whether the <term>opposing parties</term> <note>original: ἀντίδικοι</note> are present or not, they shall receive a judge who, following the decision of Honoratus, will examine the <term>Canopic property</term> <note>original: τὴν Κανωπῖτιν — likely referring to an estate or land located in the Canopic district near Alexandria</note> so that neither the creditor may profit nor the debtor, and neither may gain an advantage." When Orestinus said again that the property was not in his possession, Maecianus said: "Whether you wish it or not, you shall restore it to him. If you do not do this, you will not only be condemned but also <term>beaten</term> <note>original: δαρήσει — a rare example of a high-ranking Roman official threatening a litigant with corporal punishment during a civil dispute</note> [...] only; if any others think themselves liable for the <term>mortgages</term> <note>original: ὑποθήκας</note>, they themselves shall see to <unclear>it</unclear> <unclear>24 letters</unclear> to receive a judge." When Crepinus said, "Whomever you give [as judge]," Maecianus said: "The <term>military tribune</term> <note>original: χιλίαρχος — a high-ranking officer in the Roman army often used for administrative or judicial tasks</note> whom we deem it right to summon."

The remains of the date show that the trial took place before the end of the reign of **Antoninus Pius**, and the <term>praefecture</term> <note>The term of office of the Roman Governor of Egypt</note> of **L. Volusius Maecianus**, which has been the subject of much dispute (cf. P. Meyer, *Hermes* xxxiii. p. 262 and Stein, *Austrian Annuals* <note>original: Oesterr. Jahreshefte</note> ii, *Supplement* Col. 107 and *ibid.* iii, Col. 222), therefore began before May **A. D. 161**. The supposed praefecture of **Postumus** (*B. G. U. 388*) in **A. D. 161** may now be finally dismissed (cf. P. Meyer in *Contributions to Ancient History* <note>original: Beiträge zur alten Geschichte</note> I. p. 478), but some doubt is thrown upon the date assigned by De Ricci (*Proceedings of the Society of Biblical Archaeology* 1902 p. 65) and P. Meyer (*cited above*) to the praefecture of **T. Furius Victorinus**, since the praefecture of **L. Volusius Maecianus** may occupy the whole period between the praefectures of **M. Sempronius Liberalis** and **M. Annius Syriacus**. 29 lines.

### VIII. WEIGHTS, MEASURES, AND COINS.

#### (a) WEIGHTS AND MEASURES.

**Aroura** <note>original: "ároura"; the standard unit of land area in Egypt, roughly equivalent to 0.66 acres or 2,750 square meters.</note> 483. 25, 33; 488. 10, 17, 27; 499. 10, 17, 39, 44; 500. 14, 17, 28; 501. 13; 504. 12, 15, 23, 46; 506. 26, 55.
**Artabe** <note>original: "artábē"; a dry measure used primarily for grain, varying by region but usually around 30 to 40 liters.</note> 494. 18; 500. 13, 15, 30, 32, 34; 501. 18, 23; 516. 10, 12; 517. 2 *and often* <note>original: "et saep."</note>; 518. 5, 6; 520. 12; 521. 11; 522. 2 *and often*; 533. 19, 20, 24; 613-4; 640.
**Double-vessel** <note>original: "diploun"; a measure or container of double capacity, often used for wine.</note> 520. 6, 8, 11, 21.
**Jar** <note>original: "kerámion"; a ceramic liquid measure, frequently used for wine or oil.</note> 472. 31, 35; 522. 6, 16, 17, 27; 533. 18.

**Obol** <note>original: "obolós"; a small coin, six of which made a drachma.</note> 513. 18; 519. 10; 520. 20, 23; 522. 6 *and often*; 574; 582; 597.
**Five-obol piece** <note>original: "pentōbolon"; a coin or sum worth five obols.</note> 574.

**Talent** <note>original: "tálanton"; a very large unit of value equivalent to 6,000 drachmae.</note> 472. 36, 52; 474. 19; 494. 29; 506. 55; 577.

<column-break/>

**Four-obol piece** <note>original: "tetrōbolon"; a coin or sum worth four obols.</note> 522. 18, 30; 574.
**Three-obol interest** <note>original: "triōboleios tokos"; likely referring to a monthly interest rate of three obols per mina.</note> 506. 12, 45.
**Three-obol piece** <note>original: "triōbolon"; a coin worth half a drachma.</note> 513. 15, 17, 21, 41, 42, 55; 520. 22, 23 <margin>in the margin</margin>; 522. 11, 24.

### IX. TAXES.

**Share-tax** <note>original: "apómoira"; a tax of 1/6th or 1/10th on the produce of vineyards and orchards, originally for temples but later claimed by the state.</note> 653.
**Money taxes** <note>original: "argyriká"; taxes required to be paid in silver or copper coin rather than in kind (like grain).</note> 533. 23; 597.
**Step-tax** <note>original: "bathmós"; possibly a tax related to stairs or a tiered category of payment.</note> 574.
**Prison-guard tax** <note>original: "desmophylakía"; a fee collected from the public to pay for the maintenance of jailers.</note> 574.
**Public dues** <note>original: "dēmosia"; a general term for state taxes or official burdens.</note> 494. 4; 499. 21; 501. 31; 504. 24, 28; 506. 38.
**Species tax** <note>original: "eîdos"; often refers to taxes paid in specialized goods or specifically identified surcharges.</note> 506. 37; 577; 633.
**Acreage tax** <note>original: "eparoúrion"; a land tax calculated based on the number of arouras owned.</note> 653.
**Ten-percent surcharge** <note>original: "epidékaton"; an additional tax of one-tenth of the primary amount.</note> 609; 610.
**Appended charges** <note>original: "hepómena"; secondary fees or "extras" added to a primary tax bill.</note> 513. 12, 32.
**Poll tax** <note>original: "laographía"; a flat-rate head tax paid by male inhabitants of Egypt who were not Roman or Greek citizens.</note> 478. 23.
**Canal-work tax** <note>original: "naúbion"; a tax paid in lieu of performing manual labor on the irrigation canals.</note> 530. 6. **naubia-tax** <note>original: "naubías"; likely a genitive case form or variant spelling.</note> p. 140.
**Freight-tax on cargo (?)** <note>original: "naû(lon?) pha(rtíōn?)"; fees for shipping or transporting goods.</note> 653.
**Shipping tax** <note>original: "naulōtikē"; a tax related to the chartering of boats or freight costs.</note> 643.
**Naval dues (?)** <note>original: "nautikón"; perhaps a tax for the maintenance of the fleet.</note> 522. 15.

<column-break/>

**Brick-making tax** <note>original: "plintheuoménē"; a tax on the production of bricks.</note> 502. 44. **on the step-tax category** 574.
**Extra payments** <note>original: "prosdiagraphómena"; common surcharges added to a main tax to cover collection costs and currency exchange.</note> 513. 14, 36, 40; 574.
**Official's fee** <note>original: "prostatikón"; a fee paid for the support of a presiding official or protector.</note> 590.
**Grain taxes** <note>original: "sitiká"; taxes collected in wheat or barley rather than money.</note> 595.
**Grain rent** <note>original: "sitikòs phóros"; rent or tax on land paid in grain.</note> 514. 1.
**Libation tax** <note>original: "spondē"; a religious tax or fee, literally meaning "a drink offering."</note> 610; 653.
**Assessment** <note>original: "télesma"; a general term for a tax payment or mandated contribution.</note> 504. 23; 506. 38.
**Mortgage tax** <note>original: "télos hypothēkēs"; a registration fee paid when a property was mortgaged.</note> 511. 4.
**Bank fee (?)** <note>original: "trap(ezitikón?)"; a small charge for using the official state bank.</note> 574.
**Pig tax** <note>original: "hyikē"; a tax on the owners of swine.</note> 574.
**Tax on mortgage** <note>original: "hypothēkēs télos"; see above.</note> 511. 4.
**Rent/Tax** <note>original: "phóros"; can mean either rent for land or a tax paid to the state for a lease.</note> 499. 16, 23, 26. **grain rent** 514. 1.
**Dike-protection tax** <note>original: "ph. phragmoû"; a tax for the maintenance of fences or dikes.</note> 580.
**Guard tax** <note>original: "phýlaktron"; a fee for the local police or village guards.</note> 502. 43.

### JULIUS AFRICANUS, CESTI XVIII

**Note on the text:** The *Cesti* (meaning "Embroidered Girdles") was an encyclopedic work covering subjects from military tactics to magic. In this passage, Africanus appears to be discussing the silence of poets regarding certain events, before transitioning into a personal account of his work in establishing or visiting libraries in the Roman Empire.

# EGYPT EXPLORATION FUND.

---

### GRAECO-ROMAN BRANCH.

*THE EGYPT EXPLORATION FUND, which has conducted Archaeological research in Egypt continuously since 1883, in 1897 started a special department, called the Graeco-Roman Branch, for the discovery and publication of remains of classical antiquity and early Christianity in Egypt.*

*The Graeco-Roman Branch issues annual volumes, each of about 300 quarto pages, with facsimile plates of the more important papyri, under the editorship of Drs. B. P. GRENFELL and A. S. HUNT.*

A subscription of One Guinea to the Branch entitles subscribers to the annual volume, and also to the annual Archaeological Report. A donation of £25 constitutes life membership. Subscriptions may be sent to the Honorary Treasurers—for England, Mr. H. A. GRUEBER; and for America, Mr. F. C. FOSTER.

I. **THE STORE CITY OF PITHOM AND THE ROUTE OF THE EXODUS.** For 1883-4. By **EDOUARD NAVILLE.** Thirteen Plates and Plans. (*Fourth and Revised Edition. In preparation.*) <note>Pithom is one of the "store cities" built for the Pharaoh by the Israelites according to the Book of Exodus.</note>
